Mobility also reshapes how AI progress affects engagement: greater capability raises engagement by increasing the value of the skill trajectory a firm offers, whereas greater reliability can raise or lower it because it reduces fallback need while also changing learning opportunities. Under worker mobility, human-AI work design becomes a problem of human-capital investment, in which allocating work today shapes future skill.

AI.tldr: This paper models how firms decide worker engagement levels when deploying autonomous AI that may fail, showing engagement serves as fallback investment without worker mobility, but with mobility it becomes human-capital investment that can reverse the pattern of which workers receive engagement, and AI capability vs. reliability have different effects on engagement decisions.
AI.motivation: Firms deploying autonomous AI must decide how much work to leave to the system vs. keep workers engaged, a tradeoff affecting both current output and future human capital development.
AI.method: A parsimonious two-period model where AI may outperform workers when functioning but may fail with positive probability; the firm chooses engagement levels that lower current output for below-benchmark workers but change future skill through learning and erosion.
AI.result: Without mobility, engagement is fallback investment targeting least-skilled workers; with mobility, sorting reverses this pattern toward higher-skill workers near the AI frontier. Greater AI capability raises engagement; greater reliability has ambiguous effects.
AI.conclusion: Under worker mobility, human-AI work design becomes a human-capital investment problem where allocating work today shapes future skill trajectories.

title: TacGen: Touch Is a Necessary Dimension of Physical-World Representation -- Addressing Tactile Data Scarcity with Scalable Vision-to-Touch Alignment and Generation
summary: Touch resolves the physical-property ambiguity left by vision: exploratory contact recovers shape, texture, compliance, and material, and visuo-haptic object representations converge in ventral visual cortex. We ask whether representation learning can reproduce this grounding. TacGen mitigates the tactile-data scarcity bottleneck by combining pre-specified V+T contrastive alignment with a latent-space residual-MLP V->T generator that synthesizes tactile latents from RGB for tactile-data scaling. With matched DINOv2 backbones, splits, and probes, V+T improves matched V-only on mass (Delta R^2=+0.570), density (Delta acc=+0.067), hardness (+0.117), and uncertainty-banded force labels (Delta R^2=+0.281); all CIs exclude zero. The same representation lifts matched-capacity TACTO manipulation 0.246->0.979 while V-only capacity scaling accounts for only 4.5% of the gap, preserving 95.5%. The generator reaches cross-seed +0.589, with real tactile +0.585 inside the seed interval; the architecture comparison shows a 13pp downstream gap between reconstruction quality and representation utility. Across five-seed SSVTP/TVL reproductions, YCB-Sight transfer, three-backbone checks, permutation/random-feature controls, hash-verified manifests, and measured-force validation checks, the evidence supports the claim that touch supplies a necessary physical evidence channel for representations of contact-dependent properties.

AI.tldr: TacGen uses visuo-haptic contrastive learning and a V→T latent generator to scale tactile data, showing that touch provides necessary physical evidence for representing contact-dependent properties, with significant improvements over vision-only models across multiple benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Vision alone leaves ambiguity in physical properties (shape, texture, compliance, material); the authors ask whether representation learning can reproduce the grounding that touch provides by resolving these ambiguities, and seek to overcome the scarcity of tactile data.
AI.method: TacGen combines pre-specified V+T contrastive alignment with a latent-space residual-MLP visual-to-tactile (V→T) generator that synthesizes tactile latents from RGB images, enabling tactile-data scaling. They use matched DINOv2 backbones, splits, and probes for evaluation.
AI.result: V+T improves over V-only on mass (ΔR²=+0.570), density (Δacc=+0.067), hardness (+0.117), and force labels (ΔR²=+0.281) with CIs excluding zero. TACTO manipulation rises from 0.246→0.979 with V-only capacity scaling accounting for only 4.5% of the gap. The generator achieves +0.589 cross-seed vs +0.585 with real tactile.
AI.conclusion: Across extensive controls and reproductions, evidence supports that touch supplies a necessary physical evidence channel for representations of contact-dependent properties that vision alone cannot capture.

title: Characterizing Large Language Model Agentic Workflows: A Study on N8n Ecosystem
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are rapidly being adopted in low-code and no-code automation platforms, where non-expert users design workflows that combine natural language understanding with external services and APIs. LLM agents are LLM systems that use LLMs as a core "brain" to reason, plan, and autonomously execute complex, multi-step tasks. In this paper, we present the first large-scale empirical study of LLM agentic workflows in low-code automation platforms. We analyze more than 6,000 publicly available n8n workflows and examine four aspects of their design: task distribution, structural and tool use patterns, reliability mechanisms, and autonomy levels. Our analysis shows that LLM workflows are not merely prompt response pipelines. Instead, LLMs are commonly embedded within broader automation structures involving control logic, external tools, communication services, storage systems, and human review points. We further find that while many workflows include lightweight post-processing or routing logic after LLM execution, explicit reliability mechanisms such as structured fallback paths, repair loops, failure-specific alerts, and human approval gates remain relatively uncommon. These results reveal a gap between the increasing deployment of LLM agents in practical automation ecosystems and the limited engineering support for reliability, safety, and governance. Overall, our study provides ten empirical findings and five research takeaways for researchers, platform developers, and practitioners seeking to understand and improve real-world LLM agentic workflows.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first large-scale empirical study of LLM agentic workflows in low-code automation platforms, analyzing over 6,000 n8n workflows to examine task distribution, structural patterns, reliability mechanisms, and autonomy levels. The study finds that LLMs are embedded in broader automation structures with control logic, tools, and human review, but reliability mechanisms remain uncommon, highlighting a gap between deployment and engineering support for safety and governance.
AI.motivation: LLMs are rapidly being adopted in low-code/no-code automation platforms by non-expert users, yet there is no large-scale empirical understanding of how LLM agentic workflows are actually designed, structured, and governed in practice. The paper aims to fill this gap.
AI.method: The authors conducted a large-scale empirical analysis of over 6,000 publicly available n8n workflows, examining four aspects: (1) task distribution, (2) structural and tool use patterns, (3) reliability mechanisms, and (4) autonomy levels.
AI.result: LLM workflows are not just prompt-response pipelines; LLMs are commonly embedded within broader automation structures involving control logic, external tools, communication services, storage systems, and human review points. However, explicit reliability mechanisms (structured fallbacks, repair loops, failure alerts, human approval gates) remain relatively uncommon.
AI.conclusion: There is a gap between the increasing deployment of LLM agents in practical automation ecosystems and the limited engineering support for reliability, safety, and governance. The study provides ten empirical findings and five takeaways for researchers, platform developers, and practitioners.

title: Empowering a Single-Frequency GNSS Receiver to Achieve High-Precision Positioning with Relative Observations
summary: Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) navigation is widely used to provide absolute, outdoor positioning in field robotics. Advances in Real-Time Kinematic (RTK) technology can achieve centimeter-level accuracy, facilitating autonomous navigation tasks. However, the cost and extra infrastructure used for RTK still hinder the application and more cost-effective solutions are desired. In this letter, we present a novel tightly-coupled state estimation framework that achieves high-precision localization by using low-cost, mass-market single-frequency GNSS receivers with any relative motion sensors (e.g., wheel encoder, camera, LiDAR). We propose a sliding-window factor graph that integrates generic relative motion with global epoch-to-anchor constraints derived from continuous carrier phase tracking. To eliminate the reliance on physical base stations, we introduce a virtual anchor mechanism: upon the initial observation of a satellite, its state is locked as a virtual reference to establish global epoch-to-anchor constraints. By substituting multi-frequency hardware redundancy with single-frequency multi-modal kinematic priors and a robust cycle-slip recovery technique, our approach ensures carrier-phase integrity on cheap receivers. Extensive real-world experiments on heterogeneous low-cost sensor suites validate that our method improves the accuracy of a single-frequency receiver from several meters to decimeter-level precision across diverse environments, providing an accurate, cost-effective and reliable alternative for autonomous navigation.

AI.tldr: A tightly-coupled state estimation framework using low-cost single-frequency GNSS receivers and relative motion sensors achieves decimeter-level localization accuracy without base stations, via a sliding-window factor graph with virtual anchor mechanism and robust cycle-slip recovery.
AI.motivation: RTK-GNSS provides centimeter-level accuracy but requires expensive multi-frequency receivers and physical base station infrastructure. The authors aim to achieve comparable precision using low-cost, mass-market single-frequency receivers without external infrastructure.
AI.method: A sliding-window factor graph tightly couples generic relative motion sensors (wheel encoder, camera, LiDAR) with global epoch-to-anchor constraints from continuous carrier phase tracking. A virtual anchor mechanism locks satellite states upon first observation to eliminate physical base stations. Single-frequency kinematic priors and robust cycle-slip recovery maintain carrier-phase integrity.
AI.result: Extensive real-world experiments with heterogeneous low-cost sensor suites demonstrate improvement from several meters (standalone single-frequency GNSS) to decimeter-level precision across diverse environments.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework offers an accurate, cost-effective, and reliable alternative to RTK-GNSS for autonomous navigation, enabling high-precision localization without expensive multi-frequency hardware or external infrastructure.

title: HiComm: Hierarchical Communication for Multi-agent Reinforcement Learning
summary: Cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) often relies on communication to mitigate partial observability, yet most existing protocols treat messages as flat dense vectors detached from the structure of the observations they summarize. This design overlooks an important source of inductive bias in many cooperative environments, where observations naturally follow a hierarchy such as groups and entities. We propose \textsc{HiComm}, a plug-in communication module that grounds messages in the sender's hierarchical observation. \textsc{HiComm} is receiver-driven: the receiver issues a query, and the hierarchy is resolved through a three-stage decoding process that first selects a group, then a sender, and then an entity within that group, returning the corresponding feature slice as the message. This converts communication from unstructured vector transmission into structured information retrieval over the sender's observation hierarchy. We instantiate this mechanism with Straight-Through Gumbel-Softmax for differentiable discrete selection and a lightweight shared projection design that attaches to standard MARL pipelines. Experiments across cooperative MARL tasks with different observation structures and coordination demands show that \textsc{HiComm} matches or outperforms representative learned communication baselines while reducing communication volume by up to $23\times$ per receiver per episode.

AI.tldr: HiComm is a plug-in communication module for cooperative MARL that replaces flat dense message vectors with structured information retrieval over the sender's hierarchical observation (group→sender→entity), reducing communication volume by up to 23× while matching or outperforming baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing MARL communication protocols treat messages as flat dense vectors detached from observation structure, overlooking the natural hierarchical inductive bias (groups and entities) present in many cooperative environments.
AI.method: HiComm uses a receiver-driven, three-stage hierarchical decoding process (select group → select sender → select entity) with Straight-Through Gumbel-Softmax for differentiable discrete selection and a lightweight shared projection design.
AI.result: Matches or outperforms representative learned communication baselines across cooperative MARL tasks while reducing communication volume by up to 23× per receiver per episode.
AI.conclusion: Grounding messages in the sender's hierarchical observation structure converts communication from unstructured vector transmission into structured information retrieval, improving efficiency without sacrificing performance.

title: Behavior Uncloning: Distilling Mode Redirection into Policy Weights without Inference-Time Steering
summary: Behavior-cloned policies often learn multiple behavior modes from demonstration datasets, including modes that are unsafe or otherwise undesired at deployment. For example, a policy trained on diverse handover demonstrations may learn to pass a knife blade-first. Standard remedies such as data curation and inference-time steering either require access to the original demonstrations for full retraining or add substantial inference-time overhead. To address this gap, we propose MoRE(Mode Redirection), which redirects policy rollouts toward desired behavior modes through a short "uncloning" step. Specifically, MoRE distills the redirection signal from a temporary mode classifier into the policy weights to steer behavior. A retain loss balances this edit by preserving desired-mode competence, allowing the standalone policy to suppress unwanted modes with zero inference-time overhead. Across eight simulated and real-world tasks, MoRE improves the average deployment success rate (SR) by 44 percentage points over the original mixed-mode policy. Among all compared adaptation and steering baselines, MoRE achieves the strongest SR and approaches the filtered-data retraining reference, while preserving task competence and inference speed. MoRE also generalizes across robot policy backbones, including Diffusion Policy and the Pi0.5 VLA, diverse task categories, and real-world deployments.

AI.tldr: MoRE (Mode Redirection) redirects behavior-cloned policies away from undesired modes by distilling a mode classifier's signal into policy weights via a short "uncloning" step, achieving strong deployment success rates with zero inference-time overhead across simulated and real-world tasks.
AI.motivation: Behavior-cloned policies learn multiple behavior modes from demonstrations, including unsafe ones (e.g., passing a knife blade-first). Existing solutions require full retraining with curated data or add inference-time overhead, lacking a lightweight method to suppress undesired modes without sacrificing efficiency.
AI.method: MoRE performs a short "uncloning" step that distills redirection signals from a temporary mode classifier into policy weights, combined with a retain loss to preserve desired-mode competence. This produces a standalone policy that suppresses unwanted modes without inference-time overhead.
AI.result: Across eight simulated and real-world tasks, MoRE improves average deployment success rate by 44 percentage points over the original mixed-mode policy, outperforms all compared adaptation and steering baselines, and approaches the filtered-data retraining reference while preserving inference speed.
AI.conclusion: MoRE generalizes across robot policy backbones (Diffusion Policy, Pi0.5 VLA), diverse task categories, and real-world deployments, offering an effective zero-overhead solution for mode redirection in behavior-cloned policies.

title: Flow Reasoning Models: Scaling Reasoning Through Iterative Self-Refinement
summary: Discrete flow models have recently shown promising performance on few-step text generation; however, when naively applied to structured reasoning tasks such as Sudoku and Zebra puzzles, they converge confidently to incorrect answers (solving only $\sim$36% of Sudoku puzzles). We introduce Flow Reasoning Models (FRMs), a training and test-time-scaling framework for structured reasoning with flow models. We make the observation that, despite their poor solve rate, flow models can act as their own verifiers. A correct answer is a stable fixed point of the denoising dynamics, returning to itself when re-noised and re-solved. This enables a test-time-scaling paradigm: propose many candidate solutions and keep those that are dynamically stable, which alone reaches high solve rates on Sudoku-Shah (~$100\%$) and Zebra ($95.9\%$). This even generalizes to harder out-of-distribution puzzles like Sudoku-Extreme ($96.1\%$), without ever training on that distribution. This pure search, however, wastes a great deal of computation generating incorrect candidate solutions. We therefore design a training recipe to improve the base model's efficiency. First, we train flow models with a self-conditioning channel and close it at inference, letting them refine their own past predictions. Second, we train models to avoid their own failed generations using direct preference optimization. These changes substantially improve the base model's efficiency, letting it reach $99.2\%$ on Sudoku in just $7$ forward passes, over $8\times$ fewer than the strongest matched masked-diffusion baseline we compare needs for the same accuracy. When combined with test-time scaling, this lets flow models solve hard out-of-distribution puzzles (e.g. Sudoku-Extreme) far more efficiently.

AI.tldr: Flow Reasoning Models (FRMs) use flow models' self-verification capability (stable fixed points of denoising dynamics) for structured reasoning, achieving ~100% on Sudoku and 95.9% on Zebra puzzles via test-time scaling, and improving efficiency with self-conditioning and preference optimization to reach 99.2% on Sudoku in just 7 forward passes.
AI.motivation: Discrete flow models applied naively to structured reasoning tasks (e.g., Sudoku, Zebra puzzles) converge confidently to incorrect answers, solving only ~36% of Sudoku puzzles, motivating the need for a framework to improve their reasoning capability.
AI.method: FRMs leverage the observation that flow models can act as their own verifiers: correct answers are stable fixed points under re-noising and re-solving dynamics. Test-time scaling proposes many candidates and retains dynamically stable ones. Training improvements include: (1) self-conditioning channel (closed at inference) for refinement; (2) direct preference optimization (DPO) to avoid failed generations.
AI.result: Test-time scaling alone: ~100% on Sudoku-Shah, 95.9% on Zebra, 96.1% on out-of-distribution Sudoku-Extreme. With training: 99.2% on Sudoku in only 7 forward passes (8× fewer than strongest masked-diffusion baseline), and more efficient out-of-distribution solving.
AI.conclusion: Flow models with self-verification via dynamic stability, combined with targeted training (self-conditioning + DPO), constitute a powerful and efficient framework for structured reasoning that generalizes to harder distributions without retraining.

title: AnyBody: Free-Form Whole-Body Humanoid Control from Arbitrary Keypoint Guidance
summary: We present AnyBody, a unified whole-body humanoid controller driven by an arbitrary subset of body keypoints chosen at deploy time. Prior physics-based trackers either rely on expensive full-body motion capture and error-prone trajectory retargeting, which bottleneck scalable data collection and policy learning, or decompose upper- and lower-body control into separate hierarchical representations, sacrificing the coordinated whole-body motions that loco-manipulation requires. We close this gap by learning a single latent motion representation that any keypoint subset can address. To achieve this, we first train a privileged teacher tracker on a large unstructured motion corpus and distill it online into a deterministic encoder-decoder student whose latent space is a unit sphere. We then train a transformer keypoint encoder that admits any subset of body keypoints through masked self-attention, aligning it to the privileged latent. Additionally, we treat the frozen decoder as a motor prior and specialize downstream tasks with a lightweight residual corrector in the latent space. We demonstrate the effectiveness of AnyBody by tracking large-scale human motions from arbitrary keypoint subsets, free-form control, flexibly teleoperating, and learning downstream behaviors including locomotion, in-air writing, and obstacle-reach.

AI.tldr: AnyBody is a unified whole-body humanoid controller that uses any subset of body keypoints (chosen at deploy time) to drive physics-based tracking and control, overcoming limitations of prior methods that required full-body motion capture or hierarchical decoupling of upper/lower body.
AI.motivation: Prior physics-based trackers either require expensive full-body motion capture with error-prone retargeting (bottlenecking scalable data collection), or decompose upper/lower body control into separate hierarchies (sacrificing coordinated whole-body motion needed for loco-manipulation).
AI.method: 1) Train a privileged teacher tracker on large unstructured motion corpus. 2) Distill it online into a deterministic encoder-decoder student with a unit sphere latent space. 3) Train a transformer keypoint encoder that accepts any subset of body keypoints via masked self-attention, aligning it to the privileged latent. 4) Use the frozen decoder as a motor prior, specializing downstream tasks with a lightweight residual corrector in latent space.
AI.result: AnyBody demonstrates effective tracking of large-scale human motions from arbitrary keypoint subsets, free-form control, flexible teleoperation, and learning downstream behaviors such as locomotion, in-air writing, and obstacle-reach.
AI.conclusion: AnyBody provides a scalable and unified framework for whole-body humanoid control from any keypoint subset, enabling coordinated whole-body motions without expensive MoCap or hierarchical decomposition.

title: Pooled Leaderboards Hide System-Specific Winners: A Reporting-Protocol Audit of Offline Root-Cause Analysis Benchmarks
summary: Offline root-cause-analysis (RCA) benchmarks commonly rank methods by a single pooled top-1 accuracy across multiple subsystems, and engineers often read the pooled winner as a recommendation for their own subsystem. We audit that reading on three public RCA benchmark families -- OpenRCA, RCAEval, and PetShop -- covering 11 subsystems and 778 matched scoring units. To keep pairwise comparisons on identical cases, the main analysis retains four methods or comparators with complete coverage: BARO, a CD-1min adapter, max-$|Z|$, and per-service alert-count. All six pairwise comparisons show subsystem-level effects of both signs, every random-effects 95\% prediction interval crosses zero, and case-level interaction tests reject exchangeability in 5 of 6 pairs. Leave-one-system-out selection picks the lower-scoring method on up to 5 of 11 held-out subsystems, with regret reaching 24.8 pp on RCAEval / Sock-Shop. We release a 320-line audit module; given a matched RCA benchmark score table, it recomputes the same per-subsystem stability checks alongside pooled scores.

AI.tldr: This paper audits RCA benchmarks and finds that pooled top-1 accuracy rankings are unreliable due to significant subsystem-level variability, with prediction intervals crossing zero and substantial regret when selecting methods for held-out subsystems.
AI.motivation: Engineers often interpret pooled winner rankings from RCA benchmarks as recommendations for their own subsystem, but this assumption has not been properly tested. The authors aim to audit whether pooled accuracy generalizes across subsystems.
AI.method: The authors analyze three RCA benchmark families (OpenRCA, RCAEval, PetShop) covering 11 subsystems and 778 scoring units. They retain four methods with complete coverage (BARO, CD-1min adapter, max-|Z|, per-service alert-count), conduct pairwise comparisons, random-effects meta-analysis, case-level interaction tests, and leave-one-system-out selection to measure regret.
AI.result: All six pairwise comparisons show subsystem-level effects of both signs; every random-effects 95% prediction interval crosses zero; case-level interaction tests reject exchangeability in 5 of 6 pairs; leave-one-system-out selection picks the lower-scoring method on up to 5 of 11 held-out subsystems, with regret reaching 24.8 pp on RCAEval/Sock-Shop.
AI.conclusion: Pooled accuracy rankings are not stable across subsystems; engineers should not treat pooled winners as universally applicable recommendations. The authors release an audit module to recompute per-subsystem stability checks alongside pooled scores.

title: CORE Planner: Contextual-memory Oriented Reinforcement-learning in Unknown Environments for Robot Navigation
comment: Accepted for publication in IEEE Transactions on Industrial Electronics
summary: Autonomous navigation in unknown environments requires a robot to efficiently reach a predefined goal while exploring without prior maps. Although progress has been made in this area, most existing works still rely on traditional planning methods with hand-crafted rules, while learning-based methods often suffer from limited environmental memory and challenges in simulation-to-real (sim-to-real) transfer. To overcome these limitations, we propose a Contextual-memory Oriented Reinforcement-learning (CORE) planner for robot navigation in unknown environments. The proposed CORE planner effectively combines the core advantages of traditional and learning-based methods. Specifically, our method uses a sparse visibility graph for structured environment representation, reducing the computational overhead of dense grid maps, and employs a Transformer network to achieve a holistic environmental understanding, thereby significantly improving navigation efficiency. Moreover, we introduce a visibility graph-based graph sparsification method and a contextual memory mechanism, which alleviates local optima and enhances computational performance in large-scale scenes. Finally, our approach achieves zero-shot sim-to-real transfer after training solely on image-based environments, requiring no fine-tuning. Experimental results show that CORE Planner consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, including the traditional FAR Planner and all learning-based baselines, across representative environments, reducing travel distance by 13\% over traditional FAR Planner and by up to 48\% relative to learning-based baselines, with larger gains observed in more complex environments. In real-world scenarios, CORE successfully navigates without human intervention, showcasing zero-shot sim-to-real transfer. Code is available at https://github.com/BBD00/core_planner.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes CORE Planner, a Contextual-memory Oriented Reinforcement-learning approach for robot navigation in unknown environments that combines traditional planning with learning-based methods, using sparse visibility graphs and Transformer networks to achieve efficient navigation and zero-shot sim-to-real transfer, outperforming state-of-the-art methods by reducing travel distance by 13-48%.
AI.motivation: Existing robot navigation methods in unknown environments have limitations: traditional planning relies on hand-crafted rules, while learning-based methods suffer from limited environmental memory and challenges in sim-to-real transfer.
AI.method: CORE Planner combines (1) sparse visibility graphs for structured environment representation to reduce computational overhead, (2) Transformer network for holistic environmental understanding, (3) visibility graph-based graph sparsification, and (4) contextual memory mechanism to alleviate local optima and enhance computational performance in large-scale scenes.
AI.result: CORE Planner reduces travel distance by 13% over traditional FAR Planner and up to 48% over learning-based baselines, achieves zero-shot sim-to-real transfer without fine-tuning, and successfully navigates real-world environments without human intervention.
AI.conclusion: The proposed CORE planner effectively bridges the gap between traditional planning and learning-based navigation, achieving superior performance and zero-shot sim-to-real transfer, with larger gains observed in more complex environments.

title: Direct Causation in International Humanitarian Law and the Challenge of AI-Mediated Civilian Cyber Operations
comment: 11 pages, 1 figure, Workshop on Technical AI Governance Research ICML 2026
summary: International humanitarian law protects civilians from direct attack unless and for such time as they take direct part in hostilities, with the ICRC's 2009 Interpretive Guidance operationalising this rule through a three-criterion cumulative test. This paper argues that AI-mediated civilian cyber operations challenge the direct causation element of this test in a structurally specific way: when a civilian deploys an autonomous multi-agent cyber system of the kind recently demonstrated in offensive AI research, the "one causal step" standard fails because harm is produced by system-generated decisions made after human disengagement, and the integral-part requirement does not extend because it presupposes downstream human contributors whose conduct can be independently classified. The framework therefore defaults to treating such deployments as indirect participation, in tension with its purpose of capturing civilians who personally take part in hostilities. Beyond the doctrinal analysis, this paper identifies goal-specification granularity as the property on which the integral-part test's concreteness component implicitly turns, classifies AI-mediated operations along a five-level spectrum, and argues that existing technical AI governance instruments do not log or report this property.

AI.tldr: This paper argues that when civilians deploy autonomous multi-agent AI cyber systems, the ICRC's "direct causation" test for direct participation in hostilities fails because harm results from system decisions made after human disengagement, leading these operations to be misclassified as indirect participation, and identifies goal-specification granularity as the unlogged property determining concreteness under the integral-part test.
AI.motivation: To address a structural gap in international humanitarian law's framework for classifying civilian cyber operations involving autonomous AI systems, specifically the direct causation element of the ICRC's 2009 Interpretive Guidance.
AI.method: Doctrinal legal analysis combined with technical classification of AI-mediated operations across a five-level spectrum, and examination of existing AI governance instruments for logging capabilities.
AI.result: The "one causal step" standard fails because harm is produced by system-generated decisions after human disengagement; the integral-part requirement does not extend because it presumes downstream human contributors; these operations default to indirect participation classification; goal-specification granularity is identified as the implicit property underlying concreteness.
AI.conclusion: Existing technical AI governance instruments do not log or report goal-specification granularity, which is needed to properly classify such operations under IHL.

title: MoPe: Motion Permanence for Robust Monocular Gaussian Mapping in Dynamic Environments
summary: Robust robot autonomy depends on scene representations that remain stable enough to support localization, navigation, and downstream decision making in dynamic environments. Monocular Gaussian Splatting SLAM provides high-fidelity mapping, but current uncertainty-aware methods still treat dynamic regions largely as per-frame observations. This makes the representation effectively memoryless: when a pedestrian slows, pauses, or reappears after occlusion, the current frame may look static, allowing dynamic content to be absorbed into the map and leaving persistent ghosting artifacts. We argue that this failure reflects a representation-level mismatch. Dynamic-ness is not an instantaneous appearance property, but a temporal property defined by motion history. Building on this view, we introduce Motion Permanence: the principle that an object's dynamic identity should persist over time rather than be re-decided from each frame independently. We realize this principle in MoPe, a memory-aware uncertainty filter for monocular Gaussian mapping. MoPe propagates the historical dynamic posterior through geometry-consistent SE(3) warping and fuses it with current-frame evidence using bounded Bayesian log-odds updates. The resulting persistent posterior guides tracking, mapping, dynamic-aware Gaussian insertion, and Gaussian-level post-cleanup. On Wild-SLAM, Bonn, and TUM sequences, MoPe improves tracking robustness and reduces residual ghosting, with the strongest gains on dynamic-human scenes that most directly violate the memoryless assumption. These results show that maintaining temporal dynamic state inside the scene representation is a practical step toward more reliable representation-centric autonomy in changing real-world environments.

AI.tldr: MoPe introduces Motion Permanence, a memory-aware uncertainty filter for monocular Gaussian Splatting SLAM that propagates historical dynamic posteriors through SE(3) warping and Bayesian fusion, significantly reducing ghosting artifacts in dynamic scenes.
AI.motivation: Current uncertainty-aware monocular Gaussian Splatting SLAM methods treat dynamic regions as per-frame observations, making them memoryless. This causes persistent ghosting artifacts when dynamic objects slow down, pause, or reappear after occlusion, as the representation re-decides dynamic identity independently per frame.
AI.method: MoPe implements Motion Permanence by: (1) propagating historical dynamic posteriors via geometry-consistent SE(3) warping, (2) fusing with current-frame evidence using bounded Bayesian log-odds updates, and (3) using the resulting persistent posterior to guide tracking, mapping, dynamic-aware Gaussian insertion, and Gaussian-level post-cleanup.
AI.result: On Wild-SLAM, Bonn, and TUM sequences, MoPe improves tracking robustness and reduces residual ghosting, with strongest gains on dynamic-human scenes that violate the memoryless assumption.
AI.conclusion: Maintaining temporal dynamic state inside the scene representation is a practical step toward more reliable representation-centric autonomy in changing real-world environments.

title: Selective Memory Retention for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
comment: Accepted at the International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML) 2026
summary: When does retention matter for memory-augmented LLM agents? We study this with TraceRetain, a lightweight framework for bounded external memory in frozen LLM agents that scores entries by interpretable features (success, age, access frequency, redundancy, specificity, similarity, downstream utility) and evicts the lowest-scoring ones at capacity. On clean ALFWorld with gpt-5-mini, external memory robustly improves over no memory across two seeds, but differences among bounded retention policies fall within Wilson 95% CIs: clean ALFWorld at T=100 to T=200 does not naturally exhibit the memory pollution retention is designed to address. Under a controlled noisy-write stress (75% synthetic distractors), unbounded memory and FIFO-K50 degrade on Precision@5 (20.2% to 12.4% and 15.8% to 3.8%) while TraceRetain-CEM is essentially unchanged (16.9% to 16.6%) and preserves 97/100 task success. The mechanism: unbounded memory has the highest mean similarity (0.87) but lowest precision, indicating failed distractors close to the query in embedding space. Held-out in-distribution evaluation shows memory-augmented policies solving 47 to 49 of 50 tasks vs. 39/50 for no memory. Bounded retention buys memory and step efficiency on saturated clean benchmarks at no task-success cost, and only differentiates from cache heuristics when streams contain noise.

AI.tldr: TraceRetain is a lightweight bounded external memory framework for frozen LLM agents that scores entries by interpretable features and evicts low-scoring ones. On clean ALFWorld, external memory helps but retention policies don't differ significantly; under noisy-write stress (75% distractors), unbounded memory and FIFO degrade while TraceRetain-CEM stays robust, preserving 97/100 task success.
AI.motivation: To study when retention truly matters for memory-augmented LLM agents, particularly whether bounded retention policies provide benefits over simpler cache heuristics, and to understand the conditions under which memory pollution occurs.
AI.method: TraceRetain framework: bounded external memory for frozen LLM agents scoring entries by interpretable features (success, age, access frequency, redundancy, specificity, similarity, downstream utility) and evicting lowest-scoring ones at capacity. Evaluated on ALFWorld with clean and noisy-write (75% synthetic distractors) settings.
AI.result: Clean ALFWorld: external memory improves over no memory but bounded retention policies don't differ significantly (within Wilson 95% CIs). Noisy-write stress: unbounded memory Precision@5 drops 20.2%→12.4%, FIFO-K50 drops 15.8%→3.8%, TraceRetain-CEM stays 16.9%→16.6% preserving 97/100 task success. Unbounded memory has highest mean similarity (0.87) but lowest precision due to failed distractors near query in embedding space. Held-out evaluation: memory-augmented policies solve 47-49/50 tasks vs 39/50 for no memory.
AI.conclusion: Bounded retention buys memory and step efficiency on saturated clean benchmarks at no task-success cost, and only differentiates from cache heuristics when streams contain noise. Unbounded memory is vulnerable to memory pollution from distractor entries that are close in embedding space.

title: PL-LIT: A LiDAR-Inertial-Thermal SLAM Using Point-Line Features and Thermographic Mapping
comment: 8 pages,International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems 2026 (IROS)
summary: Thermal imaging is resilient to adverse conditions, such as intense illumination, low-light operation, and fog, and can therefore mitigate odometry degradation when visible-spectrum imagery becomes unreliable. Nevertheless, most thermal cameras employ automatic gain control (AGC), and thermal images often present low global contrast despite containing informative edge structures. These characteristics undermine brightness constancy and cause conventional optical flow tracking-based odometry pipelines that fundamentally rely on the brightness constancy assumption across consecutive frames. To address these issues, we propose a general LiDAR-Inertial-Thermal SLAM system that accommodates both visible-light and thermal cameras. PL-LIT combines an online photometric calibration module with a deep neural network for point-line feature extraction, enabling more stable and repeatable thermal tracking. For state estimation, we design a tightly coupled LiDAR-Inertial-Thermal formulation within an Error-State Iterated Kalman Filter (ESIKF). We further introduce a line-feature constraint scheme ensuring the reliability of geometric constraints across varying thermal appearances. In addition, PL-LIT builds a probabilistic thermal-intensity voxel map, which supports real-time thermal anomaly detection. Extensive experiments demonstrate that PL-LIT exhibits generality and robustness in visible-light environments, achieves state-of-the-art performance on long-range thermal infrared datasets, and provides practical safety inspection functionality based on thermographic mapping.

AI.tldr: PL-LIT is a LiDAR-Inertial-Thermal SLAM system that combines online photometric calibration, deep neural network point-line feature extraction, and an ESIKF-based tightly coupled formulation to achieve robust odometry under adverse visual conditions, while also enabling real-time thermal anomaly detection via probabilistic thermographic mapping.
AI.motivation: Thermal cameras are resilient to adverse conditions (low light, fog, intense illumination) but suffer from automatic gain control (AGC) causing low global contrast and violating brightness constancy, which degrades conventional optical flow tracking and odometry pipelines that rely on this assumption.
AI.method: PL-LIT integrates (1) online photometric calibration to compensate for AGC effects, (2) a deep neural network for stable point-line feature extraction, (3) a tightly coupled LiDAR-Inertial-Thermal formulation within an Error-State Iterated Kalman Filter (ESIKF), (4) a line-feature constraint scheme for robust geometric constraints across varying thermal appearances, and (5) a probabilistic thermal-intensity voxel map for real-time thermal anomaly detection.
AI.result: The system demonstrates generality and robustness in visible-light environments, achieves state-of-the-art performance on long-range thermal infrared datasets, and provides practical safety inspection functionality via thermographic mapping.
AI.conclusion: PL-LIT effectively addresses the challenges of thermal imaging for SLAM by combining photometric calibration, learned features, and multi-sensor fusion, enabling reliable operation in adverse conditions and offering additional safety inspection capabilities.

title: Measuring Graph-to-Graph Semantic Similarity in Knowledge Graphs: An Empirical Evaluation of Knowledge Graph Embeddings
comment: 9 pages, 2 figures, 6 tables. Accepted as a poster at The 2nd Frontiers in Graph Machine Learning for the Large Model Era (GMLLM'26) Workshop, co-located with KDD 2026
summary: A Knowledge Graph (KG) represents facts as structured triples and is widely used to organize relational knowledge across diverse domains. Just as textual information ranges from words and sentences to complete documents, KG information can be interpreted at multiple levels, from entities, relations, and triples to subgraphs and entire KGs. However, existing KG embedding methods mainly focus on entities, relations, and triples, leaving graph-level semantics largely unaddressed. Conventional graph-level methods, which typically compare graphs based on structural patterns, are also insufficient because structural similarity alone cannot guarantee semantic similarity between KGs. To evaluate how well different methods capture such graph-level semantic information, we study graph-to-graph semantic similarity, which determines whether a pair of KGs represents semantically corresponding underlying information. To obtain reliable ground-truth correspondences, we construct a semantic matching dataset by modifying text documents, extracting KGs from both original and modified documents, and transferring their known correspondences to KG pairs. We compare text-based, structure-based, and KG embedding-based approaches on each dataset. For the KG embedding-based approach, we introduce two scoring functions: \textit{EmbPairSim}, which uses maximal pairwise entity similarity, and \textit{AvgEmbSim}, which uses a frequency-weighted centroid. Experiments on WikiText-2 and CC-News show that \textit{EmbPairSim} achieves up to 5.3 pp higher MRR than Sentence-BERT while using substantially fewer parameters. These results suggest that KGE representations can serve as compact and effective signals for graph-to-graph semantic similarity in KGs. Our code is available at https://github.com/SeungRyeolBaek/KG-to-KG-Semantic-Similarity.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses graph-to-graph semantic similarity in Knowledge Graphs (KGs) by constructing a semantic matching dataset from text document modifications and introducing two KG embedding-based scoring functions (EmbPairSim and AvgEmbSim), with EmbPairSim achieving up to 5.3 pp higher MRR than Sentence-BERT using fewer parameters.
AI.motivation: Existing KG embedding methods focus on entity, relation, and triple levels, neglecting graph-level semantics. Meanwhile, conventional graph-level methods rely on structural similarity, which is insufficient because structural similarity does not guarantee semantic similarity between KGs.
AI.method: The authors construct a semantic matching dataset by modifying text documents, extracting KGs from original and modified documents, and transferring known correspondences to KG pairs. They compare text-based, structure-based, and KG embedding-based approaches. For KG embeddings, they propose EmbPairSim (maximal pairwise entity similarity) and AvgEmbSim (frequency-weighted centroid).
AI.result: On WikiText-2 and CC-News, EmbPairSim achieves up to 5.3 pp higher MRR than Sentence-BERT while using substantially fewer parameters.
AI.conclusion: KGE representations can serve as compact and effective signals for graph-to-graph semantic similarity in KGs.

title: LAMP: Long-Horizon Adaptive Manipulation Planning for Multi-Robot Collaboration in Cluttered Space
summary: Multi-robot manipulation requires jointly reasoning about contact formations, robot motions under coupled dynamics, and collision avoidance. Systematically searching over this large space is difficult and becomes increasingly intractable as the number of robots grows, the task horizon lengthens, or the scene becomes more cluttered. Existing approaches therefore either learn to solve the problem end-to-end via reinforcement learning or restrict planning to a simpler surrogate problem, such as planning object motions while learning short-horizon contact primitives. However, neither paradigm scales to the problem instances we target: longhorizon multi-robot manipulation in extremely dense environments. In this paper, we propose a Long-horizon Adaptive Manipulation Planning (LAMP) framework with two planners that enable tractable search over the full coupled space by combining a learned generative manipulation model: a LAMPA* planner that systematically searches over the coupled objectrobot space, and LAMP-Lazy: a lazy planner that enables real-time replanning through deferred evaluation. Experiments in challenging simulated environments demonstrate that our approach solves complex long-horizon tasks in highly cluttered environments that prior methods cannot handle.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes LAMP, a framework combining two planners (LAMPA* and LAMP-Lazy) with a learned generative manipulation model for long-horizon multi-robot manipulation in extremely dense environments, outperforming prior methods that don't scale to such settings.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches (end-to-end RL or restricted planning with short-horizon primitives) fail to scale to long-horizon multi-robot manipulation in extremely dense, cluttered environments due to the intractability of searching the coupled space of contact formations, robot motions, and collision avoidance.
AI.method: LAMP framework with two planners: LAMPA* systematically searches the coupled object-robot space, and LAMP-Lazy enables real-time replanning via deferred evaluation, both leveraging a learned generative manipulation model.
AI.result: In challenging simulated environments, LAMP solves complex long-horizon tasks in highly cluttered settings that prior methods cannot handle.
AI.conclusion: The LAMP framework enables tractable search over the full coupled manipulation space, achieving scalability to long-horizon multi-robot tasks in dense environments where existing approaches fail.

title: Evidence-Informed LLM Beliefs for Continual Scientific Discovery
summary: Open-ended scientific discovery with large language models (LLMs) increasingly operates as a long-horizon loop of hypothesis search and verification, where a reward signal guides which hypotheses to test next. A notable recent example is AutoDiscovery, which uses "Bayesian surprise" - the belief shift an LLM undergoes after observing evidence for a hypothesis - as both a discovery metric and a reward for search. We first observe that AutoDiscovery treats surprisal as a static quantity, while surprisal in human reasoning is non-stationary - it is defined relative to beliefs that evolve with experience, a prerequisite for continual scientific discovery. We address this mismatch with evidence-informed LLM beliefs: priors updated with evidence from previous hypotheses to compute non-stationary surprisal for new hypotheses. We compare in-context belief-updating mechanisms and find that embedding-based retrieval-augmented generation over prior discoveries best anticipates eventual posteriors, identifying 37.5% of static surprisals as spurious. We then modify search to avoid these spurious rewards and prioritize hypotheses that remain surprising under non-stationary beliefs. Concretely, we introduce two complementary changes to the original search procedure: belief-update filtering and diversity maximization. Across five discovery domains, our method increases accumulated non-stationary surprisal by 30.62% on average compared to the original search procedure, demonstrating that continual scientific discovery with LLMs requires not only better belief measurement but also search procedures that avoid redundancy and encourage diversity.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies a key limitation in LLM-driven scientific discovery: static Bayesian surprise used as a reward signal fails to account for evolving beliefs. The authors propose evidence-informed LLM beliefs with non-stationary surprisal, using retrieval-augmented generation for belief updating, and introduce belief-update filtering and diversity maximization to improve search. Their method increases accumulated non-stationary surprisal by 30.62% across five domains.
AI.motivation: Current LLM-based scientific discovery systems like AutoDiscovery use static Bayesian surprise as a reward signal, ignoring that surprise in human reasoning is non-stationary—it depends on beliefs that evolve with accumulated evidence. This mismatch limits continual scientific discovery.
AI.method: The authors propose (1) evidence-informed LLM beliefs where priors are updated with evidence from previous hypotheses using in-context belief-updating mechanisms, finding embedding-based RAG over prior discoveries works best; (2) belief-update filtering to remove spurious static surprisals (37.5% identified); (3) diversity maximization to prioritize hypotheses that remain surprising under non-stationary beliefs.
AI.result: The method increases accumulated non-stationary surprisal by 30.62% on average across five discovery domains compared to the original AutoDiscovery search procedure.
AI.conclusion: Continual scientific discovery with LLMs requires not only better belief measurement (non-stationary surprisal) but also search procedures that avoid redundancy and encourage diversity.

title: SPACE: Swarm Pheromone Fields for Adaptive Collision-Aware Exploration
summary: Massive robot swarms can explore unknown environments quickly, but adding robots eventually stops helping. Doorways and dense traffic create congestion, increasing inter-robot contacts and reducing the value of each additional robot. We study this safety-efficiency tradeoff for ground swarms of tens to hundreds of robots. We present SPACE, Swarm Pheromone Fields for Adaptive Collision-Aware Exploration. Inspired by ant foraging, SPACE maintains a shared environmental field with an attractive frontier pheromone, a repellent explore pheromone, and a fast robot-density field. Coordination is decentralized and mediated through this field. We evaluate SPACE on real building floorplans, namely sixteen home layouts from the HouseExpo dataset and eight campus floors from the KTH dataset, with swarms of up to two hundred and fifty-six robots. SPACE lies on the empirical Pareto frontier. It attains the lowest inter-robot contact rate at every congested swarm size, four to seventeen times fewer than a greedy nearest-frontier planner, while keeping coverage time within about two percent of that near time-optimal planner. The results indicate that, at this scale, coordination mainly improves safety rather than coverage time.

AI.tldr: SPACE uses pheromone-inspired fields for decentralized robot swarm coordination, achieving the lowest collision rates (4-17x fewer contacts) while maintaining near-optimal coverage time (~2% difference) in real floorplan environments with up to 256 robots.
AI.motivation: Massive robot swarms face diminishing returns due to congestion through doorways and dense traffic, increasing inter-robot contacts and reducing the value of additional robots. The safety-efficiency tradeoff needs to be addressed for ground swarms of tens to hundreds of robots.
AI.method: SPACE (Swarm Pheromone Fields for Adaptive Collision-Aware Exploration) maintains a shared environmental field with three components: attractive frontier pheromone, repellent explore pheromone, and a fast robot-density field. Coordination is decentralized and mediated through this field, inspired by ant foraging.
AI.result: Evaluated on 16 home layouts (HouseExpo) and 8 campus floors (KTH) with swarms up to 256 robots. SPACE achieves 4-17x fewer inter-robot contacts compared to greedy nearest-frontier planner while keeping coverage time within ~2% of that near time-optimal planner, lying on the empirical Pareto frontier.
AI.conclusion: At this scale, coordination mainly improves safety rather than coverage time, as the coordination mechanism reduces collisions without substantially sacrificing exploration speed.

title: AI Trading's Alpha Singularity: Emergent Market Reasoning through Agent-to-Agent Self-Evolution
summary: Automated alpha mining holds the scoring function fixed and varies the search algorithm over it. A search that converges against a fixed scorer overfits whatever the scorer cannot penalize, a primary cause of the out-of-sample generalization gap. We treat the scoring function as a search artifact alongside the alpha factors and study what conditions make this joint search admissible. Sealed Joint Search (SJS) is a framework: a set of structural conditions on information flow in an autonomous-discovery system that prevent joint search from collapsing into self-confirmation while keeping the evaluator sealed. Conditions cover role decomposition, typed inter-role communication, provenance-sealed reads, versioned stores, and substrate-local promotion. Agora tests SJS empirically: five LLM agent classes communicate via three channels, evolving eight skill libraries, with alpha libraries built on AlphaGen operators. Three evaluators write reports aggregated into one brief, carrying forward disagreement instead of voting. We run Agora for 100 rounds on CSI 1000 and evaluate on a 91-day 2026 holdout sealed from all LLM inputs. Agora achieves holdout Sharpe +1.87; best baseline +1.334 at favorable seed and -0.755 cross-seed mean. Pre-loading Agora's two metrics into a frozen-library ablation recovers only +0.40 of the +2.25 Sharpe gap, and adding PPO without library evolution worsens the gap. The two metrics emerge rather than being designed. Caveats: single-seed run, short-side concentrated signal, intended for long-short.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Sealed Joint Search (SJS), a framework that treats the scoring function as a search artifact alongside alpha factors to prevent overfitting in automated alpha mining. Implemented via Agora—a multi-agent LLM system with five agent classes, three communication channels, and eight skill libraries—it achieves a holdout Sharpe of +1.87 on CSI 1000, significantly outperforming baselines, with the key insight that joint search requires structural information-flow constraints to avoid self-confirmation bias.
AI.motivation: Standard automated alpha mining fixes the scoring function while varying the search algorithm, causing the search to overfit what the scorer cannot penalize, leading to poor out-of-sample generalization. The authors aim to solve this by treating the scoring function itself as a search artifact and establishing conditions that prevent this joint search from collapsing into self-confirmation.
AI.method: SJS imposes structural conditions: role decomposition, typed inter-role communication, provenance-sealed reads, versioned stores, and substrate-local promotion. Agora implements this with five LLM agent classes (Generator, Verifier, Librarian, Evaluator, Summarizer) communicating via three channels, evolving eight skill libraries. Alpha factors use AlphaGen operators. Three evaluators write separate reports aggregated into a brief carrying forward disagreement rather than voting. The system runs 100 rounds on CSI 1000, evaluated on a 91-day 2026 holdout completely sealed from LLM inputs.
AI.result: Agora achieves a holdout Sharpe of +1.87. The best baseline reaches +1.334 at a favorable seed but only -0.755 cross-seed mean. Pre-loading Agora's two metrics into a frozen-library ablation recovers only +0.40 of the +2.25 Sharpe gap. Adding PPO without library evolution worsens the gap. The two key metrics emerge rather than being explicitly designed.
AI.conclusion: Jointly searching over both the scoring function and alpha factors, under proper information-flow constraints (SJS), substantially outperforms fixed-scorer approaches. The framework prevents self-confirmation and overfitting by design. Caveats include single-seed run, short-side concentrated signal, and intended use for long-short strategies.

title: Understanding LLM Intervention Explanations in Multi-Party Human-Robot Interaction
comment: Accepted for 2026 36th IEEE International Conference on Robot and Human Interactive Communication
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly embedded in social robots to support natural group interactions, yet their role in complex multi-party settings remains underexplored. In particular, it is unclear how LLM-driven robots decide when and why to intervene in group conversations. This paper investigates the intervention explanations generated by an LLM-based orchestrator in a multi-party interaction involving three human participants and two robots. We conducted a between-subjects study with 24 groups (66 university students), comparing a homogeneous condition (two robots with the same role, i.e., a mover) and a heterogeneous condition (two robots with different roles, i.e., a mover and an opposer). At each conversational turn, the LLM orchestrator decided whether to intervene and generated a textual explanation of its decision. We performed a thematic analysis of 610 intervention explanations, identifying five recurring themes. Results show that explanations are facilitation-oriented, emphasizing agreement, participation, and interaction flow. While patterns remain stable across conditions, role differentiation emerges: the mover supports coordination, whereas the opposer drives goal-oriented interventions. These findings contribute to explainable AI by characterizing how LLM-driven systems justify intervention decisions in real-time, multi-party human-robot interaction.

AI.tldr: This paper studies how LLM-driven robots justify intervention decisions in multi-party human-robot interactions, revealing five recurring themes in explanations that emphasize facilitation, with role differentiation between a coordinator (mover) and a goal-driver (opposer).
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used in social robots for group interactions, but how LLM-driven robots decide when and why to intervene in complex multi-party settings remains underexplored.
AI.method: Between-subjects study with 24 groups (66 university students) comparing homogeneous (two movers) vs. heterogeneous (mover + opposer) robot roles; thematic analysis of 610 LLM-generated intervention explanations.
AI.result: Five recurring themes identified; explanations are facilitation-oriented (agreement, participation, interaction flow); patterns stable across conditions, but role differentiation emerges (mover supports coordination, opposer drives goal-oriented interventions).
AI.conclusion: Characterizes how LLM-driven systems justify intervention decisions in real-time multi-party HRI, contributing to explainable AI in social robotics.

title: A Cognition-Emotion-Personality Framework for Modeling Human-Like Awareness and Behavior in Emergency Evacuations
summary: Agent-based evacuation simulations are widely used to study crowd behavior during emergencies, but many models rely on assumptions such as perfect event awareness, complete exit knowledge, and fully rational decision-making. This paper presents an extended evacuation framework that integrates cognitive, emotional, social, and personality-related mechanisms into a unified model of human behavior under uncertainty. The framework incorporates a dynamic event-awareness mechanism based on a continuous Event Certainty Level, a memory-based representation of exit knowledge subject to acquisition, forgetting, and recall, a continuous fear model in which panic emerges as a high-intensity state, and an OCEAN-based personality representation. Neuroticism is explicitly integrated into the emotional model, influencing fear generation, escalation, social contagion, and recovery. Behavioral heterogeneity is further captured through individualized decision thresholds that affect responses to perceived risk. The framework is evaluated through simulation experiments examining the effects of spatial familiarity, memory robustness, decision sensitivity, emotional dynamics, and personality variation. Results show that cognitive, emotional, and personality-driven processes substantially influence evacuation dynamics, reducing evacuation efficiency and generating realistic crowd phenomena such as delays, confusion, injuries, and socially influenced behaviors. The proposed framework provides a more realistic representation of human behavior in emergency evacuations and supports systematic investigation of the interactions between cognition, emotion, personality, and crowd dynamics.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an extended evacuation framework that integrates cognitive, emotional, social, and personality (OCEAN-based) mechanisms into agent-based evacuation simulations, moving beyond traditional assumptions of perfect awareness and rationality. The model incorporates dynamic event awareness, memory-based exit knowledge, continuous fear dynamics (including panic), neuroticism-driven emotional processes, and individualized decision thresholds. Simulation experiments show these factors reduce efficiency and produce realistic crowd behaviors like delays, confusion, and social influences.
AI.motivation: Existing agent-based evacuation models rely on unrealistic assumptions (perfect event awareness, complete exit knowledge, fully rational decision-making), failing to capture the cognitive, emotional, and personality-driven processes that influence real human behavior during emergencies.
AI.method: The framework integrates (1) a dynamic event-awareness mechanism with continuous Event Certainty Level; (2) memory-based exit knowledge with acquisition, forgetting, and recall; (3) a continuous fear model where panic emerges as high-intensity state; (4) OCEAN-based personality with neuroticism integrated into fear generation, escalation, social contagion, and recovery; and (5) individualized decision thresholds for behavioral heterogeneity. Evaluated through simulation experiments examining spatial familiarity, memory robustness, decision sensitivity, emotional dynamics, and personality variation.
AI.result: Cognitive, emotional, and personality-driven processes substantially influence evacuation dynamics, reducing evacuation efficiency and generating realistic crowd phenomena including delays, confusion, injuries, and socially influenced behaviors.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework provides a more realistic representation of human behavior in emergency evacuations and supports systematic investigation of interactions between cognition, emotion, personality, and crowd dynamics.

title: MTD-Map: Single-Stage Long-Term LiDAR Map Maintenance Framework via Mixture Transition Distribution
summary: While robust map maintenance has advanced significantly, existing studies have focused on specific tasks, especially dynamic object removal or change detection. In this paper, we take a holistic view of the map maintenance problem and propose MTD-Map, a single-stage framework that handles both dynamic object removal and change detection without separate task-specific modules. MTD-Map employs an explicit representation that compactly encodes the direction and duration of occupancy transitions through Mixture Transition Distribution (MTD) modeling. We develop a recursive MTD formulation that encodes historical occupancy patterns into an augmented state to capture high-order temporal dependencies. Furthermore, a stability-driven adaptive strategy balances noise suppression with the preservation of quasi-static structures. Extensive experiments verify that MTD-Map robustly removes dynamic objects and achieves competitive change detection performance, subsequently reducing computational costs. Our project page is available at: https://taeyoung96.github.io/mtd_map/.

AI.tldr: MTD-Map is a single-stage framework for holistic map maintenance that handles both dynamic object removal and change detection using Mixture Transition Distribution modeling, recursive state encoding, and adaptive stability-driven strategies.
AI.motivation: Existing map maintenance studies address dynamic object removal or change detection as separate, task-specific problems. The authors aim to unify these tasks into a single, holistic framework.
AI.method: MTD-Map uses Mixture Transition Distribution (MTD) modeling to compactly encode occupancy transition direction and duration. A recursive MTD formulation captures high-order temporal dependencies, and a stability-driven adaptive strategy balances noise suppression with quasi-static structure preservation.
AI.result: The method robustly removes dynamic objects, achieves competitive change detection performance, and reduces computational costs.
AI.conclusion: MTD-Map effectively unifies dynamic object removal and change detection in a single-stage framework, demonstrating strong performance and efficiency.

title: PolicyGuard: A Dialogue-Grounded Sub-Agent Verifier for Policy Adherence in LLM Agents
summary: LLM agents handle user requests on behalf of organizations through tool calls and must follow the company policies stated in their system prompts. Prior work approaches this as a safeguarding problem -- external checks that block non-compliant agent actions. We argue that policy adherence is a broader problem: real workflows unfold across many turns, require explicit user confirmation and prerequisite reads, and hinge on the content of the dialogue rather than on any single argument value. Meeting this bar requires (i) full conversation context, (ii) self-reasoning over the policy and the current dialogue, and (iii) conversation-specific remediation that guides the agent's next turn -- three capabilities that prior safeguard work has often underestimated. We introduce POLICYGUARD, a sub-agent verifier that shares the agent's view of the dialogue, reasons over the policy in context, and provides actionable feedback for the agent's next turn. On tau^2-BENCH airline across three vendors (GPT-5.4, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Gemini 2.5 Pro) with four trials per setting, POLICYGUARD improves PASS4 by +12.0 / +6.0 / +12.0 pp. Per-call analyses show POLICYGUARD achieves higher policy-violation recall while blocking roughly half as often as argument-level guards.

AI.tldr: POLICYGUARD is a sub-agent verifier that improves LLM agent policy adherence by using full conversation context, self-reasoning over policies, and providing actionable remediation feedback, achieving +6-12 pp improvement in PASS4 across three LLM vendors on tau^2-BENCH airline benchmark.
AI.motivation: Prior work frames policy adherence as a safeguarding problem with external checks on individual arguments, but real workflows require multi-turn compliance, user confirmations, prerequisite reads, and dialogue-level reasoning—capabilities that existing safeguards underestimate.
AI.method: POLICYGUARD is a sub-agent verifier that shares the agent's dialogue view, reasons over the policy in context, and generates actionable feedback to guide the agent's next turn, rather than just blocking non-compliant actions.
AI.result: On tau^2-BENCH airline across GPT-5.4, Claude Sonnet 4.6, and Gemini 2.5 Pro (4 trials each), POLICYGUARD improves PASS4 by +12.0, +6.0, and +12.0 pp respectively, with higher policy-violation recall and roughly half the blocking rate of argument-level guards.
AI.conclusion: Policy adherence for LLM agents requires conversation-level reasoning and actionable remediation, not just argument-level blocking; POLICYGUARD demonstrates that sub-agent verification with contextual policy reasoning is more effective and less disruptive.

title: Learning Transferable Dynamics Priors from Action to World Modeling
summary: We study action-conditioned world modeling as a scalable way to learn transferable dynamics priors for robot learning. By pretraining a model to predict how actions drive visual scene evolution, the resulting world model captures reusable interaction dynamics beyond appearance-level video generation. Concretely, we pretrain a multi-view interactive base diffusion world model, A2World, on large-scale robot manipulation data with real action annotations. We validate the learned dynamics priors from two complementary perspectives. First, we adapt A2World into a task- or scene-specialized real-world simulator, A2World-sim, whose long-horizon rollouts support simulator-based policy evaluation and scalable what-if analysis by replacing real-robot rollouts with world model rollouts. Second, starting from the same pretrained weights, we adapt A2World into a video-action joint prediction model, A2World-policy, that predicts actions under visual and instruction conditioning. Experiments across simulation benchmarks and real-robot settings demonstrate that action-conditioned world model pretraining yields transferable dynamics priors that benefit both simulator-centric and policy-centric robot learning.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes A2World, a multi-view interactive base diffusion world model pretrained on large-scale robot manipulation data with real action annotations. It serves as both a task/scene-specialized simulator (A2World-sim) for long-horizon rollouts and a video-action joint prediction model (A2World-policy) for policy learning, demonstrating that action-conditioned world model pretraining yields transferable dynamics priors beneficial for robot learning.
AI.motivation: To learn transferable dynamics priors for robot learning via action-conditioned world modeling, enabling reusable interaction dynamics beyond appearance-level video generation.
AI.method: Pretrained a multi-view interactive base diffusion world model (A2World) on large-scale robot manipulation data with real action annotations. Adapted into A2World-sim (task/scene-specialized simulator) and A2World-policy (video-action joint prediction model).
AI.result: The learned dynamics priors benefit both simulator-centric (long-horizon rollouts for policy evaluation and what-if analysis) and policy-centric (action prediction under visual and instruction conditioning) robot learning across simulation benchmarks and real-robot settings.
AI.conclusion: Action-conditioned world model pretraining produces transferable dynamics priors that can be effectively adapted for both world simulation and policy learning in robot manipulation tasks.

title: SurgVLA-Bench: Towards Evaluating Vision-Language-Action Models for Laparoscopic Surgical Robotics
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models represent a promising direction for embodied intelligence in surgical robotics. Despite the prevalence of VLA benchmarks for general robotics, standardized evaluation platforms specifically designed for surgical contexts remain absent. To address this limitation, we present SurgVLA-Bench, the first comprehensive benchmark for evaluating VLA models in laparoscopic surgical robotics. Leveraging the SurRoL simulation platform, we construct a hierarchical task taxonomy ranging from atomic actions to complete surgical procedures, complemented by a multi-dimensional evaluation framework assessing action accuracy and semantic consistency. We then systematically evaluate two representative paradigms, including autoregressive models such as OpenVLA, and flow matching models such as $π_{0}$, $π_{0.5}$, and SmolVLA. Our experiments show that autoregressive models tend to excel in semantic understanding, while flow matching models often achieve higher task precision but may face generalization trade-offs. However, even the best-performing models remain far from satisfactory, as the constrained endoscopic field of view, restricted viewing angles, and frequent occlusions persist as fundamental physical bottlenecks. The code and data are available at https://github.com/VCL-HNU/SurgVLA

AI.tldr: SurgVLA-Bench is the first benchmark for evaluating Vision-Language-Action models in laparoscopic surgical robotics, revealing that autoregressive models excel in semantic understanding while flow matching models achieve higher task precision, but all models still struggle with physical constraints like limited endoscopic field of view and occlusions.
AI.motivation: Existing VLA benchmarks exist for general robotics but no standardized evaluation platform is available for surgical contexts, hindering progress in surgical embodied intelligence.
AI.method: Built on the SurRoL simulation platform, SurgVLA-Bench constructs a hierarchical task taxonomy from atomic actions to complete surgical procedures, with a multi-dimensional evaluation framework assessing action accuracy and semantic consistency. It evaluates autoregressive models (OpenVLA) and flow matching models (π₀, π₀.₅, SmolVLA).
AI.result: Autoregressive models excel in semantic understanding; flow matching models achieve higher task precision but face generalization trade-offs. Even the best models underperform due to constrained endoscopic field of view, restricted viewing angles, and occlusions.
AI.conclusion: SurgVLA-Bench provides the first comprehensive VLA benchmark for surgical robotics, identifies performance gaps between model paradigms, and highlights persistent physical bottlenecks (limited FOV, occlusions) as fundamental challenges for surgical VLA models.

title: CORE: Common Outcome Regularities from Action-Free Visual Demonstrations for Robot Manipulation
summary: Robot imitation learning often relies on costly robot demonstrations, while abundant action-free visual demonstrations, such as human videos, are difficult to use because they lack robot-executable actions and suffer from embodiment gaps. We propose CORE, a policy learning framework that extracts Common Outcome Regularities from visual demonstrations. Rather than transferring explicit actions across embodiments, CORE exploits a key observation: although successful trajectories for the same task can be diverse, their terminal states often share stable object configurations, spatial relations, and contact constraints. CORE first trains a terminal outcome encoder with contrastive and auxiliary temporal objectives, then aggregates successful terminal embeddings into visual goal prototypes, and finally injects these prototypes as global goal conditions into robot policies. Compared with language instructions, visual goal prototypes provide more concrete geometric and physical constraints for task completion. Across Meta-World, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world manipulation, CORE improves the average success rate of the corresponding policy backbones by up to +3.9, +11.1, and +17.0 percentage points, respectively, and outperforms text-conditioned variants under the evaluated settings.

AI.tldr: CORE extracts common outcome regularities (terminal state patterns) from action-free visual demonstrations to generate visual goal prototypes that improve robot policy learning without requiring robot-action labels.
AI.motivation: Robot imitation learning suffers from the high cost of collecting robot demonstrations with executable actions, while abundant action-free visual demonstrations (e.g., human videos) are underutilized due to the lack of robot-executable actions and embodiment gaps.
AI.method: (1) Train a terminal outcome encoder with contrastive and auxiliary temporal objectives. (2) Aggregate successful terminal embeddings into visual goal prototypes. (3) Inject these prototypes as global goal conditions into robot policies, replacing or augmenting language instructions.
AI.result: Improves average success rates by up to +3.9% (Meta-World), +11.1% (RoboTwin 2.0), and +17.0% (real-world manipulation) over baseline policy backbones, and outperforms text-conditioned variants.
AI.conclusion: Visual goal prototypes derived from action-free demonstrations provide more concrete geometric and physical constraints than language instructions, enabling effective policy learning without costly robot action labels.

title: When Summaries Distort Decisions: Information Fidelity in LLM-Compressed Financial Analysis
summary: Financial decision-makers face more information than they can directly inspect, making context compression necessary. Yet when large language models (LLMs) compress financial source material, they can alter the investment judgment supported by the original source. We frame this problem as information fidelity: compression loses fidelity when it changes the decision induced by the source. In agentic systems, such losses may recur across intermediate steps and amplify throughout the decision process. Across financial filings and earnings-call transcripts, we find that LLM-based compression can produce fluent and factually plausible compressed contexts that nevertheless alter downstream decisions. We analyze two diagnostic patterns associated with fidelity loss: decontextualization, where salient evidence is retained but separated from the caveats and contextual qualifiers needed for correct interpretation, and model dependency, where different compressors expose different views of the same source.
