Second, when the robot misunderstands intent, users cannot quickly detect errors until assistive motion diverges significantly, requiring substantial corrective input. We address this by introducing legible motion into shared autonomy, where robot actions must both advance toward the goal and clearly reveal which goal has been inferred, enabling users to understand the robot's beliefs and adjust control accordingly. The robot modulates communication strength through confidence-aware adaptive authority allocation by providing assertive legible assistive actions when confident while increasing user authority when uncertain, transforming shared autonomy into transparent bidirectional collaboration. User studies including simulation and physical experiments with a six-degree-of-freedom robot arm demonstrate that legible shared autonomy significantly improves users' understanding of robot beliefs and reduces user control effort compared to standard shared autonomy.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces legible motion into shared autonomy systems to make the robot's inferred goals transparent to users, improving understanding and reducing control effort.
AI.motivation: Traditional shared autonomy systems provide efficient but ambiguous assistive motion that fails to reveal which goal the robot has inferred, causing wasted user effort when the robot is correct and delayed error detection when the robot is incorrect.
AI.method: Legible motion is incorporated into shared autonomy where robot actions simultaneously advance toward the goal and clearly reveal which goal has been inferred. Confidence-aware adaptive authority allocation modulates communication strength: assertive legible assistance when confident, increased user authority when uncertain.
AI.result: User studies with simulation and physical experiments using a six-degree-of-freedom robot arm show that legible shared autonomy significantly improves users' understanding of robot beliefs and reduces user control effort compared to standard shared autonomy.
AI.conclusion: Legible shared autonomy transforms shared autonomy into transparent bidirectional collaboration, enabling users to perceive robot beliefs and adjust control accordingly, improving overall human-robot team performance.

title: UCOB: Learning to Utilize and Evolve Agentic Skills via Credit-Aware On-Policy Bidirectional Self-Distillation
summary: Skill memories can improve agentic reinforcement learning by reusing past experience as textual guidance, but retrieved skills are not oracular: they may help in one state while misleading the same policy in another. This makes the common privileged-teacher assumption fragile, namely that a skill-conditioned prompt can be treated as a fixed teacher for the no-skill prompt. We introduce UCOB, a framework for learning to utilize and evolve agentic skills via credit-aware on-policy bidirectional self-distillation. UCOB treats skill-conditioned and no-skill prompts as two on-policy context views of the same model, compares their return-to-go within the same task and anchor state, and uses the higher-return view as the local teacher. This local credit signal internalizes useful skill-conditioned behavior, corrects misleading skill usage, and guides task/state skill memory updates, utility-aware retrieval, and reflection self-training. Experiments on agentic tasks, including ALFWorld, WebShop, and Search-QA, show that UCOB outperforms skill-free RL, skill-memory baselines, and self-distillation methods across model scales, with up to 23.5 and 18.0 point gains over SOTA baselines on ALFWorld and WebShop. Ablations and analyses further validate its core mechanisms and efficiency.

AI.tldr: UCOB is a framework for agentic reinforcement learning that uses credit-aware on-policy bidirectional self-distillation between skill-conditioned and no-skill prompts, improving over skill-free RL and skill-memory baselines on ALFWorld, WebShop, and Search-QA.
AI.motivation: Retrieved skill memories in agentic RL are not oracular—they may help in one state but mislead in another. The common privileged-teacher assumption (treating skill-conditioned prompts as fixed teachers) is fragile and suboptimal.
AI.method: UCOB treats skill-conditioned and no-skill prompts as two on-policy context views of the same model, compares their return-to-go within the same task and anchor state, and uses the higher-return view as the local teacher. This enables internalizing useful skill-conditioned behavior, correcting misleading skill usage, and guiding skill memory updates, utility-aware retrieval, and reflection self-training.
AI.result: UCOB outperforms skill-free RL, skill-memory baselines, and self-distillation methods across model scales, with up to 23.5 and 18.0 point gains over SOTA baselines on ALFWorld and WebShop. Ablations and analyses validate its core mechanisms and efficiency.
AI.conclusion: Credit-aware bidirectional self-distillation effectively addresses the non-oracular nature of retrieved skill memories, enabling more robust skill utilization and evolution in agentic RL tasks.

title: TACO: A Test and Check Framework for Robust Pose Graph Optimization
summary: Pose Graph Optimization (PGO) is one of the most widely adopted approaches for solving Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) problems. However, PGO approaches are particularly sensitive to outliers, which can substantially degrade the quality of the estimated trajectories. These outliers arise from incorrect place recognition associations caused by perceptual aliasing in the environment. In this paper, we present TACO (short for Test And Check Optimization), a robust optimization framework designed to filter out outliers from PGO systems. Rather than explicitly modeling measurements as inliers or outliers, TACO finds an approximation to the maximally consistent set of measurements incrementally through two complementary components: (i) The test component, namely the Incremental Probabilistic Consensus (IPC) algorithm, evaluates the consistency of each incoming loop closure online. (ii) The check component dubbed Switchable Outlier Sanitization leverages the existing Switchable Constraints to periodically sanitize any inconsistent measurements from the consistent set that IPC may have mistakenly included. We evaluate TACO on 2D SLAM and 3D Visual SLAM datasets against several state-of-the-art methods. The results show robustness comparable to state-of-the-art offline methods while preserving the computational efficiency required for online deployment, achieving a success rate above 90% in 2D and 83% in 3D across outlier rates up to 50%, with mean convergence times of approximately 45 ms and 100 ms, respectively. We release an open-source implementation of our method with this paper.

AI.tldr: TACO is a robust optimization framework for Pose Graph Optimization that filters outliers via an incremental test component (IPC) and a periodic check component (Switchable Outlier Sanitization), achieving over 90% success in 2D and 83% in 3D with 45ms/100ms convergence times even at 50% outlier rates.
AI.motivation: PGO approaches are highly sensitive to outliers from incorrect place recognition due to perceptual aliasing, which degrades trajectory estimation quality in SLAM systems.
AI.method: TACO combines (i) Incremental Probabilistic Consensus (IPC) for online consistency evaluation of loop closures and (ii) Switchable Outlier Sanitization using Switchable Constraints to periodically remove mistakenly included inconsistent measurements.
AI.result: Success rates above 90% in 2D and 83% in 3D with outlier rates up to 50%, mean convergence times ~45ms (2D) and ~100ms (3D), matching offline robustness while maintaining online computational efficiency.
AI.conclusion: TACO achieves state-of-the-art robustness comparable to offline methods with the efficiency needed for online deployment, and is released as open-source.

title: OSWorld2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks
comment: 68 pages, 42 figures. Equal contribution: Mengqi Yuan, Zilong Zhou, and Xinzhuang Xiong
summary: Existing computer-use benchmarks fail to capture the realism, complexity, and long-horizon demands of real-world computer use, limiting their ability to reveal the limitations of frontier agents. We introduce OSWorld 2.0, a benchmark of 108 long-horizon computer-use workflows across everyday and professional tasks, designed to capture complex and challenging real-world phenomena. Each task represents a realistic end-to-end workflow that takes human users a median of about 1.6 hours to complete and requires an average of 318 tool calls with Claude Opus 4.7 using maximum thinking, compared with about 30 in OSWorld 1.0. OSWorld 2.0 targets challenge phenomena that are common in real workflows yet underrepresented in prior benchmarks, spanning interaction-design challenges such as streaming interaction and dynamic environments, as well as agent-pattern challenges such as cross-source reasoning, implicit-state inference, and visual-spatial precision. Tasks are grounded in authentic input artifacts and cross-referenced against realistic stateful user profile data, and include separate safety reports auditing safety-sensitive execution. Under our primary binary-completion metric at 500 steps, Claude Opus 4.8 with maximum thinking and batched tool calls scores best but still completes only 20.6% of tasks at a 54.8% partial score; GPT-5.5 is far more token-efficient yet plateaus near 13%. These results show that current agents are still far from professional-level computer use: rather than stumbling on basic GUI control or coding, they lose track of constraints, miss information that arrives mid-task, guess rather than ask the user, and skip verification, struggling most when a task hinges on hidden state they must recover.

AI.tldr: OSWorld 2.0 is a benchmark of 108 long-horizon computer-use workflows (median ~1.6 hours per task, ~318 tool calls each) that reveals frontier agents remain far from professional-level computer use; the best model (Claude Opus 4.8) completes only 20.6% of tasks, as agents struggle with constraint tracking, mid-task information, hidden state recovery, and verification rather than basic GUI control or coding.
AI.motivation: Existing computer-use benchmarks fail to capture the realism, complexity, and long-horizon demands of real-world computer use, limiting their ability to reveal the limitations of frontier agents.
AI.method: 108 long-horizon workflows across everyday and professional tasks, median ~1.6 hours human completion time, ~318 tool calls per task with Claude Opus 4.7. Targets challenge phenomena: streaming interaction, dynamic environments, cross-source reasoning, implicit-state inference, visual-spatial precision. Grounded in authentic artifacts and stateful user profiles with safety audits.
AI.result: Claude Opus 4.8 with maximum thinking and batched tool calls completes 20.6% of tasks (54.8% partial score); GPT-5.5 plateaus near 13%. Agents fail not on basic GUI or coding but on constraint tracking, mid-task information, guessing instead of asking, skipping verification, and recovering hidden state.
AI.conclusion: Current agents are still far from professional-level computer use; the benchmark exposes foundational reasoning and interaction gaps beyond GUI control.

title: Normalizing Flow-Enhanced Message Passing for Multirobot Collaborative Localization
summary: Accurate, robust, and adaptive localization is essential for various robotic operations. This paper proposes a new message passing (MP) algorithm for realizing collaborative localization in a distributed manner. The algorithm unifies Gaussian belief propagation (GBP) and mean-field (MF) approximation, where GBP preserves dependencies among robot states, and MF enables estimation of noise statistics. To effectively handle non-conjugate terms from nonlinear measurement models, the algorithm adopts a parametric formulation in which these terms are treated by gradient estimators. Beyond linearization and sampling, we further design a normalizing flow (NF)-based gradient estimator, enabling learnable sampling. End-to-end training tunes NF parameters according to the behavior of MP, improving the overall estimation performance. To support estimation of practical robotic states that involve rotations, the method is then extended to Lie group state spaces. Finally, the method is applied to multirobot localization task fusing odometry, global navigation satellite system (GNSS) measurements, and inter-robot ultra wideband (UWB) ranging. Simulations and experiments on autonomous surface vehicles (ASVs) demonstrate its improved accuracy, robustness, and adaptability.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a distributed collaborative localization algorithm that unifies Gaussian belief propagation and mean-field approximation, uses normalizing flow-based gradient estimators for handling nonlinear measurements, extends to Lie group state spaces for rotations, and demonstrates improved accuracy, robustness, and adaptability on multi-robot localization tasks with ASVs.
AI.motivation: Accurate, robust, and adaptive localization is essential for various robotic operations; existing methods face challenges in handling nonlinear measurements, non-conjugate terms, and rotational states in a distributed manner.
AI.method: The algorithm unifies Gaussian belief propagation (GBP) and mean-field (MF) approximation; GBP preserves dependencies among robot states, MF enables noise statistics estimation. A parametric formulation with gradient estimators handles non-conjugate terms from nonlinear measurement models, with a normalizing flow (NF)-based gradient estimator enabling learnable sampling. End-to-end training tunes NF parameters. The method extends to Lie group state spaces for rotations.
AI.result: The method is applied to multi-robot localization fusing odometry, GNSS, and inter-robot UWB ranging. Simulations and experiments on autonomous surface vehicles (ASVs) demonstrate improved accuracy, robustness, and adaptability.
AI.conclusion: The proposed MP algorithm unifying GBP and MF with NF-based gradient estimators and Lie group extensions achieves superior performance for distributed collaborative localization in robotic systems.

title: Learned Coordination Conventions in Cooperative MARL: Measuring the Translation Gap Between Theory-Informed Roles and Learned Routing
comment: 8 pages, 1 figures. Poster Accepted at NExT-Game 2026: New Frontiers in Game-Theoretic Learning, ICML 2026 Workshop
summary:
Role-semantic assignments provide priors over how heterogeneous agents may coordinate, but cooperative MARL systems instead settle on conventions through decentralized, non-stationary learning, with no guarantee that the resulting structure matches those priors. We study this translation gap between theory-informed role expectations and learned coordination structure through a diagnostic combining a role-routing matrix, formation sensitivity ($Δ_{\max}$), and gradient/occlusion attribution across three-role MiniGrid and SMACv2 (Terran) environments.
  We show that label-conditioned attention produces substantially more concentrated and role-specific routing than flat MLP baselines, remains stable under 3v3--9v9 scaling, transfers zero-shot across team sizes, and is invariant to ally-slot padding. A 5-seed re-evaluation shows partial alignment between learned conventions and designer-specified priors while revealing where small-n noise can manufacture apparent strategic divergence. We present these results as an empirical framework for measuring coordination structure in cooperative MARL rather than as a new equilibrium concept or causal explanation.

AI.tldr: The paper examines the gap between theory-informed role expectations and learned coordination structures in cooperative MARL, proposing a diagnostic framework (role-routing matrix, Δmax, gradient/occlusion attribution) to measure alignment. Label-conditioned attention produces more concentrated role-specific routing than MLP baselines, transfers zero-shot across team sizes, and shows partial alignment with designer-specified priors.
AI.motivation: To understand and measure the translation gap between theoretically expected role-semantic assignments and the emergent coordination structures learned by decentralized cooperative MARL systems.
AI.method: Diagnostic framework combining a role-routing matrix, formation sensitivity (Δmax), and gradient/occlusion attribution; tested on three-role MiniGrid and SMACv2 (Terran) environments comparing label-conditioned attention vs. flat MLP baselines.
AI.result: Label-conditioned attention yields more concentrated, role-specific routing, remains stable under 3v3–9v9 scaling, transfers zero-shot across team sizes, and is invariant to ally-slot padding. Partial alignment between learned conventions and designer priors is observed, with small-n noise potentially creating apparent strategic divergence.
AI.conclusion: The paper presents an empirical framework for measuring coordination structure in cooperative MARL, not a new equilibrium concept or causal explanation.

title: AUSLUN: A Fixed-Hover UAV--USV System for GNSS-Denied Maritime Search and Navigation
summary: Global navigation satellite system (GNSS) denial can prevent an unmanned surface vehicle (USV) from both finding a distant vessel and maintaining a globally referenced approach. This paper presents AUSLUN (Automatic UAV Search, Localization, and USV Navigation), a fixed-hover aerial-surface system that uses a coastal unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV), which estimates its own pose through visual-inertial odometry (VIO), as a long-range sensing and navigation anchor. The central design shifts sensing motion from UAV translation to a zoom pod and closes the loop through three coupled elements: polygon-aware annular pod scanning, modality-aware bearing-range localization, and target-relative USV guidance with visual-loss recovery. The same gated recursive estimator uses laser range for the non-cooperative target and datalink range for the cooperative USV. Search-planning simulations show that the adaptive yaw bounds reduce scan time and redundant coverage relative to a matched fixed-sector scan, and GPS-referenced field data show that the gated recursive estimator outperforms non-recursive baselines in localization accuracy. An integrated maritime mission further demonstrates the complete search-to-navigation sequence, including a deliberately triggered visual-loss recovery. These results establish the feasibility and operating boundary of fixed-hover UAV assistance for stationary-target approach in coastal GNSS-denied environments. The source code and a video demonstration are publicly available at https://github.com/xirhxq/pod_search and https://youtu.be/S-5RkJs35JI.

AI.tldr: AUSLUN is a fixed-hover UAV-USV system for coastal GNSS-denied environments where a UAV uses VIO and a zoom pod to search, localize, and guide a USV toward a non-cooperative stationary target, with a gated recursive estimator for bearing-range fusion and visual-loss recovery.
AI.motivation: GNSS denial prevents USVs from finding distant vessels and maintaining globally referenced approaches, motivating a UAV-based sensing and navigation anchor that operates without satellite positioning.
AI.method: The system shifts sensing motion from UAV translation to a zoom pod, with three coupled elements: polygon-aware annular pod scanning, modality-aware bearing-range localization using a gated recursive estimator (laser range for non-cooperative targets, datalink range for cooperative USV), and target-relative USV guidance with visual-loss recovery.
AI.result: Adaptive yaw bounds reduce scan time and redundant coverage vs. fixed-sector scans (simulation); gated recursive estimator outperforms non-recursive baselines in localization accuracy (GPS-referenced field data); integrated maritime mission demonstrates complete search-to-navigation sequence including visual-loss recovery.
AI.conclusion: Establishes feasibility and operating boundary of fixed-hover UAV assistance for stationary-target approach in coastal GNSS-denied environments.

title: SCARCE: Scalable Cascade Analysis for Rare-event Characterisation via Embeddings
summary: Rare events govern the safety profile of modern AI systems, yet their probabilities are extremely difficult to estimate: direct Monte Carlo requires prohibitive sample budgets. Subset Simulation (SS) addresses this by decomposing a rare-event probability into moderate conditional probabilities over nested intermediate events. However, classical SS requires a handcrafted scalar performance function whose sublevel sets define those events, demanding detailed knowledge of the failure geometry and limiting transfer to new domains. We propose SCARCE (Scalable Cascade Analysis for Rare-event Characterisation via Embeddings), which replaces the performance function with learned latent representations and geometric rulers that score proximity to failure regions. Adaptive thresholding constructs nested intermediate events directly from data. We formalise SCARCE through a non-negative supermartingale, yielding a high-probability upper envelope that remains valid under early stopping. On MNIST misclassification, where dense Monte Carlo provides ground truth, SCARCE achieves approximately 400--500 times lower mean absolute error than grid-searched traditional SS while eliminating systematic over-counting. We then study PAIR-style LLM jailbreaks under a fleet-level threat model with adversarial fraction $η$. On Llama-Guard-3-8B hidden states, a PCA-based ruler attains 2.6% mean relative error for $η\geq 10^{-3}$ against finite-sample references whose average bootstrap relative half-width is 27.9%, and transfers to a GCG-style corpus with 2.93% relative error after recalibration. A directional criterion $\mathrm{KL}(p_{\mathrm{good}}\,\|\,p_{\mathrm{bad}})$ ranks rulers consistently with estimation error (Spearman $ρ=0.83$).

AI.tldr: SCARCE replaces handcrafted performance functions in Subset Simulation with learned latent embeddings and geometric rulers to estimate rare-event probabilities in AI systems, achieving 400-500x lower error than classical SS on MNIST misclassification and under 3% relative error on LLM jailbreak detection.
AI.motivation: Rare events govern the safety profile of modern AI systems, but direct Monte Carlo estimation requires prohibitive sample budgets. Classical Subset Simulation needs handcrafted scalar performance functions requiring detailed knowledge of failure geometry, limiting transfer to new domains.
AI.method: SCARCE replaces the handcrafted performance function with learned latent representations and geometric rulers that score proximity to failure regions. It uses adaptive thresholding to construct nested intermediate events from data, and is formalized through a non-negative supermartingale for a high-probability upper envelope valid under early stopping.
AI.result: On MNIST misclassification: 400-500x lower mean absolute error than grid-searched traditional SS. On Llama-Guard-3-8B hidden states for PAIR-style jailbreaks: 2.6% mean relative error (η≥10⁻³) vs finite-sample references with 27.9% avg bootstrap half-width, transferring to GCG-style corpus with 2.93% relative error after recalibration. KL divergence ranks rulers consistently with estimation error (Spearman ρ=0.83).
AI.conclusion: SCARCE demonstrates that learned latent representations can effectively replace handcrafted performance functions for rare-event estimation via Subset Simulation, achieving substantial accuracy gains and transferability across domains, with a theoretically grounded supermartingale framework ensuring validity under early stopping.

title: Trust Your Instincts: Confidence-Driven Test-Time RL for Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become indispensable for pushing Vision-Language-Action Models (VLAs) beyond static imitation learning. However, existing RL methods typically require external environmental feedback, relying on predefined success signals to guide policy updates. In this work, we show that VLA models possess useful internal evaluative capabilities: in discrete-action VLAs, trajectories with higher generation confidence are significantly more likely to succeed. Based on this observation, we introduce T^2VLA (Test-time VLA), an architecture-agnostic test-time RL framework that enables VLA models to achieve self-bootstrapping policy improvement. Instead of relying on external rewards, T^2VLA leverages trajectory-level similarity to high-confidence expert demonstrations as an intrinsic reward signal. In addition, we propose a Confidence-Driven Dual Expert Bootstrapping mechanism, which dynamically balances a Local Pseudo-Expert for exploration and a Global Expert Pool for training stability. Extensive experiments on the LIBERO and RoboTwin benchmarks show that T^2VLA consistently outperforms supervised baselines and approaches oracle RL performance with ground-truth rewards, achieving effective improvement without external reward feedback. Furthermore, T^2VLA adapts to distinct VLA paradigms, including both OpenVLA-OFT and the pi series.

AI.tldr: T^2VLA is a test-time RL framework that enables Vision-Language-Action Models to bootstrap policy improvement without external rewards, using trajectory-level similarity to high-confidence expert demonstrations as intrinsic reward and a Confidence-Driven Dual Expert Bootstrapping mechanism.
AI.motivation: Existing RL methods for VLA models require external environmental feedback (success signals), which limits applicability. The authors aim to leverage VLA models' internal evaluative capabilities—specifically, higher generation confidence correlates with trajectory success—to enable self-bootstrapping policy improvement without external rewards.
AI.method: T^2VLA uses trajectory-level similarity to high-confidence expert demonstrations as an intrinsic reward signal instead of external rewards. It introduces a Confidence-Driven Dual Expert Bootstrapping mechanism with a Local Pseudo-Expert (for exploration) and a Global Expert Pool (for stability). The framework is architecture-agnostic and operates at test time.
AI.result: On LIBERO and RoboTwin benchmarks, T^2VLA consistently outperforms supervised baselines and approaches oracle RL performance with ground-truth rewards, achieving effective improvement without external reward feedback. It adapts to distinct VLA paradigms including OpenVLA-OFT and the pi series.
AI.conclusion: VLA models can achieve self-bootstrapping policy improvement via test-time RL using internal confidence signals as intrinsic rewards, eliminating the need for external environmental feedback.

title: SFBench: The SciFy Scientific Feasibility Benchmark
summary: We present SFBench, a benchmark dataset for evaluating systems that assess the feasibility of scientific claims. SFBench includes 197 claims in materials science, each annotated with a ground-truth feasibility score on a five-point scale along with an explanation of that assessment. The collection differs from previous collections in several important ways: 1) it defines a complex task that requires reasoning over claims of varying scientific feasibility; 2) its claims are not extracted from existing scientific publications but are created de novo, greatly reducing the chances that LLMs have trained on them; 3) claims and ground truth are established by subject matter experts, not by artificial intelligence; and 4) unlike many benchmarks that ask about question/answer pairs, provide multiple choice answers, or ask questions requiring short, fixed answers, SFBench explanations are completely open-ended. We describe the benchmark design, data creation process, and evaluation metrics, and we report baseline results using recent GPT models.

AI.tldr: SFBench is a new benchmark dataset of 197 materials science claims, each annotated by experts with feasibility scores and open-ended explanations, designed to evaluate how well systems (e.g., LLMs) can assess the plausibility of scientific claims. It avoids LLM contamination via de novo creation and uses expert-driven ground truth.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks for scientific claim evaluation often suffer from LLM data contamination, reliance on AI-generated ground truth, and constrained output formats (e.g., multiple-choice). SFBench addresses these gaps by introducing a complex, open-ended feasibility assessment task with expert-annotated, de novo claims.
AI.method: The authors created 197 de novo claims in materials science (not extracted from existing publications), each annotated by subject-matter experts with a five-point feasibility score and a free-text explanation. They designed the benchmark, define evaluation metrics, and report baseline results using recent GPT models.
AI.result: The paper presents the benchmark dataset and reports baseline performance results from recent GPT models on the feasibility assessment task.
AI.conclusion: SFBench provides a more rigorous and less contaminated benchmark for evaluating scientific claim feasibility, with open-ended expert explanations as ground truth, and establishes baselines for future work.

title: Critical Interval MSE: Toward Reliable Offline Validation for Robot Manipulation Policies
summary: Real-world evaluation is the gold standard for robot policies because it tests them against the physical conditions and deployment challenges they are ultimately designed to handle. However, real-world evaluation is also the bottleneck for iterating on robot policies: it is costly, difficult to reproduce, and often too sparse to reliably compare nearby model variants. A straightforward proxy for performance is validation loss on expert demonstrations, but this proxy is often poorly correlated with real-world performance. In this paper, we introduce Critical Interval MSE (CI-MSE), an intuitively simple yet effective offline validation metric. CI-MSE restricts error computation to task-critical segments and pairs it with simple action-alignment procedures that better match rollout-time behavior. Across simulation and real-world experiments, CI-MSE yields a stronger correlation between validation error and rollout performance than raw MSE. Across a wide range of policy checkpoints, CI-MSE achieves a Spearman's rank correlation of $-0.87$, much closer to the ideal value of $-1$ than raw MSE's $-0.61$, demonstrating a significant improvement. We show through sensitivity analysis that our metric is robust to a wide range of hyperparameters. We further study the effectiveness of CI-MSE under evaluation distribution shifts and suggest design boundaries when using this metric. In summary, this paper provides a simple and reliable offline validation tool for accelerating policy iteration. Project webpage: https://ci-mse.github.io/

AI.tldr: CI-MSE is an offline validation metric that restricts error computation to task-critical segments and uses action-alignment procedures, achieving significantly better correlation with real-world robot policy performance (Spearman's ρ = -0.87) than raw MSE (-0.61).
AI.motivation: Real-world evaluation is the gold standard for robot policies but is costly, difficult to reproduce, and too sparse for reliable comparison of model variants. Existing offline proxies like validation loss on expert demonstrations correlate poorly with real-world performance.
AI.method: CI-MSE (Critical Interval MSE) restricts error computation to task-critical segments and pairs it with simple action-alignment procedures that better match rollout-time behavior.
AI.result: Across simulation and real-world experiments, CI-MSE achieves Spearman's rank correlation of -0.87 (close to ideal -1), significantly outperforming raw MSE's -0.61. The metric is robust to a wide range of hyperparameters.
AI.conclusion: CI-MSE provides a simple, reliable offline validation tool for accelerating policy iteration, with demonstrated effectiveness and robustness under evaluation distribution shifts.

title: Budgeted Act-or-Defer Multi-Agent LLM Deliberation with Local Reliability Bounds
summary: Multi-agent deliberation among LLMs can improve reasoning, but deployment requires deciding when the current answer is reliable enough to act on and when it should be escalated to human review. We formulate this as budgeted act-or-defer decision making. At each round, the system maps the debate prefix to a low-dimensional state, computes a $k$-nearest-neighbor lower confidence bound on state-conditional correctness using calibration data, and acts only when the bound exceeds a user-specified reliability threshold. The certificate controls wrong actions through the decomposition $β= δ+ α+ \varepsilon_{\mathrm{act}}$, separating calibration failure, residual action risk, and representation gap. The guarantee is conditional, not distribution-free: it relies on a valid local bias envelope and an action-region representation-gap bound, and each assumption is paired with falsification-style diagnostics. Because the same absolute wrong-action budget has different meanings across tasks of different difficulty, we set budgets relative to each task's final-round error using training data only, and evaluate safety by normalized budget usage $\mathrm{WA}/β$. On six benchmarks against nine baselines, the method uses 9--12% of the pre-declared budget on activated datasets, reaching up to 84% automation and 96% acted-on accuracy; on stress-test datasets, it defers rather than forcing unreliable automation. Rather than relying on per-task post-hoc threshold search, the method prospectively converts a user-declared wrong-action budget into an auditable act-or-defer operating point before deployment, under explicitly stated assumptions.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a budgeted act-or-defer framework for multi-agent LLM deliberation, where decisions are made to act or defer to human review based on a k-nearest-neighbor lower confidence bound on correctness, with formal guarantees on wrong-action rates via decomposition into calibration failure, residual action risk, and representation gap, and relative budget setting per task difficulty.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent LLM deliberation improves reasoning but lacks a principled mechanism for deciding when an answer is reliable enough to act on versus when it should be escalated to human review, motivating a budgeted act-or-defer decision framework with formal reliability guarantees.
AI.method: Formulates budgeted act-or-defer decision making; at each round, maps debate prefix to low-dimensional state, computes k-NN lower confidence bound on state-conditional correctness from calibration data, acts only when bound exceeds reliability threshold. Wrong-action budget decomposed as β = δ + α + ε_act (calibration failure, residual action risk, representation gap). Budgets set relative to task difficulty using training data; evaluated via normalized budget usage WA/β.
AI.result: On six benchmarks against nine baselines, the method uses 9-12% of pre-declared budget on activated datasets, reaching up to 84% automation and 96% acted-on accuracy; on stress-test datasets it defers rather than forcing unreliable automation.
AI.conclusion: The method prospectively converts a user-declared wrong-action budget into an auditable act-or-defer operating point before deployment under explicitly stated assumptions, without requiring per-task post-hoc threshold search.

title: Pondering the Way: Spatial-perceiving World Action Model for Embodied Navigation
summary: Existing world model-based planners for visual navigation typically follow a verification-centric paradigm, decoupling goal intent from trajectory synthesis. This approach suffers from candidate dependence, heavy computational overhead, and inconsistencies between sampled actions and predicted visuals. To address these issues, we propose SWAM (Spatial-perceiving World Action Model), a task-centric joint observation-action generation framework. Given start and goal RGB observations, SWAM performs single-pass inference to simultaneously generate intermediate RGB-D sequences and corresponding action trajectories, promoting goal-consistent trajectory generation and improved spatial feasibility. While SWAM leverages depth pseudo-labels during training to internalize spatial priors, it requires only monocular RGB input at inference time. We further introduce a visual-guided action refinement module and a trajectory-scale regularization loss to enforce fine-grained alignment between motion and visual cues while stabilizing predictions across varying distances. Extensive experiments show that SWAM significantly outperforms state-of-the-art two-stage planners in success rate, trajectory accuracy, and inference efficiency, while demonstrating robust zero-shot generalization to unseen environments.

AI.tldr: SWAM is a task-centric joint observation-action generation framework that simultaneously predicts RGB-D sequences and action trajectories from monocular RGB input in a single pass, outperforming two-stage planners in navigation success rate, accuracy, and efficiency.
AI.motivation: Existing world model-based planners decouple goal intent from trajectory synthesis, leading to candidate dependence, high computational cost, and inconsistency between sampled actions and predicted visuals.
AI.method: SWAM performs single-pass inference to jointly generate intermediate RGB-D observations and corresponding action trajectories. It uses depth pseudo-labels during training (monocular RGB at inference), a visual-guided action refinement module, and a trajectory-scale regularization loss.
AI.result: SWAM significantly outperforms state-of-the-art two-stage planners in success rate, trajectory accuracy, and inference efficiency, with robust zero-shot generalization to unseen environments.
AI.conclusion: The task-centric joint generation paradigm effectively resolves inconsistencies between action and visual prediction, offering a more efficient and spatially feasible alternative to verification-centric planners.

title: Safety from Honesty in a Disinterested AI Predictor
summary: As AI systems become more capable, training procedures that optimize for downstream outcomes risk introducing implicit agency: goal-directed behavior that designers never specified. We present a formal safety argument for the Scientist AI (SAI) Predictor, trained to approximate the Bayesian posterior conditioned on a dataset of "epistemically contextualized" natural-language statements. We argue that such a Predictor can honestly predict agents, actions, and their consequences without itself being an agent that selects outputs to achieve goals. This rests on data representation and on the training procedure. Epistemic contextualization of text distinguishes latent factual claims from communication acts, so expressions of goals are treated as evidence to be explained rather than drives the model adopts. With a posterior-seeking training objective, this is intended to drive the Predictor toward calibrated, cautious predictions. Training proceeds so downstream effects of deploying a prediction never serve as a reward signal; any agency the system needs is supplied by explicit scaffolding constrained by guardrails. We prove that, under assumptions on the training dynamics and on the argued sparsity of dangerous Predictors, the probability that training produces a Predictor whose guarded deployment carries residual harm above a specified threshold is small: a dangerous Predictor would have to underestimate harm in a coordinated way across many queries while such coordinated patterns are rare under the initialization distribution and receive no direct training signal. Safety and accuracy are jointly supported in this framework, since the constraints that secure accuracy are the same ones that make coordinated deception costly. These guarantees against misalignment and agency arising from within the Predictor itself do not preclude the use of the Predictor as part of an agentic system.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a formal safety argument for a Bayesian posterior-approximating Predictor trained on epistemically contextualized natural-language data, showing that it can make honest predictions without becoming an agent.
AI.motivation: As AI systems grow more capable, optimizing for downstream outcomes can inadvertently produce implicit agency—goal-directed behavior not specified by designers. The authors seek a training framework that avoids this risk.
AI.method: The approach uses epistemic contextualization of text (distinguishing factual claims from communication acts), a posterior-seeking training objective that treats goal expressions as evidence, and decouples training from downstream deployment rewards. Safety is argued via a proof that dangerous coordinated predictions are rare under initialization and receive no training signal.
AI.result: Under assumptions on training dynamics and sparsity of dangerous Predictors, the probability of producing a Predictor whose guarded deployment causes residual harm above a threshold is small. Coordinated deception is costly because the same constraints that ensure accuracy make it so.
AI.conclusion: Safety and accuracy are jointly supported: the constraints securing accuracy also prevent coordinated deception. The Predictor itself is non-agentic, though it can be used within an agentic system.

title: Sphere-VIO: Fast and Robust Visual-Inertial Odometry via Unified Spherical Representation for Heterogeneous Multi-Camera Systems
summary: Multi-camera visual-inertial odometry (VIO) overcomes the inherent limitations of pure visual systems by expanding the field of view. However, existing algorithms are typically tailored for fixed camera setups and lack unified compatibility with heterogeneous multi-camera systems. Meanwhile, due to the absence of a unified cross-camera representation and association mechanism, current methods struggle to achieve a balance among robust cross-camera feature tracking, stable depth estimation, and reliable real-time performance. To address these issues, we present Sphere-VIO, a lightweight filter-based VIO framework with unified spherical representation for heterogeneous multi-camera systems. Specifically, we first propose a Unified Spherical Panorama Model (USPM) that supports all standard camera models and enables bidirectional fast mapping between multi-camera images and a shared spherical space without sequential stitching, simplifying cross-camera feature management and improving triangulation efficiency. Second, we design a parallel-accelerated depth-guided semi-direct tracking pipeline, namely Hierarchical Omnidirectional Feature Alignment (HOFA), with global spherical constraints for robust cross-camera matching, and fuse multi-camera depth observations into a standard depth filter for stable initialization. Finally, we develop a multi-camera-adapted ESKF backend that employs spherical bearing residuals and Schur complement marginalization to minimize computational overhead, enabling accurate real-time state estimation on resource-constrained devices. Extensive experiments on public benchmarks and a custom omnidirectional dataset show that Sphere-VIO achieves superior trade-offs between accuracy, robustness, efficiency, and cross-camera generality.

AI.tldr: Sphere-VIO is a lightweight filter-based visual-inertial odometry framework using unified spherical representation for heterogeneous multi-camera systems, featuring a Unified Spherical Panorama Model, hierarchical feature alignment, and an ESKF backend with spherical bearing residuals, achieving superior accuracy, robustness, efficiency, and cross-camera generality.
AI.motivation: Existing VIO algorithms are tailored for fixed camera setups and lack unified compatibility with heterogeneous multi-camera systems. Current methods also struggle to balance robust cross-camera feature tracking, stable depth estimation, and reliable real-time performance due to the absence of a unified cross-camera representation and association mechanism.
AI.method: (1) Unified Spherical Panorama Model (USPM) supporting all standard camera models for bidirectional mapping between multi-camera images and a shared spherical space. (2) Hierarchical Omnidirectional Feature Alignment (HOFA) with depth-guided semi-direct tracking and global spherical constraints for robust cross-camera matching, plus multi-camera depth fusion into a standard depth filter. (3) Multi-camera-adapted ESKF backend using spherical bearing residuals and Schur complement marginalization for efficient real-time state estimation.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on public benchmarks and a custom omnidirectional dataset demonstrate Sphere-VIO achieves superior trade-offs between accuracy, robustness, efficiency, and cross-camera generality compared to existing methods.
AI.conclusion: Sphere-VIO effectively addresses the limitations of existing VIO systems for heterogeneous multi-camera setups by providing a unified spherical representation and lightweight filter-based framework that balances accuracy, robustness, efficiency, and generality across different camera configurations.

title: Diversity is the Strength of the AI Crowd
comment: Accepted at the ICML 2026 Workshop on Forecasting as a New Frontier of Intelligence, Seoul, South Korea, 2026
summary: Top AI forecasting systems are approaching superforecaster-level accuracy on future world events, but still rely primarily on off-the-shelf LLMs combined with forecasting-specific context gathering and scaffolding. We study how to improve this recipe through ensembling: given a fixed number of samples, which off-the-shelf model forecasts should be combined to maximize accuracy? On binary questions from the Metaculus AI Benchmark, we find that individual accuracy is not enough: many frontier LLMs make highly correlated predictions, limiting the value of additional forecasts from the same or similar models. Instead, the strongest ensembles combine accurate but diverse forecasters, with models such as \model{Grok 4} contributing disproportionately because their predictions are less correlated with other frontier LLMs. These results suggest that the strength of the AI crowd comes not from sampling more forecasts indiscriminately, but from combining forecasts across models with complementary errors, motivating forecasting systems that explicitly optimize for both model quality and diversity.

AI.tldr: Ensembling diverse, accurate LLMs improves forecasting accuracy more than simply adding more forecasts from similar models; Grok 4 contributes disproportionately due to low correlation with other frontier LLMs.
AI.motivation: Top AI forecasting systems approach superforecaster accuracy but rely on off-the-shelf LLMs with context gathering and scaffolding; the paper studies how to improve this via ensembling—which combination of model forecasts maximizes accuracy given a fixed sample budget.
AI.method: On binary questions from the Metaculus AI Benchmark, the authors compare individual accuracy vs. ensemble accuracy, analyzing prediction correlations among frontier LLMs and measuring how diversity (low correlation) enhances ensemble performance.
AI.result: Individual accuracy alone is insufficient; frontier LLMs produce highly correlated predictions. The strongest ensembles combine accurate but diverse forecasters; Grok 4 is especially valuable due to lower correlation with other frontier models.
AI.conclusion: The strength of AI crowds comes from combining forecasts across models with complementary errors, not from indiscriminately sampling more forecasts. Forecasting systems should explicitly optimize for both model quality and diversity.

title: Flying to Image-Specified Objects: 3D Quadrotor Navigation via Cross-Graph Memory and Viewpoint Planning
summary: Instance-Specific Image-Goal Navigation (InstanceImageNav) requires a robot to navigate toward the exact object instance depicted in a query image. Extending this task to quadrotors is challenging due to continuous 3D control, limited field of view (FOV), and safety constraints, which make successful navigation highly dependent on selecting informative viewpoints. We propose a hierarchical navigation framework for quadrotor InstanceImageNav that separates high-level decision making from low-level motion execution. Instead of navigating directly to spatial locations, the system generates viewpoint-aware action nodes around frontier regions and potential target objects, enabling the robot to explore while maintaining informative viewpoints for detecting the target instance. A lightweight semantic memory maintains object-level and observation-level context, allowing semantic cues to propagate to candidate action nodes for decision making. A learning-based policy selects the most promising action node, and a trajectory planner generates dynamically feasible 3D flight paths for safe execution. Experiments in simulation demonstrate consistent improvements over strong baselines, and real-world quadrotor flights validate the practicality and robustness of the proposed framework.

AI.tldr: A hierarchical navigation framework for quadrotors to navigate toward specific object instances shown in a query image, using viewpoint-aware action nodes, semantic memory, and a learning-based policy for safe 3D flight.
AI.motivation: Extending InstanceImageNav to quadrotors is challenging due to continuous 3D control, limited FOV, and safety constraints, making viewpoint selection critical for success.
AI.method: A hierarchical framework separating high-level decision making from low-level motion execution: generates viewpoint-aware action nodes around frontiers and potential targets, uses lightweight semantic memory for object/observation context, employs a learning-based policy to select action nodes, and a trajectory planner for feasible 3D paths.
AI.result: Consistent improvements over strong baselines in simulation; real-world quadrotor flights validate practicality and robustness.
AI.conclusion: The proposed hierarchical framework with viewpoint-aware exploration and semantic memory effectively enables quadrotor InstanceImageNav in both simulated and real-world settings.

title: Sample-Efficient Learning of Probabilistic Causes for Reachability in Markov Decision Processes with Probabilistic Guarantees
comment: Accepted to UAI2026 as oral presentation
summary: Probabilistic model checking for Markov decision processes (MDPs) provides quantitative guarantees, but often offers limited insight into why undesired outcomes occur. Probability-raising (PR) causality addresses this by identifying states whose visitation increases the probability of reaching designated states. Existing PR-cause identification methods, however, use MDP modifications not well-suited for learning: the gap between conditional and unconditional reachability probabilities can be hard to detect from transition samples, and construction requires reachability probabilities of the MDP, which are unavailable when transition probabilities are unknown. We study unknown MDPs and propose a learning approach with probabilistic guarantees for PR-cause identification. Our key ingredient is a restart-based MDP modification that reduces PR-cause checking to two conditional reachability queries without using reachability values of the original MDP. We prove correctness, establish sample-complexity bounds, and develop an anytime learning-and-checking algorithm based on two-sided value iteration that progressively classifies states as causal, non-causal, or undecided. Experiments on two benchmarks demonstrate reliable and fast identification of PR causes.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a learning-based approach for identifying probability-raising causes in unknown Markov decision processes, using a restart-based modification that enables PR-cause checking without requiring reachability probabilities of the original MDP.
AI.motivation: Existing PR-cause identification methods rely on MDP modifications that require reachability probabilities of the original MDP, making them unsuitable for unknown MDPs where transition probabilities are unavailable. This limits the applicability of causality analysis in learning settings.
AI.method: The authors propose a restart-based MDP modification that reduces PR-cause checking to two conditional reachability queries, eliminating the need for original MDP reachability values. They develop an anytime learning-and-checking algorithm based on two-sided value iteration that progressively classifies states as causal, non-causal, or undecided, with sample-complexity bounds.
AI.result: The approach is proven correct with established sample-complexity bounds. Experiments on two benchmarks demonstrate reliable and fast identification of PR causes.
AI.conclusion: The restart-based approach effectively enables PR-cause identification in unknown MDPs, offering a practical learning-based solution with probabilistic guarantees.

title: RoamFlow: Reinforcement-Aligned One-Step Action MeanFlow Policy for Image-Goal Navigation
summary: Image-goal navigation is a key challenge in embodied robotics, where an agent must reach a target specified solely by a goal image. While existing reinforcement learning approaches map perceptual observations directly to actions, they struggle to model long-horizon dependencies, often leading to suboptimal trajectories. To address this limitation, we propose RoamFlow, a generative navigation framework that leverages MeanFlow to predict the average velocity field for trajectory synthesis, enabling efficient few-step generation and reducing inference latency. We further adopt a two-stage training strategy that combines expert imitation for stable initialization with reinforcement learning for task-specific policy refinement. Extensive experiments in both Habitat simulation and real-world robotic platforms demonstrate that RoamFlow achieves efficient inference while maintaining strong navigation performance under real-time constraints.

AI.tldr: RoamFlow is a generative navigation framework using MeanFlow for trajectory synthesis with a two-stage training strategy (expert imitation + RL), achieving efficient inference and strong navigation performance in both simulation and real-world settings.
AI.motivation: Existing RL approaches for image-goal navigation struggle to model long-horizon dependencies, leading to suboptimal trajectories.
AI.method: Proposes RoamFlow, a generative navigation framework using MeanFlow to predict average velocity fields for trajectory synthesis with few-step generation, combined with a two-stage training strategy: expert imitation for stable initialization followed by reinforcement learning for policy refinement.
AI.result: Achieves efficient inference with reduced latency while maintaining strong navigation performance under real-time constraints, validated in both Habitat simulation and real-world robotic platforms.
AI.conclusion: RoamFlow effectively addresses long-horizon dependency issues in image-goal navigation, offering a practical solution for real-time embodied robotics applications.

title: Toward Secure and Reliable PDDL Formalization of Large Language Models with Planner-in-the-Loop Feedback
summary: Planning often requires symbolic specifications that are both executable and verifiable. For large language models deployed in autonomous or decision-support systems, failures in such formalization may lead to unverifiable decisions, execution failures, or unsafe downstream behavior. We present NL-PDDL-Bench, a multi-domain benchmark for natural-language-to-PDDL specification construction with planner-verified executability and controlled difficulty scaling by object count. We further propose a planner-in-the-loop framework that uses validator and planner diagnostics to revise non-executable specifications through localized edits. Building on this infrastructure, we develop a planner-grounded optimization recipe that combines parameter-efficient Low-Rank Adaptation supervised fine-tuning, offline planner-derived preference pairs for Direct Preference Optimization, and inference-time planner-in-the-loop repair, without requiring online planner calls during training. We also provide a unified evaluation suite for parseability, solvability, specification similarity, and outcome-aware plan-level consistency against planner references. Experiments on representative model families show substantial gains in planner success and plan-level agreement, with improved robustness under difficulty scaling and cross-domain variation. These results highlight the value of externally verifiable formalization for reliable deployment of LLMs in safety- or security-sensitive planning systems. Code and data are available at: https://github.com/ibasicplan/NL-PDDL-Bench

AI.tldr: The paper introduces NL-PDDL-Bench, a benchmark for translating natural language to PDDL planning specifications, and proposes a planner-in-the-loop framework combining supervised fine-tuning, preference optimization, and inference-time repair to improve executability and plan-level consistency, demonstrating substantial gains across model families.
AI.motivation: Planning in autonomous/decision-support systems requires symbolic specifications that are both executable and verifiable. Failures in formalizing natural language into such specifications (e.g., PDDL) lead to unverifiable decisions, execution failures, or unsafe behavior, motivating the need for reliable NL-to-PDDL translation with formal guarantees.
AI.method: The authors propose (1) NL-PDDL-Bench, a multi-domain benchmark with controlled difficulty scaling; (2) a planner-in-the-loop framework that uses validator/planner diagnostics to revise non-executable specs; (3) a planner-grounded optimization recipe combining LoRA-based supervised fine-tuning, offline DPO from planner-derived preference pairs, and inference-time repair—all without online planner calls during training.
AI.result: Experiments show substantial gains in planner success and plan-level agreement, with improved robustness under difficulty scaling and cross-domain variation across representative model families.
AI.conclusion: Externally verifiable formalization is valuable for reliable deployment of LLMs in safety- or security-sensitive planning systems.

title: OpenSPM: An Environment-Transferable Robotic Key Spatial Pose Memory and Closed-Loop High-Frequency Flow-Matching Action Generation Model
summary: Open-environment tabletop robotic manipulation requires systems to possess semantic understanding, precise geometric pose estimation, and high-frequency action generation. While end-to-end vision-language-action (VLA) models excel at semantic generalization, they often lack explicit geometric constraints for fine-grained tasks and require costly training. To bridge the gap between high-level semantics and low-level physical execution, we propose OpenSPM, an open environment spatial persistent memory framework consisting of spatial pose memory and flow-matching action generation model. OpenSPM first leverages semantically conditioned 3D perception and Kalman filtering to track continuous 6D poses. It then extracts key spatial poses from human demonstrations, keeping them as transferable, object-centric spatial persistent memory entries. During inference, OpenSPM retrieves relevant memory entries in terms of natural language instructions, transfers the spatial poses to new scenes using SE(3) transformations, and generates high-frequency action chunks via a lightweight conditional flow-matching model. Combined with real-time proprioceptive state feedback and terminal residual correction, the system effectively suppresses trajectory error accumulation. Evaluated on ten LIBERO-GOAL tasks, OpenSPM achieves an 85.6% success rate and an equivalent control frequency of 1033.3 Hz, while requiring minimal inference AI computing power. Extensive ablations illustrate that structured spatial persistent memory and closed-loop residual correction play a crucial role in reliable, high-frequency robotic manipulation.

AI.tldr: OpenSPM is an open-environment spatial persistent memory framework for tabletop robotic manipulation that combines semantic 3D perception, Kalman-filtered 6D pose tracking, key spatial pose extraction from demonstrations, SE(3)-based pose transfer, and lightweight flow-matching action generation. It achieves 85.6% success rate and 1033.3 Hz control frequency on LIBERO-GOAL tasks with minimal compute.
AI.motivation: Existing VLA models lack explicit geometric constraints for fine-grained tasks and require costly training; there is a gap between high-level semantics and low-level physical execution that needs bridging for open-environment manipulation.
AI.method: OpenSPM uses (1) semantically conditioned 3D perception + Kalman filtering for continuous 6D pose tracking, (2) extraction of key spatial poses from demonstrations stored as object-centric memory entries, (3) retrieval via natural language + SE(3) transfer to new scenes, and (4) high-frequency action chunks via a lightweight conditional flow-matching model with proprioceptive feedback and terminal residual correction.
AI.result: 85.6% success rate and 1033.3 Hz equivalent control frequency across ten LIBERO-GOAL tasks, requiring minimal inference AI computing power.
AI.conclusion: Structured spatial persistent memory and closed-loop residual correction are critical for reliable, high-frequency robotic manipulation in open environments.

title: GUICrafter: Weakly-Supervised GUI Agent Leveraging Massive Unannotated Screenshots
summary: Data, as the fundamental substrate of modern intelligence, has greatly driven the development of current foundation models. Naturally, researchers aim to extend this paradigm to the domain of GUI agents, hoping to build strong GUI agents through a similar paradigm. However, GUI agent data cannot be directly harvested from the internet, making it costly and difficult to collect at scale. As a result, current GUI agents suffer from poor cross-device generalization and limited visual grounding ability for fine-grained GUI elements. As an attempt to address data challenge in GUI agents, we propose GUICrafter, a weakly-supervised GUI agent leveraging massive unannotated screenshots to substantially reduce the reliance on expensive human annotations. GUICrafter explores a curriculum learning framework for training GUI agents through two progressive stages. First, the model learns visual grounding from large-scale unannotated screenshots and webpages, leveraging the rich contextual signals inherent in GUI interactions without human annotations. Then, in Stage 2, we leverage a small amount of high-quality data to calibrate the model via reinforcement learning. Experiments show that GUICrafter achieves competitive, or even superior, performance to advanced systems like UI-TARS while using only 0.1% of its data. Furthermore, under the same amount of annotated data, GUICrafter surpasses all previous methods such as GUI-R1. Code, data, and models are available at https://github.com/fansunqi/GUICrafter.

AI.tldr: GUICrafter is a weakly-supervised GUI agent that leverages massive unannotated screenshots via curriculum learning (visual grounding pretraining + RL fine-tuning with minimal annotations), achieving competitive performance to UI-TARS using only 0.1% of its data.
AI.motivation: GUI agent data is costly and difficult to collect at scale (cannot be directly harvested from the internet like text data), leading to poor cross-device generalization and limited visual grounding for fine-grained GUI elements.
AI.method: A curriculum learning framework with two stages: Stage 1 learns visual grounding from large-scale unannotated screenshots/webpages using contextual signals inherent in GUI interactions; Stage 2 uses a small amount of high-quality data to calibrate the model via reinforcement learning.
AI.result: GUICrafter achieves competitive or superior performance to UI-TARS while using only 0.1% of its data; under the same amount of annotated data, it surpasses all previous methods including GUI-R1.
AI.conclusion: Weakly-supervised learning with unannotated screenshots can substantially reduce reliance on expensive human annotations for GUI agents while maintaining strong performance.

title: REPAIR-Bench: A Benchmark for Robot Error Perception And Interaction Recovery
summary: Understanding how users perceive and respond to robot failures is essential for building robust and trustworthy robot systems. Prior work, however, (i) often treats failures as independent events, (ii) emphasizes binary failure detection, (iii) with rule-based recovery modeling. We present REPAIR-Bench, built on 214 interaction trials from 41 participants, the benchmark spans four induced failure types and provides synchronized facial action units, head pose, speech transcripts, and post-interaction affect and recovery reports. The benchmark spans three novel evaluation tasks that jointly capture the lifecycle of failure in human-robot interaction (HRI): (i) failure detection over inter-dependent interaction sessions, modeling longitudinal user adaptation across repeated failures; (ii) visual failure-type classification beyond binary success/failure formulations; and (iii) user-centered recovery prediction, inferring users' preferred recovery strategies from interaction context rather than relying on manually designed or rule-based strategies. In baseline experiments, hierarchical recurrent modeling improved failure detection over a single-session model (strict F1: 0.80 vs. 0.68), achieved a failure localization mean signed error of -0.51 s, median absolute error of 2.97 s and, for recovery prediction, a QLoRA-tuned Mistral-7B reached Hit@5=0.76 and F1@5=0.32. REPAIR-Bench provides both the HRI and Medical HRI communities with a standardized framework for (1) evaluating robot failures and (2) building transparent, adaptive, and trustworthy recovery systems.

AI.tldr: REPAIR-Bench is a benchmark built on 214 interaction trials from 41 participants that models the full lifecycle of robot failures in HRI across three tasks: longitudinal failure detection, visual failure-type classification, and user-centered recovery prediction, showing hierarchical recurrent models outperform single-session baselines (F1: 0.80 vs 0.68) and QLoRA-tuned Mistral-7B achieves Hit@5=0.76 for recovery prediction.
AI.motivation: Prior work treats failures as independent events, focuses on binary failure detection, and uses rule-based recovery modeling, lacking a comprehensive benchmark that captures user adaptation across repeated failures, distinguishes failure types, and infers user-preferred recovery strategies.
AI.method: The authors built REPAIR-Bench from 214 interaction trials (41 participants) with four induced failure types, synchronized facial action units, head pose, speech transcripts, and post-interaction reports. They defined three evaluation tasks: (1) longitudinal failure detection using hierarchical recurrent modeling, (2) visual failure-type classification beyond binary success/failure, and (3) user-centered recovery prediction using QLoRA-tuned Mistral-7B.
AI.result: Hierarchical recurrent modeling improved failure detection over single-session models (strict F1: 0.80 vs 0.68), failure localization mean signed error of -0.51s (median absolute error 2.97s), and QLoRA-tuned Mistral-7B achieved Hit@5=0.76 and F1@5=0.32 for recovery prediction.
AI.conclusion: REPAIR-Bench provides a standardized framework for the HRI and Medical HRI communities to evaluate robot failures and build transparent, adaptive, and trustworthy recovery systems.

title: DeepTrans Studio: Turning Expert Interventions into Shared Team Knowledge in Agentic Translation Workflows
comment: 4 pages, 2 figures. Accepted to CSCW 2026 Demo. Code and demo video: https://github.com/hint-lab/deeptrans-studio, https://youtu.be/cNpafhHAEjg
summary: Professional translation is often a team-based process: translators, reviewers, and project managers must coordinate terminology, legal force, and accountability across documents. Yet many LLM-based translation tools treat human corrections as isolated edits. Expert decisions made in one segment or by one member are rarely captured as reusable knowledge for the rest of the team. We present DeepTrans Studio, a collaborative translation workspace that lets professionals intercept selected nodes in an agentic translation workflow, review evidence, revise AI outputs, and save approved decisions to a shared team memory. During the demo, attendees will role-play translators and reviewers, resolve preset terminology and legal-modal risks, and see how their decisions are propagated to downstream segments and surfaced in a teammate's workspace as reusable precedents. The demo illustrates how human interventions in AI-mediated work can become shared, traceable knowledge rather than one-off corrections.

AI.tldr: DeepTrans Studio is a collaborative translation workspace that captures human expert decisions as reusable, shared knowledge within an agentic translation workflow, enabling team-based terminology and legal consistency across documents.
AI.motivation: Professional translation is team-based (translators, reviewers, project managers) requiring coordination of terminology, legal force, and accountability, but existing LLM-based tools treat human corrections as isolated, non-reusable edits.
AI.method: DeepTrans Studio allows professionals to intercept nodes in an agentic workflow, review evidence, revise AI outputs, and save approved decisions to a shared team memory that propagates to downstream segments and teammates.
AI.result: In the demo, attendees role-play translators and reviewers, resolve terminology and legal-modal risks, and observe decisions propagate across segments and appear in teammates' workspaces as reusable precedents.
AI.conclusion: Human interventions in AI-mediated translation work can become shared, traceable knowledge rather than one-off corrections.

title: WARP: Whole-Body Retargeting for Learning from Offline Human Demonstrations
summary: Direct transfer from human demonstration to learnable robot action is a crucial step towards scalable whole-body mobile manipulation. While human data scales better than mobile teleoperation, it requires overcoming significant embodiment gaps. Existing retargeting methods yield imprecise or inconsistent solutions, causing action multi-modality that prevents supervised policies from reliably converging. We present Whole-body-Aware Retargeting from human Pose (WARP), an offline pipeline that explicitly models embodiment differences to extract precise, unique whole-body actions. WARP leverages a closed-form Shoulder-Elbow-Wrist (SEW) geometric solver for exact end-effector tracking while preserving whole-body structural intent. Paired with lazy mobile-base control, it extracts accurate, consistent robot trajectories. Evaluations show WARP provides highly reliable data for open-loop real-world replay. To our knowledge, WARP is the first framework to achieve zero-shot whole-body mobile manipulation directly from offline human demonstrations, eliminating the need for human-in-the-loop teleoperation action data. More details on https://warp-retarget.github.io/

AI.tldr: WARP is an offline retargeting pipeline that uses a closed-form SEW geometric solver and lazy mobile-base control to extract precise, unique whole-body robot actions from human pose demonstrations, enabling zero-shot whole-body mobile manipulation without teleoperation data.
AI.motivation: Existing retargeting methods for transferring human demonstrations to robot actions produce imprecise or inconsistent solutions, leading to action multi-modality that prevents supervised policies from converging reliably. The goal is to overcome embodiment gaps and enable scalable whole-body mobile manipulation without human-in-the-loop teleoperation.
AI.method: WARP (Whole-body-Aware Retargeting from human Pose) is an offline pipeline that explicitly models embodiment differences. It uses a closed-form Shoulder-Elbow-Wrist (SEW) geometric solver for exact end-effector tracking while preserving whole-body structural intent, combined with lazy mobile-base control to extract accurate, consistent robot trajectories.
AI.result: WARP provides highly reliable data for open-loop real-world replay. It is the first framework to achieve zero-shot whole-body mobile manipulation directly from offline human demonstrations, eliminating the need for human-in-the-loop teleoperation action data.
AI.conclusion: WARP enables scalable, precise whole-body mobile manipulation directly from offline human demonstrations by explicitly modeling embodiment gaps and using geometric solvers, removing the dependency on teleoperation data collection.

title: DEEPMED Search: An Open-Source Agentic Platform for Medical Deep Research with Introspective Verification
comment: 5 pages, 2 figures, 2 tables. Accepted to IJCAI-ECAI 2026 Demo Track. Project website: https://www.deepmedsearch.cloud. Demo video: https://youtu.be/4U4aok8yLpk
summary: Navigating the deluge of heterogeneous medical data, from academic literature (PubMed) to clinical guidelines (Web) and private knowledge bases, remains a critical bottleneck for evidence-based medicine. While commercial black-box tools lack transparency, standard open-source RAG implementations frequently suffer from reasoning drift when handling complex, long-tail queries. We present DEEPMED Search, a fully open-source, agentic platform designed for transparent medical deep research. Built on a high-performance Next.js architecture, DEEPMED Search features a source-adaptive router that autonomously dispatches sub-queries to PubMed, web search, or local graph-based knowledge bases based on information density. Crucially, the platform integrates an introspective verification module, powered by a causal-consistent multi-agent debate framework, to validate retrieved evidence against diagnostic logic before synthesis. To demonstrate its robustness, we showcase DEEPMED Search's ability to autonomously decompose high-difficulty rare disease queries, filter out confounding noise, and generate structured, citation-backed research reports in minutes. By open-sourcing this software, we provide the community with a robust infrastructure to democratize access to trustworthy, glass-box medical reasoning in research and prototyping settings.

AI.tldr: DEEPMED Search is an open-source, agentic medical deep research platform that uses a source-adaptive router and causal-consistent multi-agent debate to decompose complex queries, validate evidence, and generate structured, citation-backed reports across PubMed, web, and local knowledge bases.
AI.motivation: Existing commercial tools are black-box and lack transparency, while standard open-source RAG systems suffer from reasoning drift on complex, long-tail medical queries, creating a critical bottleneck for evidence-based medicine.
AI.method: A high-performance Next.js architecture with a source-adaptive router that dispatches sub-queries to PubMed, web, or local graph-based knowledge bases based on information density, plus an introspective verification module using a causal-consistent multi-agent debate framework to validate evidence against diagnostic logic before synthesis.
AI.result: The platform autonomously decomposes high-difficulty rare disease queries, filters confounding noise, and generates structured, citation-backed research reports in minutes.
AI.conclusion: By open-sourcing DEEPMED Search, the authors aim to democratize access to trustworthy, glass-box medical reasoning for research and prototyping.

title: Seeing Touch from Motion: A Unified Modality-Aware Visuo-Tactile Policy with Tactile Motion Correlation
summary: Visuo-Tactile policies leveraging optical tactile sensors have shown great promise in contact-rich manipulation. These sensors achieve high spatial resolution and multi-dimensional force sensing by utilizing an internal camera to monitor the deformation of their elastic gel surface, thereby indirectly inferring tactile cues. Despite their advantages, extracting fine-grained contact states necessary for contact-rich manipulation remains an open challenge. Existing methods typically use either raw images or cumulative motion fields to represent tactile cues. However, both are prone to perception ambiguity. Raw tactile images mainly capture appearance changes, while cumulative motion fields only reflect the aggregate gel deformation. Consequently, distinct fine-grained contact states can exhibit highly similar patterns, making it difficult to explicitly distinguish subtle contact variations. To address this issue, we explore the dynamic priors of tactile motion and discover that the correlation between transient and cumulative motion can explicitly distinguish fine-grained contact states. Based on this insight, we propose a motion-aware tactile representation to facilitate contact-rich manipulation. Beyond tactile representation, effective fusion of tactile and visual modalities is also critical. Most existing fusion methods either directly concatenate features from each modality or train modality-specific networks separately and fuse their outputs. However, these strategies struggle to simultaneously model cross-modal interactions and preserve modality-specific characteristics. In this work, we take advantage of the Mixture-of-Transformers architecture and propose a unified modality-aware visuo-tactile policy that captures cross-modal complementarity while maintaining modality-specific properties.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a motion-aware tactile representation using the correlation between transient and cumulative motion to distinguish fine-grained contact states, combined with a Mixture-of-Transformers architecture for unified visuo-tactile policy learning that preserves both cross-modal interactions and modality-specific properties in contact-rich manipulation.
AI.motivation: Existing tactile representations (raw images or cumulative motion fields) suffer from perception ambiguity where distinct fine-grained contact states produce similar patterns, making subtle contact variations difficult to distinguish for contact-rich manipulation.
AI.method: 1) A motion-aware tactile representation that leverages the correlation between transient and cumulative motion to explicitly distinguish fine-grained contact states. 2) A unified visuo-tactile policy based on Mixture-of-Transformers architecture that models cross-modal complementarity while preserving modality-specific properties.
AI.result: The proposed motion-aware tactile representation can explicitly distinguish fine-grained contact states that are ambiguous under raw images or cumulative motion fields alone. The Mixture-of-Transformers fusion effectively captures cross-modal interactions while maintaining modality-specific characteristics.
AI.conclusion: Leveraging dynamic priors of tactile motion (transient-cumulative correlation) provides a more discriminative tactile representation for contact-rich manipulation, and the modality-aware fusion architecture improves visuo-tactile policy learning over naive concatenation or separate modality-specific training.

title: Rethinking Generative Reconstruction Attacks against Graph Neural Network Models
