summary: The application of graph data in numerous disciplines raises the need for gathering and analyzing huge volumes of data, some of which is private and sensitive. The non-Euclidean nature of the graph data makes the analysis computationally challenging, leading to the use of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) in the age of AI. GNNs may inadvertently leak sensitive data they are trained on, which raises serious data security issues, including the model inversion attack. In this study, we analyze GNNs' vulnerabilities by introducing two novel graph inversion (i.e., reconstruction) attacks: graph-label conditioned (GLC) attack and embedding-label conditioned (ELC) attack, utilizing targetmodel predictions and their intermediate representations, respectively. We perform a comprehensive analysis of our introduced privacy attacks and compare them with existing baselines across three benchmark graph datasets (i.e., NCI1, PROTEINS, and AIDS) and four graph distributional/structural metrics (i.e., FGD, EGD, MMD, and GKS). Our work demonstrates that an adversary can use the generator-discriminator technique to reconstruct high-quality graphs in real-world black-box attack scenarios against GNNs. Additionally, we present a variant of our attacks (Ours--) with 50% reduced queries, achieving good or comparable reconstruction attack performance. In addition, we show that GNNs are highly vulnerable to privacy attacks, varying Laplacian noise-scales.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces two novel graph reconstruction attacks (GLC and ELC) against Graph Neural Networks, demonstrating that adversaries can reconstruct high-quality graphs using generator-discriminator techniques in black-box settings, with a query-efficient variant achieving comparable performance.
AI.motivation: Graph data is increasingly used across disciplines but contains sensitive information. GNNs, while computationally efficient for non-Euclidean graph data, may inadvertently leak private training data through model inversion attacks, raising serious data security concerns.
AI.method: Two novel graph inversion attacks: (1) Graph-label conditioned (GLC) attack using target model predictions, and (2) Embedding-label conditioned (ELC) attack using intermediate representations. Both employ a generator-discriminator framework. A query-efficient variant (Ours--) reduces queries by 50%. Evaluation uses three benchmark datasets (NCI1, PROTEINS, AIDS) and four metrics (FGD, EGD, MMD, GKS).
AI.result: The attacks successfully reconstruct high-quality graphs in real-world black-box scenarios. The query-efficient variant achieves good or comparable reconstruction performance with 50% fewer queries. GNNs show high vulnerability across varying Laplacian noise scales.
AI.conclusion: GNNs are highly vulnerable to privacy attacks, and adversaries can effectively reconstruct private graph data using the proposed methods, highlighting critical security risks in graph-based machine learning.

title: Heterogeneous Tactile Transformer
summary: Tactile sensors are inherently heterogeneous: a model trained on one sensor cannot be directly used on another, which limits learning contact-rich manipulation policies from diverse tactile data at scale. To bridge this gap, we propose the Heterogeneous Tactile Transformer (HTT), a framework that learns shared tactile representations across heterogeneous sensors. HTT consists of sensor-specific encoders and a shared transformer trunk, and is pretrained with per-modality masked reconstruction together with cross-modal alignment between paired sensors. Pretraining uses our novel Heterogeneous Paired Tactile (HPT) dataset, containing 1.6M synchronized paired frames across four vision- and array-based tactile sensors. Across distinct tactile perception and real-world manipulation tasks, HTT is shown to learn transferable representations that adapt to new tasks and previously unseen sensors. Dataset, code, and model checkpoints will be released upon publication at https://jxbi1010.github.io/htt-gh-page/.

AI.tldr: HTT is a framework that learns shared tactile representations across heterogeneous sensors via sensor-specific encoders, a shared transformer, masked reconstruction pretraining, and cross-modal alignment using a new 1.6M paired frame dataset (HPT), enabling transfer across different tactile sensors and tasks.
AI.motivation: Tactile sensors are inherently heterogeneous, so a model trained on one sensor cannot be directly transferred to another, limiting scalable learning of contact-rich manipulation policies from diverse tactile data.
AI.method: HTT uses sensor-specific encoders with a shared transformer trunk, pretrained via per-modality masked reconstruction and cross-modal alignment between paired sensors on the HPT dataset (1.6M synchronized paired frames across four vision- and array-based tactile sensors).
AI.result: HTT learns transferable representations that adapt to new tasks and previously unseen sensors across distinct tactile perception and real-world manipulation tasks.
AI.conclusion: HTT effectively bridges the gap between heterogeneous tactile sensors, enabling representation transfer and scalable learning for contact-rich manipulation.

title: CLQT: A Closed-Loop, Cost-Aware, Strategy-Consistent Benchmark for Diagnostic Evaluation of LLM Portfolio-Management Agents
summary: LLM agents are increasingly cast as autonomous portfolio managers, and benchmarks have moved from financial question-answering to sequential trading. Yet most still rank agents by returns over a fixed window -- a weak proxy, since a period's return is dominated by the market path and apparent alpha can dissolve once look-ahead leakage is controlled. Such a ranking certifies neither sound reasoning, nor a consistent strategy, nor a durable edge. We introduce CLQT, which reframes closed-loop trading evaluation as diagnosis rather than ranking: an instrument that localizes where and why an agent's process succeeds or fails. CLQT is a fully closed-loop, cost-aware, strategy-consistent, temporally-gated environment whose agents run a five-stage cycle: gather, synthesize, allocate, execute, reflect. Each round emits a complete DecisionRound sealed into a recompute-verifiable hash chain, so every metric is reconstructable from the trail. Six pillars form the substrate: a hard TimeGate, institutional transaction- and financing-cost modeling, strategy-consistency scoring, three-tier memory, a Model-Context-Protocol tool layer, and mandate-aware synthesis. The same agent runs as a constrained committee of specialized roles or a single full-autonomy orchestrator, making process scaffolding an experimental variable. From the audit trail we compute a five-axis capability scorecard (APM-CS: Coherence, Acuity, Composure, Discipline, Reliability), with Coherence judged partly by a held-out, out-of-cohort LLM to curb self-preference bias. We validate it on a contamination-controlled multi-model backtest with an ablation grid and a live broker track on unseen, post-cutoff data, against a repeated-run noise floor. CLQT separates outcome from capability, yielding not a model ranking but a durable, extensible map of agent competencies and limitations.

AI.tldr: CLQT reframes closed-loop trading agent evaluation from ranking-based to diagnostic-based, using a temporally-gated, cost-aware environment with a verifiable audit trail and a five-axis capability scorecard to localize where and why an agent's process succeeds or fails.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks rank LLM trading agents by returns over fixed windows, which is a weak proxy: returns are dominated by market path, apparent alpha vanishes after controlling for look-ahead leakage, and rankings certify neither sound reasoning, consistent strategy, nor durable edge.
AI.method: CLQT is a closed-loop, cost-aware, strategy-consistent, temporally-gated environment where agents follow a five-stage cycle (gather, synthesize, allocate, execute, reflect). Each round produces a DecisionRound sealed into a recompute-verifiable hash chain. Six pillars are used: TimeGate, institutional cost modeling, strategy-consistency scoring, three-tier memory, Model-Context-Protocol tool layer, mandate-aware synthesis. Agents run as either a constrained committee of specialized roles or a single orchestrator. A five-axis capability scorecard (APM-CS: Coherence, Acuity, Composure, Discipline, Reliability) is computed, with Coherence judged partly by a held-out, out-of-cohort LLM to mitigate self-preference bias.
AI.result: Validation is performed via a contamination-controlled multi-model backtest with an ablation grid and a live broker track on unseen post-cutoff data, against a repeated-run noise floor. CLQT separates outcome from capability, yielding a durable, extensible map of agent competencies and limitations rather than a model ranking.
AI.conclusion: CLQT reframes trading agent evaluation as diagnosis rather than ranking, providing a more robust and informative assessment of agent capabilities that goes beyond simple return-based metrics.

title: SIR: Structured Image Representations for Explainable Robot Learning
summary: Existing robot policies based on learned visual embeddings lack explicit structure and are sensitive to visual distractions. Thus, the representations that drive their behaviour are often opaque, making their decision-making process difficult to interpret. To address this, we introduce Structured Image Representations (SIR), a method that leverages Scene Graphs (SGs) as an intermediate representation for robot policy learning. Our approach first constructs a fully connected graph, using image-derived features as initial node representations. Then, a module learns to sparsify this graph end-to-end, creating a task-relevant sub-graph that is passed to the action generation model. This process makes our model intrinsically explainable. Evaluations on RoboCasa show that our sparse graph policies outperform image-based baselines on average with 19.5% vs 14.81% success rate. Most importantly, we show that the learned sparse graphs are a powerful tool for model analysis. By analysing when the model's sub-graph deviates from human expectation, such as by including distractor nodes or omitting key objects, we successfully uncover dataset biases, including spurious correlations and positional biases. https://github.com/intuitive-robots/SIR_Model

AI.tldr: SIR method uses Scene Graphs as intermediate representations for robot policy learning, creating task-relevant sparse sub-graphs that improve interpretability and performance (19.5% vs 14.81% success rate) while enabling detection of dataset biases.
AI.motivation: Existing robot policies based on learned visual embeddings lack explicit structure, are sensitive to visual distractions, and have opaque representations that make decision-making difficult to interpret.
AI.method: SIR first constructs a fully connected graph from image-derived features as initial node representations, then learns to sparsify this graph end-to-end to create a task-relevant sub-graph, which is passed to the action generation model.
AI.result: Sparse graph policies outperform image-based baselines on RoboCasa (19.5% vs 14.81% success rate). The learned sparse graphs effectively detect dataset biases by analyzing deviations from human expectations (e.g., distractor nodes, missing key objects).
AI.conclusion: SIR provides intrinsically explainable robot policies via structured intermediate representations, and the sparse graphs serve as a powerful tool for model analysis to uncover dataset biases like spurious correlations and positional biases.

title: The CRISTAL Method: Neurosymbolic analysis from AI-synthesized world models
summary: This project introduces the CRISTAL Method (Coherent Reliable Intentional Synthesis of Truthful Analysis Logic), a neurosymbolic framework for automating complex analysis workflows, with fundamental investment analysis as a primary use case. This domain poses major challenges: high structural uncertainty, noisy and subjective data, tight attention budgets, and the need for justified, reproducible decisions. Human analysts often struggle in this domain due to cognitive biases and limitations, suggesting significant value in automation. But while LLM-based agents have been proposed as analytical aids, their limitations -- poor numerical reasoning, unawareness of uncertainty, and lack of reproducibility -- hinder their effectiveness in this context. CRISTAL addresses these gaps through a principled blend of statistical model synthesis, continuous learning, and active learning. Starting from a natural-language prior knowledge curriculum, CRISTAL builds a dynamic, interpretable probabilistic program that enables full Bayesian inference, including uncertainty quantification and budget-aware data acquisition. CRISTAL continually refines its world model during analysis, leveraging LLMs for code synthesis and learning. We validate CRISTAL on a novel benchmark of synthetic equities with rich financial and textual data. On a company classification task, CRISTAL achieves Bayes-optimal accuracy with just 5 examples and a 5-second budget, outperforming state-of-the-art LLMs that plateau around 40\% accuracy even with order-of-magnitude more input data and compute.

AI.tldr: CRISTAL is a neurosymbolic framework that blends statistical model synthesis, continuous learning, and active learning to automate complex analysis workflows. It builds interpretable probabilistic programs from natural-language priors, enabling Bayesian inference with uncertainty quantification. Validated on synthetic equity classification, it achieves Bayes-optimal accuracy with just 5 examples and 5 seconds, outperforming LLMs that plateau at ~40% accuracy with far more data and compute.
AI.motivation: Complex analysis domains like fundamental investment suffer from high structural uncertainty, noisy/subjective data, tight attention budgets, and the need for justified, reproducible decisions. Human analysts are limited by cognitive biases, while LLM-based agents exhibit poor numerical reasoning, unawareness of uncertainty, and lack of reproducibility, motivating a more principled automated approach.
AI.method: CRISTAL uses a neurosymbolic approach: (1) starts from a natural-language prior knowledge curriculum, (2) builds a dynamic interpretable probabilistic program enabling full Bayesian inference with uncertainty quantification and budget-aware data acquisition, (3) continually refines its world model during analysis, (4) leverages LLMs for code synthesis and learning.
AI.result: On a synthetic equities company classification task, CRISTAL achieves Bayes-optimal accuracy using only 5 examples and a 5-second budget, while state-of-the-art LLMs plateau around 40% accuracy even with order-of-magnitude more input data and compute.
AI.conclusion: CRISTAL effectively addresses the gaps of LLM-based agents in complex analysis by combining probabilistic programming, active learning, and continuous refinement, achieving superior sample and computational efficiency with interpretable, uncertainty-aware outputs.

title: TacEvo: Self-Evolving Architecture Discovery for Robotic Tactile Perception via LLM-Driven Quality-Diversity Search
summary: Vision-based tactile sensing converts contact-induced surface deformation into images, enabling robots to infer contact forces and fine surface textures that are not accessible through conventional vision alone. However, tactile images are sensor- and physics-specific, so effective architectures often require expert intuition and extensive manual iteration. Existing neural architecture search (NAS) pipelines can reduce this burden, but they are often computationally expensive and restricted to hand-designed search spaces, which limits architectural novelty and diversity. We introduce TacEvo, a self-evolving architecture discovery framework that improves network designs from downstream feedback. TacEvo uses an LLM to generate code-level mutations and crossovers, and a MAP-Elites quality-diversity loop that preserves diverse elite architectures while preferentially reusing prompts that consistently yield improvements. Exploration is guided by two behavioural descriptors, Architectural Diversity and Efficiency Ratio, which encourage coverage across structural variations and compute-size trade-offs. On ViTacTip force regression and grating classification, TacEvo achieves high autonomous generation reliability (96.0%/94.5% trainable) and improves best validation fitness over 20 generations by 56.1%/96.1%. In a 20-seed post-search high-fidelity evaluation, TacEvo matches the expert baseline on force prediction and outperforms it on fine-grained grating classification. These results suggest that LLM-driven self-evolving search constitutes a practical paradigm for AI-assisted scientific discovery in specialised robotic sensing.

AI.tldr: TacEvo is a self-evolving neural architecture search framework that uses an LLM for code-level mutations and a MAP-Elites quality-diversity loop to automatically discover high-performance tactile sensing networks, achieving 96% generation reliability and up to 96.1% fitness improvement over 20 generations.
AI.motivation: Vision-based tactile sensing requires specialized neural architectures that are difficult to design manually; existing NAS methods are computationally expensive and limited by hand-designed search spaces, lacking architectural novelty and diversity.
AI.method: TacEvo uses an LLM to generate code-level mutations and crossovers of network architectures, combined with a MAP-Elites quality-diversity loop that preserves elite architectures guided by two behavioral descriptors: Architectural Diversity and Efficiency Ratio. The framework preferentially reuses prompts that consistently yield improvements.
AI.result: ViTacTip experiments show 96.0%/94.5% trainable generation reliability, 56.1%/96.1% best validation fitness improvement over 20 generations, and matching/exceeding expert baselines on force regression and fine-grained grating classification respectively.
AI.conclusion: LLM-driven self-evolving search constitutes a practical paradigm for AI-assisted scientific discovery in specialized robotic sensing domains like tactile perception.

title: Beyond Triplet Plausibility: Relation Set Completion in Knowledge Graphs
summary: Knowledge graphs (KGs) organize real-world knowledge as triplets and underpin many downstream applications. Due to their inherent incompleteness, knowledge graph completion (KGC) is widely studied and is typically formulated as triplet prediction, with link prediction as the dominant paradigm. However, this formulation focuses on the incompleteness of triplet-wise information and overlooks the incompleteness of entity-relation compatibility information. To address this limitation, we introduce a relation set completion task (RSC), which complements the link prediction task and aims to reason about missing relations that are semantically compatible with a given entity. We further propose a Relation Set Embedding model (RelSetE), which models latent patterns among the observed relations of entities to infer missing ones. To evaluate RelSetE, we derive three benchmark datasets from standard KG benchmarks. Extensive experiments demonstrate that RelSetE effectively captures entity-relation compatibility patterns and performs favorably in inferring missing relations of entities. Code and data are publicly available.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a Relation Set Completion task (RSC) to address incompleteness of entity-relation compatibility information in KGs, and proposes RelSetE, a model that captures latent patterns among observed relations to infer missing ones, achieving strong results on derived benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing KGC methods focus on triplet-level incompleteness via link prediction, but ignore the incompleteness of entity-relation compatibility information (i.e., which relations an entity should have).
AI.method: The authors propose Relation Set Embedding (RelSetE), which models latent patterns among observed relations of entities to infer missing semantically compatible relations. They also derive three benchmark datasets from standard KG benchmarks for evaluation.
AI.result: RelSetE effectively captures entity-relation compatibility patterns and performs favorably in inferring missing relations of entities.
AI.conclusion: The proposed RSC task complements link prediction, and RelSetE demonstrates strong capability in reasoning about missing relations compatible with entities, with code and data publicly released.

title: Automating the Design of Embodied AgentArchitectures
summary: Embodied agents are typically built as hand-designed compositions of perception, memory, planning, and action modules. This modularity exposes a large architectural design space, but current systems still rely on researcher intuition to choose where information is stored, how observations are processed, and how model calls are connected. Agent Architecture Search (AAS) automates such design for text-domain agents, but has not been systematically evaluated on perceptual embodied agents through simulator rollouts. We study this transfer. We introduce AgentCanvas, a typed-graph runtime that hosts embodied executors as editable node-and-wire programs with simulator-aware execution and episode-level logs, and KDLoop, a coding-agent search procedure that cycles through proposal, critique, experiment, and distillation, with triggered reflection after stalls. We evaluate three AAS variants across four embodied executors spanning vision-language navigation, embodied question answering, and language-conditioned manipulation. The resulting 3x4 matrix shows that architecture-level search can produce deployable and directional success-rate gains on embodied tasks, while one apparent high-scoring candidate is rejected as leak-bearing. At the same time, the experiments expose constraints that are muted in text-domain AAS: optimization signals can be masked by rollout noise, search can become trapped in local edit basins, and episode-level credit assignment only partially emerges even when detailed logs are available. These results characterize both the promise and the current limits of automated architecture search for embodied agents.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates the transfer of Agent Architecture Search (AAS) from text-domain agents to embodied agents, introducing AgentCanvas (a typed-graph runtime for embodied executors) and KDLoop (a coding-agent search procedure). Through a 3x4 evaluation matrix across three AAS variants and four embodied tasks (VLN, EQA, language-conditioned manipulation), they find architecture-level search can improve success rates but faces challenges including rollout noise, search plateaus, and limited credit assignment.
AI.motivation: Embodied agents are typically hand-designed with modular perception, memory, planning, and action components, but this exposes a large design space that relies on researcher intuition. While Agent Architecture Search (AAS) has automated such design for text-domain agents, it has not been systematically evaluated on perceptual embodied agents through simulator rollouts. The authors aim to study this transfer.
AI.method: The authors introduce AgentCanvas, a typed-graph runtime for embodied executors as editable node-and-wire programs with simulator-aware execution and episode-level logs, and KDLoop, a coding-agent search procedure that cycles through proposal, critique, experiment, and distillation with triggered reflection after stalls. They evaluate three AAS variants across four embodied executors spanning vision-language navigation, embodied question answering, and language-conditioned manipulation.
AI.result: The 3x4 evaluation matrix shows architecture-level search can produce deployable and directional success-rate gains on embodied tasks, though one apparent high-scoring candidate was rejected as leak-bearing. Constraints exposed include optimization signals masked by rollout noise, search trapped in local edit basins, and episode-level credit assignment only partially emerging despite detailed logs.
AI.conclusion: The results characterize both the promise and current limits of automated architecture search for embodied agents, showing feasibility of AAS transfer to embodied domains while highlighting unique challenges not present in text-domain AAS.

title: AI Training Manager: Bounded Closed-Loop Control of Adaptive Training Recipes
summary: We present the AI Training Manager, a bounded LLM-based supervisory controller for adaptive machine learning training. Standard training pipelines often rely on fixed recipes or single-axis schedulers, which can struggle with mid-run failures such as severe overfitting, loss imbalance, exploration collapse, or unsafe exploration. Rather than replacing mathematical optimizers or acting as an unconstrained coding agent, the manager operates through a schema-conditioned interface: it reads structured telemetry snapshots from an active run, audits a constrained action space, and returns validated updates to training parameters such as learning rate, regularization strength, loss-weight coefficients, and exploration settings. We evaluate this architecture across supervised language modeling and reinforcement learning. On TinyStories, the manager detects and corrects overfitting, achieving a validation loss 60% lower than the baseline while producing auditable intervention logs. In this supervised setting, we additionally show that manager inference does not need to block the training loop: training can continue while a manager response is pending, and validated updates can be applied asynchronously once available. In a robotic manipulation reinforcement-learning task, we use the same bounded decision interface in an episodic closed-loop setting, where manager updates are applied at evaluation or checkpoint boundaries. The manager mitigates both conservative and unsafe exploration regimes. These results suggest that schema-conditioned LLMs can serve as bounded supervisory managers for live training runs, complementing conventional optimizers and schedulers with interpretable, multi-axis intervention capabilities

AI.tldr: The paper presents AI Training Manager, a bounded LLM-based supervisory controller that reads structured telemetry from active training runs and returns validated parameter updates (learning rate, regularization, loss weights, exploration settings). Evaluated on TinyStories (supervised LM) and robotic RL, it corrects overfitting (60% lower validation loss), mitigates exploration issues, and supports asynchronous updates without blocking training.
AI.motivation: Standard training pipelines with fixed recipes or single-axis schedulers struggle with mid-run failures such as severe overfitting, loss imbalance, exploration collapse, or unsafe exploration.
AI.method: A schema-conditioned LLM interface that reads structured telemetry snapshots, audits a constrained action space, and returns validated updates to training parameters (learning rate, regularization, loss-weight coefficients, exploration settings). Supports both synchronous (RL episodic) and asynchronous (supervised LM) intervention modes without blocking training loops.
AI.result: On TinyStories, the manager achieves 60% lower validation loss than baseline with auditable logs. In robotic RL, it mitigates both conservative and unsafe exploration regimes.
AI.conclusion: Schema-conditioned LLMs can serve as bounded supervisory managers for live training runs, complementing conventional optimizers and schedulers with interpretable, multi-axis intervention capabilities.

title: SA-VLA: State-aware tokenizer for improving Vision-Language-Action Models' performance
summary: Discrete action tokenization provides a compact interface for autoregressive VLA policies, but accurately recovering continuous robot actions from discrete codes remains challenging. Existing tokenizers typically map each discrete code to a fixed continuous action prototype, ignoring the robot's current proprioceptive state. This limitation is particularly pronounced in manipulation, where the same action token may require different continuous controls under different joint configurations, object poses, and contact conditions. We therefore propose SA-VLA, a state-aware action tokenizer that conditions action decoding on robot state. We study two state-injection mechanisms for VQ-based action tokenization: cross-attention between state and action features, and a lightweight state adapter that predicts action-wise modulation factors for state-conditioned action modulation and reconstruction. The adapter formulation expands the effective support of a finite codebook by allowing each discrete token to represent a family of state-dependent continuous actions, while preserving the efficiency and compatibility of discrete action modeling. Integrated into an LLM-based VLA policy, SA-VLA supports both autoregressive and parallel action-token decoding with minimal changes to the model interface. On 12 RoboTwin manipulation tasks, SA-VLA improves the average success rate from 0.29 to 0.56 over the strongest tokenizer baseline. In zero-shot sim-to-real experiments on three real-world tasks, it further improves average success from 0.15 to 0.33 over the strongest tokenizer baseline. These results demonstrate that state-conditioned action decoding is a simple and effective mechanism for reducing the compression gap in discrete VLA policies.

AI.tldr: SA-VLA introduces a state-aware action tokenizer for VLA policies that conditions action decoding on robot proprioceptive state, improving discrete-to-continuous action recovery and achieving significant gains on manipulation tasks (0.29→0.56 success on RoboTwin, 0.15→0.33 in sim-to-real).
AI.motivation: Existing discrete action tokenizers map each code to a fixed continuous prototype, ignoring the robot's proprioceptive state (joint configurations, object poses, contact conditions). This creates a compression gap that hurts manipulation accuracy, as the same action token may require different continuous controls under different states.
AI.method: SA-VLA proposes two state-injection mechanisms for VQ-based action tokenization: (1) cross-attention between state and action features, and (2) a lightweight state adapter that predicts action-wise modulation factors for state-conditioned action reconstruction. The adapter expands the effective support of a finite codebook by letting each token represent a family of state-dependent continuous actions, while maintaining discrete modeling efficiency.
AI.result: On 12 RoboTwin manipulation tasks, SA-VLA improves average success rate from 0.29 to 0.56 over the strongest tokenizer baseline. In zero-shot sim-to-real on three real-world tasks, it improves average success from 0.15 to 0.33.
AI.conclusion: State-conditioned action decoding is a simple and effective mechanism for reducing the compression gap in discrete VLA policies, enabling better continuous action recovery from discrete codes with minimal architectural changes.

title: SafePyramid: A Hierarchical Benchmark for In-context Policy Guardrailing
summary: In real-world applications, guardrails are often expected to identify unsafe user-model interactions according to application-specific safety policies, rather than relying on predefined risk taxonomies. In this work, we study this setting under the paradigm of in-context policy guardrailing, where guardrails predict safety violations based on policy specifications provided in context. To systematically evaluate this capability, we introduce SafePyramid, a safety benchmark comprising 1,000 multi-turn conversations across 10 domains and 3,000 corresponding application-specific policies, which together contain 61,699 distinct natural-language rules. SafePyramid organizes the evaluation into three difficulty levels: L0 evaluates individual-rule understanding, L1 evaluates reasoning over rule dependencies, and L2 evaluates adaptation of full novel policy frameworks defined in context. To ensure benchmark quality, we employ a rigorous multi-stage pipeline to construct and validate the benchmark. Using SafePyramid, we evaluate 10 frontier LLMs and 5 policy-configurable guardrails and find that in-context policy guardrailing remains highly challenging: even the best-performing model, GPT-5.5, exactly identifies the full set of violated rules in only 54.0%, 35.3%, and 12.9% cases on L0, L1, and L2, respectively. These results highlight the limitations of current guardrails and call for stronger in-context policy guardrails that can reliably execute policies, resolve rule dependencies, and adapt to novel policy frameworks.

AI.tldr: SafePyramid is a benchmark with 1,000 multi-turn conversations, 3,000 policies, and 61,699 rules across 10 domains, evaluating in-context policy guardrailing at three difficulty levels. Even the best model (GPT-5.5) achieves only 54.0%, 35.3%, and 12.9% accuracy on L0, L1, and L2, showing this task remains highly challenging.
AI.motivation: Real-world guardrails need to enforce application-specific safety policies beyond predefined risk taxonomies, motivating the need for in-context policy guardrailing where models reason over policies provided in context.
AI.method: The authors construct SafePyramid using a rigorous multi-stage pipeline, creating 1,000 multi-turn conversations, 3,000 policies, and 61,699 rules across 10 domains, with evaluation at three difficulty levels: L0 (individual rules), L1 (rule dependencies), and L2 (novel policy frameworks).
AI.result: 10 frontier LLMs and 5 policy-configurable guardrails were evaluated. GPT-5.5 performed best but only exactly identified violated rules in 54.0% (L0), 35.3% (L1), and 12.9% (L2) of cases, revealing severe limitations.
AI.conclusion: In-context policy guardrailing remains highly challenging; current guardrails struggle to reliably execute policies, resolve rule dependencies, and adapt to novel frameworks, calling for stronger solutions.

title: AERIS: Aerial-Edge Role-Driven Intelligence at Runtime via Orchestrated Language-Model Swarm
comment: 10 pages, 11 figures. Preprint version of the submitted manuscript
summary: Integrating large language models into robotic systems holds promise for enhancing autonomy, yet practical deployment remains constrained by strict heartbeat-constrained scheduling and limited computational power. We propose AERIS: an edge deployment framework for aerial platforms. It organizes dedicated small language models combined with lightweight perception and control modules into roles that can be instantiated at runtime, and dynamically rebinds them across different executors as resources change, thereby pushing intelligent capabilities to the edge. AERIS achieves long-horizon instruction decomposition through an attention-subgoal alignment mechanism, which involves annotating the currently active instruction step in messages, thereby progressively approaching long-term objectives. We evaluate AERIS on a high-fidelity UAV Vision-and-Language Navigation benchmark. Under a heartbeat-timed execution mechanism, AERIS maintains a stable perception-decision-control loop between a low-frequency planner and a high-frequency controller, supporting real-time closed-loop operation. We further validate its deployability through two real-world experiments focused on planning and fast response. A demonstration video is provided in the supplementary materials.

AI.tldr: AERIS is an edge deployment framework for aerial platforms that integrates small language models with lightweight modules through role-based instantiation and dynamic rebinding, using attention-subgoal alignment for long-horizon tasks. It achieves stable real-time closed-loop operation under heartbeat-timed execution, validated on UAV VLN benchmarks and real-world experiments.
AI.motivation: Integrating LLMs into robotic systems (especially aerial platforms) is promising but faces constraints from heartbeat-constrained scheduling and limited edge computational power, creating a gap between intelligent capabilities and practical deployment.
AI.method: AERIS organizes dedicated small language models with lightweight perception/control modules into instantiable roles that dynamically rebind across executors as resources change. It uses attention-subgoal alignment to annotate active instruction steps in messages for long-horizon decomposition, and operates under a heartbeat-timed mechanism with a low-frequency planner and high-frequency controller in a stable perception-decision-control loop.
AI.result: Evaluated on a high-fidelity UAV VLN benchmark, AERIS maintains stable real-time closed-loop operation under heartbeat-timed execution. It was further validated through two real-world experiments focused on planning and fast response.
AI.conclusion: AERIS effectively pushes intelligent capabilities to the edge for aerial robots by dynamically managing small language models and lightweight modules, enabling practical deployment under strict real-time scheduling constraints.

title: A causal modeling perspective on decision theory
summary: Decision theory provides a formal framework for how agents should make choices under uncertainty, drawing on ideas from philosophy, probability, and causality. Despite significant progress, the field still lacks a unified modeling language, and key concepts - such as the distinction between subjective and objective elements, or what it means for a decision theory to perform well - are often left implicit. This can make it difficult to evaluate and compare competing theories, particularly in controversial cases. In this paper, we address these issues by introducing a formal framework for decision theory based on nonparametric structural equation models (NPSEMs), a well-established tool in causal inference. NPSEMs provide a unified foundation for representing agents, counterfactuals, and causal relationships, allowing for unambiguous definitions of EDT and CDT. Building on this foundation, we propose a novel decision theory - personal decision theory - which instructs agents to maximize a subjective model of their own counterfactual utility. We introduce a formal performance metric based on hypothetical interventions that enforce a given decision theory across a population - such as might be achieved through education or policy -- and show that, under certain assumptions, personal decision theory is optimal with respect to this metric. Throughout, we use the smoking lesion problem as a running example and conclude with a formal analysis of Newcomb's problem. Our aim is to provide decision theory with a clearer modeling language and firmer evaluative ground, thereby enabling more rigorous comparisons and facilitating conceptual progress in the field.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a formal framework for decision theory using nonparametric structural equation models (NPSEMs) to unify representations of agents, counterfactuals, and causality. It proposes "personal decision theory" — maximizing a subjective model of one's own counterfactual utility — and shows it is optimal under a population-level intervention-based performance metric.
AI.motivation: Decision theory lacks a unified modeling language; key concepts like subjective vs. objective elements and performance criteria are often implicit, hindering rigorous evaluation and comparison of competing theories.
AI.method: The authors use nonparametric structural equation models (NPSEMs) from causal inference as a unified foundation to represent agents, counterfactuals, and causal relationships, enabling unambiguous definitions of EDT and CDT. They then propose personal decision theory and introduce a formal performance metric based on hypothetical interventions that enforce a given decision theory across a population.
AI.result: Personal decision theory is shown to be optimal under the proposed population-level intervention-based performance metric, given certain assumptions. The framework is demonstrated on the smoking lesion problem and Newcomb's problem.
AI.conclusion: The work provides decision theory with a clearer modeling language and firmer evaluative ground, enabling more rigorous comparisons and facilitating conceptual progress in the field.

title: Self-supervised Geometry Reasoning for LiDAR Simultaneous Localization and Mapping
summary: LiDAR simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) relies on local geometric quantities such as covariances, correspondences, and surface structures. However, most existing pipelines rely on hand-crafted estimates of local geometry and use them as fixed inputs to LiDAR SLAM, which can make the estimated local geometry noisy and unstable in sparse regions of a point cloud or when using low-resolution LiDAR. To address this issue, this paper introduces a self-supervised framework that learns an explicit symbolic representation of local geometry and uses it to improve LiDAR SLAM recursively. Specifically, each point is represented as a Gaussian distribution, allowing local geometry to be described by a covariance. Without dense geometry labels or ground-truth poses, the framework learns by maximizing the likelihood of local geometry, with self-supervision derived from consistency relations over symbolic geometric representations, including predicted covariances, correspondences, and trajectory from SLAM. The learned geometry is then fed back into LiDAR SLAM, forming a reciprocal loop in which improved geometry enhances localization and mapping, and improved localization provides cleaner supervision for subsequent geometry reasoning. This framework is backend-agnostic and can be plugged into existing LiDAR SLAM pipelines without architectural changes. Experiments on KITTI under varying LiDAR resolutions show that the proposed method improves both odometry and global registration.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a self-supervised framework that learns explicit symbolic representations of local geometry (modeled as Gaussian distributions/covariances) and uses them to improve LiDAR SLAM recursively by maximizing likelihood of local geometry via consistency relations, forming a reciprocal loop between geometry learning and SLAM that is backend-agnostic.
AI.motivation: Existing LiDAR SLAM pipelines rely on hand-crafted estimates of local geometry (covariances, correspondences, surface structures), which are noisy and unstable in sparse point cloud regions or when using low-resolution LiDAR.
AI.method: A self-supervised framework representing each point as a Gaussian distribution to describe local geometry via covariance. It learns by maximizing likelihood of local geometry without dense labels or ground-truth poses, using self-supervision from consistency relations over predicted covariances, correspondences, and trajectory. The learned geometry is fed back into SLAM in a reciprocal loop. It is backend-agnostic and pluggable into existing pipelines.
AI.result: Experiments on KITTI under varying LiDAR resolutions show improved odometry and global registration compared to baselines.
AI.conclusion: The self-supervised learning of local geometry representations effectively improves LiDAR SLAM performance, especially under sparse or low-resolution conditions, and the framework is flexible enough to integrate into existing SLAM pipelines.

title: HippoSpark: An On-Demand Experience System for LLM Reasoning
summary: Distilling historical trajectories into reusable experience to enhance future problem-solving has become a focal point of recent LLM research. However, existing methods predominantly operate at the task level, leveraging general summaries or rules under the assumption that analogous tasks share universal solution patterns. This approach often fails in complex reasoning, which typically falters at local bottlenecks that require precise, state-specific guidance rather than broad heuristics. We introduce HippoSpark, a state-level experience system that performs on-demand retrieval tailored to the immediate needs of the current reasoning state. Across mathematical, scientific, and programming benchmarks, HippoSpark consistently outperforms both standard prompting and task-level experience baselines. Our findings reveal that the most effective experience systems are those that provide actionable guidance at critical bottlenecks rather than serving as generic task-level context. Our code is available at https://github.com/DanlingMeng/HippoSpark.

AI.tldr: HippoSpark is a state-level experience system that retrieves on-demand guidance for specific reasoning states, outperforming standard prompting and task-level experience across math, science, and programming benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing task-level experience systems fail in complex reasoning because they provide only broad heuristics, whereas complex reasoning falters at local bottlenecks requiring precise, state-specific guidance.
AI.method: HippoSpark performs on-demand retrieval of state-level experience tailored to the immediate needs of the current reasoning state, rather than relying on task-level summaries or rules.
AI.result: HippoSpark consistently outperforms both standard prompting and task-level experience baselines across mathematical, scientific, and programming benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: The most effective experience systems provide actionable guidance at critical bottlenecks rather than serving as generic task-level context.

title: KYON: Semi-Modular Wheel-Legged Quadruped With Agile Bimanual Capability
summary: This paper presents KYON, a hybrid wheel-legged quadruped robot equipped with a bimanual upper body for loco-manipulation tasks. The platform features a semi-modular design with a reconfigurable lower legs, enabling both wheeled and legged locomotion depending on the environment. A design approach that places actuators in the base and uses transmission mechanisms reduces distal inertia, improving agility and dynamic performance. The robot integrates a whole-body control framework together with a reinforcement learning based policy to handle nonlinear dynamics and enhance robustness to disturbances for the execution of locomotion and manipulation tasks, independently. Experimental results demonstrate effective dynamic locomotion and bimanual manipulation, validating the platform's capability to operate in complex and unstructured scenarios.

AI.tldr: KYON is a hybrid wheel-legged quadruped robot with a bimanual upper body for loco-manipulation, featuring semi-modular reconfigurable legs, distal inertia reduction via base-mounted actuators, and a whole-body control framework with RL-based policy for robust locomotion and manipulation in complex environments.
AI.motivation: To create a hybrid wheel-legged quadruped platform with bimanual manipulation capabilities that can operate effectively in complex and unstructured scenarios by combining dynamic locomotion and manipulation.
AI.method: Semi-modular design with reconfigurable lower legs for wheeled/legged locomotion; base-mounted actuators with transmission mechanisms to reduce distal inertia; whole-body control framework integrated with reinforcement learning-based policy for handling nonlinear dynamics and disturbance robustness.
AI.result: Effective dynamic locomotion and bimanual manipulation demonstrated; platform validated for operation in complex and unstructured scenarios.
AI.conclusion: The KYON platform successfully combines hybrid locomotion with bimanual manipulation capabilities, validated through experimental results in challenging environments.

title: SAGA: Scene-Aware, Goal-Evolving Agents for Long-Horizon CivRealm Strategy Planning
summary: Long-horizon strategic planning in complex strategy games demands concurrent reasoning across multiple decision domains under imperfect information and sparse reward. Existing LLM-based agents suffer from three systematic failures: scene blindness from raw tile coordinates, context overflow and domain coupling from monolithic state dumps, and shallow cross-game learning that treats each episode in isolation. We present SAGA, an LLM multi-agent framework with three mechanisms each directly targeting one class of failure: (i) a Map-Semantic Scene Graph that encodes typed spatial relations among game entities into per-unit natural-language context, resolving spatial blindness without global token inflation; (ii) a Tool-Augmented Planner that pulls fine-grained domain state on demand and dispatches per-domain directives to dedicated specialist controllers, eliminating context overflow, domain coupling, and mechanical constraint violations; and (iii) a Dual-Horizon Feedback Loop that combines periodic within-game goal generation with structured cross-game causal post-mortem, enabling principled strategic evolution without manual reward engineering. Evaluated on FreeCiv, SAGA attains the highest mean civilization score -- the environment's sole sparse objective reward -- with lower variance than the two strongest baselines, and is the only method that significantly surpasses every baseline on infrastructure construction, the resource axis most readily sacrificed under multi-objective conflict. It outscores the two strongest baselines in most head-to-head games while cutting output tokens (the dominant decoding cost) by 27%. Equipped with the cross-game evolution module, SAGA reaches the highest end-of-chain score across five successive episodes. Ablation studies confirm that each architectural component contributes independently to this advantage.

AI.tldr: SAGA is an LLM multi-agent framework for long-horizon strategic planning in complex games, featuring Map-Semantic Scene Graph, Tool-Augmented Planner, and Dual-Horizon Feedback Loop to address scene blindness, context overflow/domain coupling, and shallow cross-game learning respectively. It achieves state-of-the-art performance on FreeCiv with higher scores, lower variance, and 27% fewer output tokens.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon strategic planning in complex strategy games requires concurrent multi-domain reasoning under imperfect information and sparse rewards. Existing LLM-based agents suffer from three systematic failures: scene blindness from raw coordinates, context overflow and domain coupling from monolithic state dumps, and shallow cross-game learning that treats each episode in isolation.
AI.method: SAGA consists of three mechanisms: (1) Map-Semantic Scene Graph encoding typed spatial relations into per-unit natural-language context; (2) Tool-Augmented Planner that pulls domain state on demand and dispatches per-domain directives to specialist controllers; (3) Dual-Horizon Feedback Loop combining periodic within-game goal generation with structured cross-game causal post-mortem for strategic evolution.
AI.result: On FreeCiv, SAGA achieves the highest mean civilization score with lower variance than two strongest baselines, is the only method significantly surpassing all baselines on infrastructure construction, outscores strongest baselines in most head-to-head games, cuts output tokens by 27%, and reaches the highest end-of-chain score across five episodes with the cross-game evolution module.
AI.conclusion: Each architectural component contributes independently to SAGA's advantage, and the framework effectively addresses all three identified failure modes of existing LLM-based agents for strategic planning.

title: ConCent: Contact-Centric Real-to-Sim-to-Real Learning from One Demonstration
summary: Sim-to-real policy transfer -- deploying policies trained in simulation in the real world -- is a promising paradigm for scaling robot manipulation without large-scale real-world data. However, transferring simulation-trained policies remains challenging due to discrepancies in contact dynamics -- particularly in contact-rich tasks where subtle differences can alter task outcomes entirely. Because interaction between the manipulated object and the environment is mediated through contact, task success depends on accurately reproducing task-relevant contacts. Accordingly, in manipulation, contact-centric fidelity -- reproducing both the contact event sequence (when, where, and how contacts occur) and the local contact dynamics (how forces and motions evolve at each contact) -- is a necessary condition for task success. Based on this insight, we propose a contact-centric real-to-sim-to-real RL framework that uses task-relevant contact event sequences extracted from real demonstrations as the learning objective. We approximate objects as groups of primitives and optimize their contact geometry in simulation so that the resulting local contact dynamics explain the observed state transitions. The contact event sequence is automatically extracted by replaying the demonstration. This sequence serves as a structured reward signal, guiding the policy toward physically plausible contact regimes validated in reality and preventing exploitation of unrealistic simulator contacts. The signal is obtained automatically, requiring no per-task reward design. Experiments on contact-rich manipulation tasks demonstrate more stable and robust sim-to-real policy transfer compared to unconstrained RL baselines.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a contact-centric real-to-sim-to-real RL framework that uses contact event sequences extracted from real demonstrations as structured reward signals to improve sim-to-real policy transfer for contact-rich manipulation tasks.
AI.motivation: Sim-to-real policy transfer in contact-rich manipulation fails because subtle discrepancies in contact dynamics between simulation and reality completely alter task outcomes. Existing methods lack a principled way to ensure contact-centric fidelity—reproducing both the contact event sequence and local contact dynamics.
AI.method: The framework extracts task-relevant contact event sequences from real demonstrations automatically. It approximates objects as groups of primitives and optimizes their contact geometry in simulation so that local contact dynamics explain observed state transitions. The extracted contact sequence serves as a structured reward signal for RL, preventing exploitation of unrealistic simulator contacts without requiring per-task reward design.
AI.result: Experiments on contact-rich manipulation tasks demonstrate more stable and robust sim-to-real policy transfer compared to unconstrained RL baselines.
AI.conclusion: Contact-centric fidelity is a necessary condition for task success in manipulation; using contact event sequences as reward signals enables more reliable sim-to-real transfer without manual reward engineering.

title: First-Order Temporal Logic Tensor Networks
summary: Most of the existing neuro-symbolic AI methods focus on the scenario of static knowledge where objects do not change according to a temporal dimension. Temporal neuro-symbolic works are still under explored and are mainly developed for time-interval logic or propositional linear temporal logic. There is a lack of models studying linear temporal logics with predicates that deal with objects whose properties and relations change through the time. We present First-Order Temporal Logic Tensor Networks (FOT-LTN) that is an extension of Logic Tensor Networks (LTN) that fills this gap by considering a linear-temporal dimension. In particular, FOT-LTN joins the syntax of First-Order Linear Temporal Logic with the fuzzy (and real-valued) semantics of LTN obtaining a framework that supports both temporal operators and quantifiers and is totally differentiable. A first evaluation regards a temporal knowledge graph completion task on two synthetic datasets showing better performance of FOT-LTN with respect to dedicated (purely neural) methods.

AI.tldr: FOT-LTN extends Logic Tensor Networks with first-order linear temporal logic to handle dynamic objects and relations over time, showing better performance on temporal knowledge graph completion tasks than purely neural methods.
AI.motivation: Existing neuro-symbolic AI methods focus on static knowledge and lack models for linear temporal logics with predicates that handle objects whose properties and relations change over time.
AI.method: FOT-LTN extends Logic Tensor Networks (LTN) by integrating First-Order Linear Temporal Logic syntax with fuzzy real-valued semantics, supporting both temporal operators and quantifiers in a fully differentiable framework.
AI.result: On two synthetic temporal knowledge graph completion datasets, FOT-LTN achieves better performance compared to dedicated purely neural methods.
AI.conclusion: FOT-LTN successfully bridges the gap in temporal neuro-symbolic AI by enabling differentiable reasoning over dynamic objects and relations in a first-order linear temporal logic setting.

title: ActiveVital: Geometry-Aware Embodied Vital Signs Monitoring for Home Healthcare Robots
summary: Home robots require reliable vital signs monitoring to support long-term companionship and safety in daily environments, yet obtaining respiration and heart rate without physical contact remains challenging in unconstrained home settings. Millimeter-wave (mmWave) radar offers a promising solution due to its phase sensitivity to sub-millimeter motions. However, mmWave measurements are fundamentally constrained by observation geometry, since only the radial component of motion is observable. Consequently, arbitrary robot-human orientations often introduce angular misalignment that destabilizes vital signs estimation. To address this limitation, we reformulate vital signs monitoring from passive signal recovery to active geometric regulation. We propose ActiveVital, a vision-guided sensing framework that treats sensing geometry as an explicit control variable for robots. It localizes the chest anchor via visual keypoints and converts alignment errors into control commands. This steers the robot-mounted radar toward near-normal incidence to the thoracic surface, maximizing radial observability within a perception-action loop. A differential phase enhancement module further stabilizes signal extraction under motion. Experiments show that ActiveVital reduces respiration interval error from 0.87 s to 0.14 s and heart rate error from 13.59 bpm to 2.22 bpm, achieving accuracy comparable to controlled static sensing while remaining robust under unconstrained robot-human configurations.

AI.tldr: ActiveVital is a vision-guided robotic framework that actively adjusts mmWave radar orientation to achieve near-normal chest incidence, reducing respiration error from 0.87s to 0.14s and heart rate error from 13.59 bpm to 2.22 bpm in unconstrained home settings.
AI.motivation: Home robots need contactless vital signs monitoring, but mmWave radar is limited by observation geometry—only radial motion is observable, and arbitrary robot-human orientations cause angular misalignment that destabilizes estimation.
AI.method: ActiveVital reformulates sensing from passive signal recovery to active geometric regulation: it uses visual keypoints to localize the chest anchor, converts alignment errors into control commands to steer the robot-mounted radar toward near-normal chest incidence, and employs a differential phase enhancement module to stabilize signal extraction under motion.
AI.result: Respiration interval error reduced from 0.87 s to 0.14 s; heart rate error reduced from 13.59 bpm to 2.22 bpm; accuracy comparable to controlled static sensing under unconstrained robot-human configurations.
AI.conclusion: Treating sensing geometry as a control variable within a perception-action loop effectively overcomes the geometric constraints of mmWave radar for vital signs monitoring in dynamic home environments.

title: Exploration and Online Transfer with Behavioral Foundation Models
summary: Zero-shot Transfer in Reinforcement Learning (RL) aims to train an agent that can generate optimal policies for any reward function, without additional learning at transfer time, while training only on reward-free trajectories. For their generality over tasks, such models are sometimes called ``Behavioral Foundation Models'' (BFMs). While they have shown strong performances and improvements in recent years, the current framework and algorithms still assume that, during the transfer phase, the agent is informed offline about the reward (the task to solve) through a dataset of state-reward pairs, which it uses to pick the best policy to deploy. However, in practice if the reward is a black-box (e.g. direct user feedback), it is not possible to generate such a dataset: it is necessary to observe the reward through interactions with the environment. In other words, the current framework of offline transfer is not aligned with the traditional RL setting of online learning through trial-and-error, which requires exploration in order to find rewards. This paper proposes to tackle this new online transfer in zero-shot RL, with the key insight that the BFM itself can be used to generate exploration policies. We show that it is possible to frame this online learning problem in terms of a bandit-like exploration-exploitation problem. More precisely, at each step the bandit algorithm recommends a policy, the BFM executes it in the environment, which yields a reward and a new state; we repeat the process until we converge to the optimal policy. In the popular context of linear reward approximation, we derive a formulation inspired by Upper Confidence Bound and show that exploration can be achieved through the minimization of the eigenvalues of an uncertainty matrix. We evaluate qualitatively and quantitatively our framework on a simple environment to validate the concept of our method.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a framework for online transfer in zero-shot RL, where a Behavioral Foundation Model (BFM) trained on reward-free trajectories is used to generate exploration policies via a bandit-like algorithm, handling black-box reward functions without offline reward datasets.
AI.motivation: Current zero-shot RL assumes offline reward datasets for transfer, but in practice rewards can be black-box (e.g., direct user feedback), requiring online interaction and exploration. The paper aims to align zero-shot RL with the traditional online RL setting of trial-and-error learning.
AI.method: The authors frame online transfer as a bandit-like exploration-exploitation problem where a BFM generates policies, and a bandit algorithm recommends a policy at each step. In the linear reward approximation setting, they derive an Upper Confidence Bound-inspired formulation where exploration is achieved by minimizing eigenvalues of an uncertainty matrix.
AI.result: The framework is evaluated qualitatively and quantitatively on a simple environment, validating the concept of using the BFM itself for exploration in online zero-shot RL transfer.
AI.conclusion: The paper introduces a new online transfer setting for zero-shot RL that removes the offline reward dataset assumption, leveraging BFMs for exploration through bandit algorithms, with promising initial validation.

title: X-Morph: Human Motion Priors for Scalable Robot Learning Across Morphologies
summary: Recent progress in humanoid behavior models has been driven in large part by abundant human motion data, but comparable motion data is scarce for non-humanoid legged robots such as quadrupeds, hexapods, and quadruped manipulators. A promising alternative is to repurpose human motion across embodiments; however, direct retargeting often produces motions that are visually plausible yet physically inconsistent or difficult to track under robot dynamics. We present X-Morph, a human-motion-to-robot-behavior pipeline that converts human motion into deployable locomotion and loco-manipulation policies for diverse non-humanoid legged morphologies. A cross-morphology retargeting stage converts human motions into kinematically plausible, intent-preserving robot references, which are then tracked by a privileged RL policy and distilled into a causal student policy. We evaluate X-Morph on three morphologically distinct platforms: a quadruped, a hexapod, and a quadruped equipped with a manipulator. The resulting policies track diverse retargeted motions, generalize to unseen human motions, and support downstream use cases including video-based teleoperation, behavior-prior control, and text-conditioned motion generation. These results suggest that large-scale human motion can serve as a substrate for learning broad, reusable behavior priors beyond humanoid robots. Project page: https://maker-rat.github.io/morph/

AI.tldr: X-Morph converts human motion into deployable locomotion and manipulation policies for diverse non-humanoid legged robots (quadrupeds, hexapods, quadruped manipulators) via cross-morphology retargeting and RL-based policy learning.
AI.motivation: Human motion data is abundant but scarce for non-humanoid legged robots; direct retargeting produces physically inconsistent motions under robot dynamics.
AI.method: Cross-morphology retargeting converts human motion into kinematically plausible robot references, tracked by a privileged RL policy, then distilled into a causal student policy.
AI.result: Policies track diverse retargeted motions, generalize to unseen human motions, and enable video-based teleoperation, behavior-prior control, and text-conditioned motion generation across three distinct morphologies.
AI.conclusion: Large-scale human motion can serve as a substrate for learning broad, reusable behavior priors beyond humanoid robots.

title: Be Faithful When Response: Returning Fluent and Grounded Answers for Vision-Language Models Reinforcement Learning
summary: Reinforcement Learning (RL) is an important paradigm for improving the reasoning capabilities of Vision-Language Models (VLMs). However, directly applying RL to rollout multimodal reasoning can lead to instability, due to the exploitation of language priors, the neglect of visual evidence, and the generation of reasoning traces that are fluent yet not visually grounded. The question arises: Can initially steer the policy toward visually faithful reasoning regime before applying reinforcement learning? To this end, we propose a Faithful Warm-Start (FWS) strategy that first curates samples with explicit vision-language causal relationships from six general VQA benchmarks to construct the FaithfulQA dataset, where each of the image-question pairs gains a certain degree of visual observations, question requirements, commonsense knowledge, domain knowledge, and the final answer. Subsequently, a VLM-based judge is employed to further purify the dataset, ensuring strong causal consistency and visual faithfulness. This warm-start stage equips the model with the capability to understand causally grounded vision-language patterns before subsequent RL optimization under sparse answer-level rewards. Experimental results show that such faithful supervision improves answer accuracy, stabilizes RL training, and reduces visually unsupported reasoning.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a Faithful Warm-Start (FWS) strategy that pre-trains Vision-Language Models on a curated FaithfulQA dataset with explicit vision-language causal relationships before applying Reinforcement Learning, improving answer accuracy, stabilizing RL training, and reducing visually unsupported reasoning.
AI.motivation: Directly applying Reinforcement Learning to Vision-Language Models for multimodal reasoning leads to instability due to exploitation of language priors, neglect of visual evidence, and generation of reasoning traces that are fluent but not visually grounded.
AI.method: (1) Construct FaithfulQA dataset by curating samples with explicit vision-language causal relationships from six general VQA benchmarks, covering visual observations, question requirements, commonsense knowledge, domain knowledge, and final answers. (2) Use a VLM-based judge to further purify the dataset for strong causal consistency and visual faithfulness. (3) Apply this faithful warm-start before subsequent RL optimization under sparse answer-level rewards.
AI.result: The faithful supervision improves answer accuracy, stabilizes RL training, and reduces visually unsupported reasoning compared to directly applying RL to multimodal reasoning.
AI.conclusion: Warm-starting the policy toward visually faithful reasoning before RL optimization is an effective strategy to mitigate instability and improve the quality of multimodal reasoning in VLMs.

title: CSAR: Containerized System Architecture for Robotics
summary: Robotic applications increasingly rely on distributed computational infrastructures that combine embedded devices, edge servers, and cloud resources. This evolution, together with the collaborative nature of robotics projects, has made the development, integration, deployment, and long-term operation of robotic systems significantly more complex. In practice, multi-user robotics software teams face persistent challenges related to dependency isolation, compatibility, reproducibility, efficient sharing of specialized hardware, and deployment across heterogeneous environments. In this paper, we present CSAR (Containerized System Architecture for Robotics), a container-centric architectural framework designed specifically for robotics teams and the edge-cloud continuum. CSAR combines LXC/LXD-based system containerization, ROS 2/DDS-based communication, and a three-layer edge infrastructure to organize computation into hardware-affine, persistent execution environments that remain decoupled from the volatility of experimental workloads. Through its Infrastructure Core, Platform and Multi-User Orchestration, and Compute and Acceleration layers, CSAR provides strong isolation, controlled resource sharing, and topology-aware networking for distributed robotic applications. To demonstrate its validity, we describe a real deployment of CSAR in an academic robotics laboratory and evaluate it through representative use cases involving edge-offloaded 3D SLAM and GPU-accelerated semantic mapping. The results indicate that CSAR simplifies software integration, improves the utilization of shared computational resources, and facilitates safe prototyping, as well as reproducible and collaborative experimentation in robotics teams. The implementation described in this paper, including deployment templates, configuration files, and documentation, is available at https://github.com/goyoambrosio/CSAR.

AI.tldr: CSAR is a container-centric architectural framework using LXC/LXD, ROS 2/DDS, and a three-layer edge infrastructure to address dependency isolation, compatibility, reproducibility, and deployment challenges in multi-user robotics teams working across the edge-cloud continuum.
AI.motivation: Robotic applications increasingly rely on distributed infrastructures (embedded devices, edge, cloud), and collaborative robotics projects face complexity in development, integration, deployment, and long-term operation. Multi-user teams struggle with dependency isolation, compatibility, reproducibility, hardware sharing, and heterogeneous deployment.
AI.method: CSAR combines LXC/LXD-based system containerization, ROS 2/DDS communication, and a three-layer edge infrastructure (Infrastructure Core, Platform and Multi-User Orchestration, Compute and Acceleration) to create hardware-affine, persistent, decoupled execution environments with strong isolation, controlled resource sharing, and topology-aware networking.
AI.result: Real deployment in an academic robotics lab with edge-offloaded 3D SLAM and GPU-accelerated semantic mapping shows CSAR simplifies software integration, improves shared resource utilization, and facilitates safe prototyping, reproducible, and collaborative experimentation.
AI.conclusion: CSAR effectively addresses robotics team challenges in the edge-cloud continuum by providing a container-centric framework that enhances dependency management, resource sharing, and collaborative development.

title: AlgoSkill: Learning to Design Algorithms by Scheduling Human-Like Skills
summary: Designing an algorithm from a natural-language problem statement requires identifying the problem structure, reading constraints, choosing a suitable paradigm, checking correctness, and refining complexity. Existing large language model (LLM) methods often rely on direct generation or generic self-refinement, leaving these steps implicit. We propose AlgoSkill, which models algorithm design as sequential decision-making over a typed library of algorithmic skills, including abstraction, constraint analysis, state design, data-structure selection, proof checking, counterexample construction, and complexity refinement. A learned scheduler proposes skills from the current design state, while a Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) controller explores skill sequences using verification feedback from compilation, testing, stress testing, and complexity analysis. Experiments on competitive programming and combinatorial optimization benchmarks show that AlgoSkill improves over direct LLM generation, chain-of-thought prompting, self-refinement, and MCTS without typed skills. Ablations show that typed skills, verification-based repair, and search-based scheduling each contribute to performance. These results support treating automatic algorithm design as verification-guided skill scheduling rather than one-shot code generation.

AI.tldr: AlgoSkill models algorithm design as sequential decision-making using typed algorithmic skills (abstraction, constraint analysis, state design, etc.) guided by a learned scheduler and MCTS with verification feedback, outperforming direct LLM generation and self-refinement on programming and optimization benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM methods for algorithm design rely on direct generation or generic self-refinement, leaving critical design steps (identifying structure, constraints, correctness checking, complexity refinement) implicit, leading to suboptimal performance.
AI.method: AlgoSkill frames algorithm design as sequential decision-making over a typed library of algorithmic skills. A learned scheduler proposes skills from the current design state, and an MCTS controller explores skill sequences using verification feedback from compilation, testing, stress testing, and complexity analysis.
AI.result: AlgoSkill outperforms direct LLM generation, chain-of-thought prompting, self-refinement, and MCTS without typed skills on competitive programming and combinatorial optimization benchmarks. Ablations confirm typed skills, verification-based repair, and search-based scheduling each contribute to performance.
AI.conclusion: Automatic algorithm design is better treated as verification-guided skill scheduling rather than one-shot code generation, with structured skills and search being key components.

title: Chronos: A Physics-Informed Full-History Framework for Non-Markovian Long-Horizon Manipulation
comment: 20 pages, 10 figures. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Robotics
summary: General-purpose robot policies should be modeled as dynamical systems, yet many VLA and generative imitation policies still rely on present observations or short windows. This Markovian shortcut fails in memory-dependent manipulation: identical observations can demand different actions after different histories. We present Chronos, a physics-informed full-history framework for non-Markovian long-horizon manipulation. The key idea is to elevate observation history from auxiliary context to the latent state of the policy dynamics. At each physical control step, Chronos forms one state-representative token by fusing observation and proprioception, so the token sequence is aligned one-to-one with physical time. A selective state space model propagates this causal historical state, which conditions a multimodal coarse action prior through implicit maximum likelihood estimation (IMLE). This prior is then refined by a second-order Schrodinger-inspired bridge that predicts acceleration fields, yielding smoother and more physically grounded robot motion. Across 16 simulated tasks and 4 real-world experiments, Chronos is evaluated on precision insertion, general manipulation, and memory-dependent long-horizon control. On RMBench, where success requires remembering task phase, Chronos achieves 73.6% average success, outperforming Markovian VLA baseline pi0.5 by +62.4 percentage points, a 6.6x relative gain, while using 10x fewer parameters. It also surpasses the memory VLA Mem-0 by 22.8 points while using over 30x fewer parameters. In real-world dual-arm experiments using a single RGB camera, Chronos achieves 78% average success over four tasks, including 72% on the three memory-dependent tasks, whereas pi0.5 achieves 7% overall and 0% on the memory-dependent subset. These results suggest that history should not be treated as auxiliary context, but as the latent state of the manipulation policy.

AI.tldr: Chronos is a physics-informed, full-history framework for non-Markovian long-horizon manipulation that treats observation history as the latent state of policy dynamics rather than auxiliary context, using a selective state space model with a Schrödinger-inspired bridge, achieving 73.6% success on RMBench (6.6x relative gain over pi0.5) and 78% on real-world tasks with 10-30x fewer parameters.
AI.motivation: General-purpose robot policies are often modeled as Markovian dynamical systems relying on present observations or short windows, which fails in memory-dependent manipulation where identical observations demand different actions after different histories. The paper aims to address this limitation by proposing a full-history framework.
AI.method: Chronos forms one state-representative token per control step by fusing observation and proprioception, creating a token sequence aligned one-to-one with physical time. A selective state space model propagates the causal historical state, conditioning a multimodal coarse action prior via IMLE, which is then refined by a second-order Schrödinger-inspired bridge predicting acceleration fields for smoother, physically grounded motion.
AI.result: On 16 simulated tasks and 4 real-world experiments: RMBench 73.6% average success (+62.4 points over Markovian pi0.5, 6.6x gain; +22.8 over Mem-0) with 10-30x fewer parameters. Real-world dual-arm: 78% average success (72% on memory-dependent tasks) vs pi0.5's 7% overall and 0% on memory-dependent subset.
AI.conclusion: History should not be treated as auxiliary context but as the latent state of the manipulation policy. The full-history non-Markovian approach significantly outperforms both Markovian and prior memory-augmented methods while being far more parameter-efficient.

title: ACPO: Agent-Chained Policy Optimization for Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
summary: Cooperative tasks in Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) require agents to collectively maximize a shared return. Under the Centralized Training with Decentralized Execution (CTDE) paradigm, policy gradients have remained difficult to compute directly. Prior methods largely follow two approaches: independent factorized updates with centralized critics, which lack general joint-improvement guarantees without value decomposition assumptions, or alternating best-response updates, which can converge to suboptimal Nash Equilibria. In this paper, we show the joint policy gradient admits an exact decentralized decomposition of per-agent terms, each formed from per-agent score functions and decentralized critics.
