Based on this decomposition, we develop Agent-Chained Policy Optimization (ACPO), where actors are trained independently, with their updates together constituting a single step on the joint policy gradient. Central to this result is a serialized view of the simultaneous joint decision in which agents commit actions one at a time, each conditioning on a belief over preceding actions. The belief acts as the coordination mechanism which ties the independent per-agent updates into a joint gradient step. We evaluate ACPO on Multi-Robot Warehouse, SMACv2, and MA-MuJoCo, where it outperforms strong baselines, with the gap widening as the number of agents grows.

AI.tldr: ACPO decomposes the joint policy gradient into exact per-agent terms using serialized belief-based coordination, enabling independent actor updates that collectively form a joint gradient step, outperforming baselines on MARL benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Compute joint policy gradients exactly under CTDE without value decomposition assumptions or suboptimal Nash convergence, addressing limitations of prior centralized-critic and alternating-best-response methods.
AI.method: Derives exact decentralized decomposition of joint policy gradient into per-agent score functions and decentralized critics. Uses a serialized view where agents commit actions sequentially, each conditioning on a belief over preceding actions. The belief acts as the coordination mechanism tying independent updates into a joint gradient step.
AI.result: ACPO outperforms strong baselines on Multi-Robot Warehouse, SMACv2, and MA-MuJoCo, with the performance gap widening as the number of agents increases.
AI.conclusion: Exact joint policy gradient decomposition via serialized belief-based coordination is effective for scalable MARL under CTDE.

title: ReactiveBFM: Reactive Closed-Loop Motion Planning Towards Universal Humanoid Whole-Body Control
summary: While current Behavior Foundation Models (BFMs) provide robust control priors for humanoids, they only execute pre-defined reference motions. As a result, they are vulnerable to environmental shifts and incapable of reactive whole-body coordination. Naively cascading them with generative motion planners fails to achieve true reactivity, as inevitable tracking discrepancies induce fatal cumulative exposure bias. To bridge this gap, we propose ReactiveBFM, a real-time closed-loop planning-control framework. At its core, we effectively mitigate exposure bias via a scheduled prefix sampling curriculum, forcing the generative planner to actively learn error-recovery behaviors from imperfect physical states rather than ground-truth trajectories. Systematically, to reconcile the severe latency mismatch between auto-regressive planning and high-frequency tracking, we introduce an asynchronous replanning mechanism. Combined with trajectory chunking to temporally ensemble spatial references, our system guarantees spatio-temporally fluid execution without physical jitter. Deployed on the Unitree G1 humanoid, ReactiveBFM demonstrates unprecedented physical agility across a vast repertoire of text-conditioned closed-loop motions. Notably, ReactiveBFM achieves zero-shot moving target reaching, showcasing intricate whole-body coordination and on-the-fly replanning. In sim-to-sim benchmarking under severe perturbations, ReactiveBFM achieves a 93.1% success rate, significantly outperforming cascaded open-loop baselines by 28.6%.

AI.tldr: ReactiveBFM is a real-time closed-loop planning-control framework that enables reactive whole-body coordination for humanoids by mitigating exposure bias through a scheduled prefix sampling curriculum and addressing latency mismatches via asynchronous replanning and trajectory chunking.
AI.motivation: Current Behavior Foundation Models (BFMs) execute only pre-defined reference motions, making them vulnerable to environmental shifts and incapable of reactive whole-body coordination. Cascading them with generative motion planners fails due to tracking discrepancies causing fatal cumulative exposure bias.
AI.method: (1) Scheduled prefix sampling curriculum to mitigate exposure bias by forcing the generative planner to learn error-recovery behaviors from imperfect physical states. (2) Asynchronous replanning mechanism to reconcile latency mismatch between auto-regressive planning and high-frequency tracking. (3) Trajectory chunking to temporally ensemble spatial references for jitter-free execution.
AI.result: Deployed on Unitree G1 humanoid, achieving zero-shot moving target reaching with intricate whole-body coordination. In sim-to-sim benchmarking under severe perturbations, achieves 93.1% success rate, outperforming cascaded open-loop baselines by 28.6%.
AI.conclusion: ReactiveBFM bridges the gap between generative motion planning and closed-loop control for humanoids, achieving unprecedented physical agility and reactivity across text-conditioned motions.

title: SAT-RTS: A systematic framework for tactical knowledge extraction and visualization-based analysis in real-time strategy games
summary: Efficient tactical knowledge extraction and analysis in real-time strategy (RTS) games micromanagement are constrained by the high-dimensional coupled state-action sequential data and the black-box decision-making process. Current research rarely provides a hierarchical visualization-based attribution analysis from the perspective of data decoupling and abstraction. To facilitate interpretable tactical knowledge extraction and visualization-based analysis in RTS games, a systematic framework named state-action-tactic analysis pipeline (SAT-RTS) is proposed. To decipher the deep-seated drivers of critical decisions in RTS learning systems, this work integrates interpretable visualization with the automated extraction of latent tactical patterns from high-dimensional sequence data. By adapting a cluster-centric BK-tree algorithm and incorporating specialized distance metrics designed to quantify multi-aspect similarities, the proposed framework facilitates robust state-stream abstraction. Furthermore, a rule-based multi-label extraction method is developed to transform unstructured state-action sequences into discrete and interpretable tactical labels, effectively bridging the gap between raw behavioral data and high-level tactical insights. By holistically integrating these computational methods into a hierarchical visualization-based pipeline, the proposed framework effectively addresses the challenges of processing massive real-time data streams while providing fitness landscape visualizations and analytical insights to decipher deep-seated tactical drivers. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed SAT-RTS significantly enhances the interpretability and efficiency of tactical analysis in complex RTS environments.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes SAT-RTS, a hierarchical visualization-based framework for extracting and analyzing interpretable tactical knowledge from high-dimensional state-action sequences in real-time strategy games, using BK-tree clustering and rule-based multi-label extraction to bridge raw data and high-level tactical insights.
AI.motivation: Tactical knowledge extraction in RTS game micromanagement is constrained by high-dimensional coupled sequential data and black-box decision-making; current research lacks hierarchical visualization-based attribution analysis from a data decoupling and abstraction perspective.
AI.method: (1) A cluster-centric BK-tree algorithm with specialized distance metrics for state-stream abstraction; (2) a rule-based multi-label extraction method to transform unstructured sequences into interpretable tactical labels; (3) integration into a hierarchical visualization-based pipeline (SAT-RTS) providing fitness landscape visualizations.
AI.result: SAT-RTS significantly enhances interpretability and efficiency of tactical analysis in complex RTS environments, as demonstrated by comprehensive experiments.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework effectively addresses the challenges of processing massive real-time data streams while providing analytical insights to decipher deep-seated tactical drivers in RTS learning systems.

title: FutureNav: Unified World-Action Modeling for Vision-and-Language Navigation
summary: Vision-and-language navigation (VLN) in continuous environments requires an agent to ground instructions in egocentric observations while maintaining spatial understanding across long action sequences. Recent navigation foundation models have shown strong progress by scaling vision-language models, but they often learn navigation primarily as direct action generation, without explicitly modeling world states or predicting their future evolution. We introduce FutureNav, a VLM-based unified world-action modeling framework for vision-and-language navigation. Specifically, FutureNav jointly encodes text, visual, and spatial features and feeds them into the LLM, and optimizes four objectives for simultaneous world and action modeling: an action policy objective for navigation action prediction, inverse and forward dynamics objectives for modeling state transitions, and a future generation objective for predicting future spatial states. This unified architecture strengthens action prediction while explicitly modeling the world, without sacrificing inference speed. Extensive experiments show that, with only a 4B-scale backbone, FutureNav achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple VLN benchmarks and substantially outperforms prior VLN methods, paving the way toward future world-action models for VLN. We will release the code and models to support future research.

AI.tldr: FutureNav is a VLM-based unified world-action modeling framework for VLN that jointly encodes text, visual, and spatial features, optimizing four objectives (action policy, inverse dynamics, forward dynamics, future generation) to simultaneously model actions and world states, achieving SOTA performance on multiple VLN benchmarks with a 4B-scale backbone.
AI.motivation: Existing navigation foundation models scale vision-language models for VLN but primarily learn navigation as direct action generation without explicitly modeling world states or predicting future state evolution, limiting their spatial understanding and long-horizon reasoning.
AI.method: FutureNav jointly encodes text, visual, and spatial features into an LLM and optimizes four objectives: (1) action policy objective for navigation action prediction, (2) inverse dynamics for modeling state transitions backward, (3) forward dynamics for modeling state transitions forward, and (4) future generation for predicting future spatial states.
AI.result: With only a 4B-scale backbone, FutureNav achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple VLN benchmarks and substantially outperforms prior VLN methods.
AI.conclusion: Unified world-action modeling strengthens action prediction while explicitly modeling world states without sacrificing inference speed, paving the way toward future world-action models for VLN.

title: Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning in StarCraft Micromanagement with Influence Maps and Cluster-based Scripts
summary: Real-time strategy (RTS) games present significant AI challenges, characterized by expansive state-action spaces arising from multi-unit coordination in continuous battlefields, and sparse delayed rewards stemming from final win/lose signals. Existing approaches face a trade-off between managing the dimensionality explosion of joint actions and maintaining the interpretability of complex state representations. This complexity is further intensified by the limitation of traditional hierarchical structures in adaptively decomposing tasks into effective tactical modules. Such difficulties are compounded by the black-box nature of deep learning models and their reliance on sparse rewards, which together result in limited sample efficiency and a lack of decision-making transparency. To address these limitations, this paper proposes HRL-IM/CBS, a hierarchical reinforcement learning framework with influence map hashing and cluster-based scripts for StarCraft micromanagement. Influence map hashing encodes global battlefield situations into compact hexadecimal codes, capturing spatial control and relative advantage. Cluster-based scripts enable dynamic local coordination through adaptive unit partitioning. The hierarchical multi-Q-table architecture decomposes decision-making into upper-level clustering strategy selection and lower-level tactical execution, with reward allocation providing dense learning signals. Experiments across six asymmetric scenarios demonstrate competitive performance against deep RL baselines while offering advantages in sample efficiency and interpretability through transparent Q-table representations.

AI.tldr: HRL-IM/CBS is a hierarchical reinforcement learning framework using influence map hashing and cluster-based scripts to address challenges in StarCraft micromanagement, achieving competitive performance with better sample efficiency and interpretability than deep RL baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing AI approaches for RTS games suffer from a trade-off between managing the dimensionality explosion of joint actions and maintaining interpretability, compounded by sparse rewards, black-box deep learning models, and limitations of traditional hierarchical structures in adaptive task decomposition.
AI.method: The framework combines (1) influence map hashing to encode battlefield states into compact hexadecimal codes, (2) cluster-based scripts for dynamic local coordination, and (3) a hierarchical multi-Q-table architecture with upper-level clustering strategy selection and lower-level tactical execution, plus reward allocation for dense learning signals.
AI.result: Experiments across six asymmetric scenarios show competitive performance against deep RL baselines with advantages in sample efficiency and interpretability through transparent Q-table representations.
AI.conclusion: HRL-IM/CBS effectively addresses the state-action space explosion and sparse reward problems in RTS game AI while maintaining interpretability, offering a promising alternative to black-box deep RL approaches.

title: HUMEMBR: Learning Human Routines for Predictive Embodied Navigation
summary: Understanding and navigating human-centered environments over extended periods of time while considering human behavior and routines remains a fundamental challenge in robotics. In real-world settings, robots may be asked to locate a specific individual, predict where that person is likely to be, or estimate when they typically leave a building. Addressing such queries requires reasoning over extensive histories of observations and capturing long-term behavioral patterns. To this end, we introduce Human-Centered Memory for Embodied Robots (HUMEMBR), a system designed for embodied question answering and routine-conditioned navigation. HUMEMBR integrates a continuous memory construction process with a parallel retrieval and querying mechanism, enabling the system to accumulate structured representations of human routines while supporting interactive, user-driven queries. Our experimental results indicate that HUMEMBR improves long-horizon reasoning about human behavior relative to full-context LLM baselines, while using substantially fewer tokens. Furthermore, we deploy HUMEMBR on a physical robot in two distinct environments, showing its ability to handle diverse queries and navigation tasks under real-world conditions.

AI.tldr: HUMEMBR is a system for embodied robots that constructs structured memories of human routines over time, enabling long-horizon reasoning and query-driven navigation while using fewer tokens than full-context LLM baselines, validated on physical robots in real-world environments.
AI.motivation: Robots navigating human-centered environments over extended periods struggle to reason about long-term human behavioral patterns (e.g., locating individuals, predicting routines), which requires handling extensive observation histories — a fundamental challenge in robotics.
AI.method: HUMEMBR integrates continuous memory construction with parallel retrieval and querying mechanisms to accumulate structured representations of human routines, supporting interactive user-driven queries and embodied question answering.
AI.result: Improves long-horizon reasoning about human behavior compared to full-context LLM baselines while using substantially fewer tokens; successfully deployed on a physical robot in two distinct real-world environments for diverse queries and navigation tasks.
AI.conclusion: Structured memory of human routines enables efficient long-horizon reasoning and practical embodied navigation in real-world settings.

title: Temporal Feature Extractors in EEG Foundation Models: A Controlled Comparison Including a Pretrained Time-Series Model
summary: Electroencephalography (EEG) foundation models aim to learn generalizable representations from large-scale brain recordings. However, the role of temporal feature extractors and whether pretrained time-series foundation models (TSFMs) can be effectively transferred to this setting remains underexplored. We conduct a controlled comparison of three temporal feature extraction strategies, including a linear baseline, a convolutional encoder, and a frozen pretrained TSFM (MOMENT), within a unified EEG foundation model. We evaluate their impact on representation quality using two downstream tasks: motor imagery and emotion recognition. Results reveal different trends across the evaluated benchmarks. On the motor imagery dataset, simple temporal representations perform competitively, whereas the emotion dataset benefits from richer temporal modeling. Although not specifically adapted to EEG, the pretrained TSFM serves as an effective temporal feature extractor, suggesting that general-purpose time-series representations can be transferred as frozen temporal feature extractors within EEG foundation models.

AI.tldr: This paper compares three temporal feature extraction strategies within EEG foundation models—linear baseline, convolutional encoder, and frozen pretrained time-series foundation model (MOMENT)—finding that simple representations suffice for motor imagery while richer temporal modeling benefits emotion recognition, and that general-purpose TSFMs can be effectively transferred as frozen extractors for EEG.
AI.motivation: To investigate the role of temporal feature extractors in EEG foundation models and determine whether pretrained time-series foundation models (TSFMs) can be effectively transferred to EEG representation learning, an area that remains underexplored.
AI.method: Conducted a controlled comparison of three temporal feature extraction strategies (linear baseline, convolutional encoder, frozen pretrained TSFM MOMENT) within a unified EEG foundation model, evaluated on motor imagery and emotion recognition tasks.
AI.result: Simple temporal representations perform competitively on motor imagery, while emotion recognition benefits from richer temporal modeling. The frozen pretrained TSFM serves as an effective temporal extractor despite not being specifically adapted to EEG.
AI.conclusion: General-purpose time-series representations can be transferred as frozen temporal feature extractors within EEG foundation models, suggesting that domain-specific EEG adaptation may not always be necessary for effective temporal encoding.

title: Vision-Language-Action Models: Experimental Insights from a Real-World UR5 Platform
summary: This project investigates whether recent Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models can be transferred from controlled research benchmarks to a real-world robotic platform, specifically a UR5e manipulator, in a reproducible and operationally meaningful manner. The work integrates real-robot data acquisition, dataset engineering (compatible with the RLDS format), and the fine-tuning and deployment of OpenVLA and OpenVLA-OFT models, with systematic validation of action representations and control interfaces. The project resulted in several foundational assets: (i) a complete real-robot data acquisition pipeline, (ii) a dataset conversion workflow aligned with RLDS standards, (iii) an initial fine-tuning and inference infrastructure for VLA models, and (iv) a structured set of experimental observations grounded in real-robot trials. These elements collectively establish a reproducible framework for evaluating learning-based manipulation systems beyond simulation. Empirically, the experiments reveal a consistent gap between promising offline indicators and unstable closed-loop behavior on the physical system: this gap cannot be attributed solely to model limitations, it is strongly influenced by action semantics, coordinate frame conventions, temporal alignment between modalities, image preprocessing consistency, and dataset coverage and quality. These observations lead to a key interpretation: the successful deployment of VLA systems in real-world settings depends less on incremental improvements in model capacity and more on precise control of the entire data-model-control pipeline. The project reframes VLA-based robotics from a primarily model-centric challenge to a system-level problem; it highlights the difficulty of running robust task execution on the real robot and provides a clear, experimentally grounded understanding of the conditions required for reliable deployment.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates transferring VLA models (OpenVLA, OpenVLA-OFT) from controlled benchmarks to a real UR5e robot, revealing a consistent gap between offline indicators and closed-loop real-world performance, and argues that successful deployment depends on precise control of the entire data-model-control pipeline rather than model improvements alone.
AI.motivation: To assess whether VLA models can be transferred from research benchmarks to a real robotic platform (UR5e) in a reproducible and operationally meaningful way, and to understand the factors causing performance degradation in real-world deployment.
AI.method: Integrated real-robot data acquisition, RLDS-compatible dataset engineering, fine-tuning and deployment of OpenVLA and OpenVLA-OFT models, with systematic validation of action representations and control interfaces on a UR5e manipulator.
AI.result: Produced four foundational assets: (i) a real-robot data acquisition pipeline, (ii) an RLDS-aligned dataset conversion workflow, (iii) initial fine-tuning/inference infrastructure for VLA models, and (iv) structured experimental observations from real-robot trials. Empirically, a consistent gap was found between offline metrics and unstable closed-loop behavior, influenced by action semantics, coordinate frames, temporal alignment, image preprocessing, and dataset quality.
AI.conclusion: Successful VLA deployment in the real world depends less on model capacity improvements and more on system-level control of the entire data-model-control pipeline. The work reframes VLA-based robotics from a model-centric to a system-level problem.

title: Propagation of~Interval Belief Structures and~Imprecise Copulas for~Neural Network Verification
summary: Quantitative verification of neural networks requires reasoning about probabilities under substantial uncertainty in both input distributions and their dependence structure. In realistic settings, this information is often only partially specified, and assuming precise probabilistic models can lead to unreliable results. We propose a sound framework for quantitative verification under imprecise probabilistic information, combining interval belief structures to represent marginal uncertainty with imprecise copulas to model uncertain dependence. We develop a propagation method for imprecisely coupled interval belief structures through feed-forward neural networks. Using mixed imprecise copula volumes, we derive sound push-forward constructions through affine transformations and activation functions. The resulting output can provide guaranteed lower and upper bounds on probabilistic safety properties, valid for all probability models compatible with the specified imprecise inputs.

AI.tldr: A framework for quantitative verification of neural networks under imprecise probabilistic information, combining interval belief structures with imprecise copulas to model uncertain dependence, yielding guaranteed lower and upper bounds on safety properties.
AI.motivation: Realistic neural network verification involves substantial uncertainty in input distributions and dependence structures; assuming precise probabilistic models can lead to unreliable results, motivating a sound framework that handles imprecise probabilistic information.
AI.method: Combines interval belief structures (for marginal uncertainty) with imprecise copulas (for uncertain dependence); propagates imprecisely coupled interval belief structures through feed-forward neural networks using mixed imprecise copula volumes; derives push-forward constructions through affine transformations and activation functions.
AI.result: The framework produces guaranteed lower and upper bounds on probabilistic safety properties that are valid for all probability models consistent with the specified imprecise inputs.
AI.conclusion: The approach provides sound quantitative verification under imprecise probabilistic information, ensuring robustness against uncertainty in both marginal distributions and dependence structures.

title: Behavior Prompting Policy: Demonstrations as Prompts for Manipulation
summary: We study behavior prompting, a paradigm that enables robots to perform new tasks at inference time given a single human demonstration, which we call a behavior prompt. To enable this capability, we present contributions in algorithm, data, and evaluation. For algorithm, we introduce Behavior Prompting Policy (BPP), an in-context visuomotor architecture that translates the behavior prompt and the current observation into robot actions. For data, we identify that task diversity is the primary driver of the prompting capability and introduce iPhUMI, a handheld manipulation interface for collecting diverse training data. For evaluation, we introduce DrawAnything and LIBERO-Gen to evaluate test-time adaptation to unseen drawing and tabletop manipulation tasks. We also demonstrate that iPhUMI serves as a practical interface for specifying behavior prompts at test time, enabling a human to command a robot via a single demonstration to complete known tasks or to define new robot capabilities. Altogether, behavior prompting provides a flexible and scalable way to teach robots new skills without the need for expensive fine-tuning. Our project website is located at https://behavior-prompting.github.io/ .

AI.tldr: This paper introduces behavior prompting, a paradigm enabling robots to perform new tasks at inference time from a single human demonstration (behavior prompt), using a novel architecture (BPP), a data collection interface (iPhUMI), and new evaluation benchmarks (DrawAnything, LIBERO-Gen).
AI.motivation: To enable robots to adapt to new tasks at inference time without expensive fine-tuning, using only a single human demonstration as a prompt.
AI.method: Behavior Prompting Policy (BPP): an in-context visuomotor architecture that maps behavior prompts and current observations to actions; iPhUMI: a handheld manipulation interface for diverse training data collection.
AI.result: BPP achieves test-time adaptation to unseen drawing and tabletop manipulation tasks on DrawAnything and LIBERO-Gen benchmarks; iPhUMI enables practical behavior prompt specification for both known and novel tasks.
AI.conclusion: Behavior prompting offers a flexible, scalable way to teach robots new skills from a single demonstration without expensive fine-tuning, with task diversity being the key driver of prompting capability.

title: Structural Certification for Reliable Physical Design with Language Models
summary: An unreliable language model can be made to produce reliable physical designs if the authority to assert is moved out of the model: the model proposes, and a deterministic engine alone certifies, returning certified, impossible, or unknown. We introduce Physics-Anchored Certification (PHACT), a propose-certify loop spanning five scientific domains, and identify what makes such a certificate trustworthy. A checker that accepts a model-supplied value can be forged; deriving the certified quantity from fixed inputs instead makes forgery impossible by construction. Across eighty adversarial trials spanning two models, two decoding temperatures, and a deliberately faulted engine, this contract produced zero false certifications.

AI.tldr: PHACT is a propose-certify loop where a language model proposes designs and a deterministic engine certifies them, achieving zero false certifications across 80 adversarial trials by deriving certified quantities from fixed inputs rather than accepting model-supplied values.
AI.motivation: Unreliable language models cannot be trusted to directly produce physical designs; authority must be shifted from the stochastic model to a deterministic certification engine to ensure reliability.
AI.method: PHACT (Physics-Anchored Certification) employs a propose-certify loop where the model proposes and a deterministic engine certifies results by deriving certified quantities from fixed inputs, making forgery impossible by construction.
AI.result: Across 80 adversarial trials spanning two models, two decoding temperatures, and a deliberately faulted engine, PHACT produced zero false certifications.
AI.conclusion: Moving authority from the model to a deterministic certifier enables reliable physical design generation from otherwise unreliable language models, with certificates that are trustworthy because they are derived from fixed inputs rather than accepted from the model.

title: Grasp-Oriented Non-Prehensile Manipulation via Learning a Graspability Field
summary: Non-prehensile manipulation is often used as a preparatory step for robotic grasping, yet existing approaches typically require a predefined target object pose. In practice, however, objects admit multiple graspable configurations and the desired pose is not known in advance. We reformulate non-prehensile manipulation for grasping as optimizing an object centric graspability objective rather than reaching a specific pose. We construct a graspable set from synthesized grasps and define a graspability field that measures how suitable an object configuration is for successful grasp execution. The scalar measure provides a dense learning signal for reinforcement learning and determines when to terminate manipulation. This yields a closed-loop manipulation-to-grasp pipeline driven by a single policy. Experiments in simulation and on a real robot show that the policy reliably reconfigures objects into graspable states and transitions to grasping without external planners or manually specified stopping conditions. The predicted graspability distance correlates with real world grasp success, which indicates that the learned representation captures grasp feasibility of object configurations.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a method for non-prehensile manipulation that optimizes object graspability rather than reaching a predefined pose, using a graspability field from synthesized grasps to guide a closed-loop manipulation-to-grasp policy via reinforcement learning.
AI.motivation: Existing non-prehensile manipulation approaches require a predefined target object pose, but objects often admit multiple graspable configurations and the desired pose is not known in advance.
AI.method: Reformulates non-prehensile manipulation for grasping as optimizing an object-centric graspability objective. Constructs a graspable set from synthesized grasps and defines a graspability field measuring how suitable an object configuration is for successful grasp execution. Uses the scalar measure as a dense learning signal for RL and to determine manipulation termination.
AI.result: The policy reliably reconfigures objects into graspable states and transitions to grasping without external planners or manually specified stopping conditions. The predicted graspability distance correlates with real-world grasp success.
AI.conclusion: The learned representation captures grasp feasibility of object configurations, enabling a closed-loop manipulation-to-grasp pipeline driven by a single policy that works in both simulation and real-world settings.

title: Open Problems in Constitutional Preference Reconstruction
summary: Pairwise preference data is widely used for training and evaluating language models (e.g., RLHF), but each datapoint records a \emph{choice}, not the rationale behind it. Methods such as Inverse Constitutional AI (ICAI) attempt to improve interpretability by compressing datasets into short ``constitutions'' of natural-language principles. We argue this framing is under-specified: a flat list of principles is not yet an executable decision rule because it leaves principle composition implicit. We use the pairwise setting as a testbed to empirically characterize three open problems in constitutional methods. First, principle quality is hard to measure: coverage and accuracy are useful but incomplete proxies for end-to-end reconstruction. Second, \emph{composition is ambiguous}: holding principles fixed, different executors (LLM judge versus majority vote) agree only $73\%$ of the time. Third, \emph{constitutions differ between LLMs}: cross-model vote agreement is $73\%$, whereas intra-model agreement is $81\%$. Across PRISM, AlpacaEval, and Chatbot Arena, we show that principle refinement (ICAI+) may be a first step towards ameliorating these problems: inter-executor agreement rises to $78\%$, and transparent executors match LLM judge accuracy ($66\%$ vs.\ $67\%$). Our results highlight that constitutions should be evaluated as \emph{constitution--executor systems}, with implications for LLMs-as-a-judge broadly.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies three open problems in constitutional methods for pairwise preference data: principle quality is hard to measure, composition is ambiguous across executors (73% agreement), and constitutions differ between LLMs (81% intra-model vs 73% cross-model agreement). The authors propose ICAI+ as a refinement approach, showing improved inter-executor agreement (78%) and comparable accuracy to LLM judges (66% vs 67%), advocating for evaluating constitutions as constitution–executor systems.
AI.motivation: Pairwise preference data records choices but not the rationale behind them. Methods like Inverse Constitutional AI (ICAI) attempt to improve interpretability by compressing datasets into short "constitutions" of principles, but this framing is under-specified because a flat list of principles is not an executable decision rule—principle composition remains implicit.
AI.method: The authors use the pairwise setting as a testbed to empirically characterize three open problems: (1) measuring principle quality via coverage and accuracy; (2) evaluating composition ambiguity by comparing different executors (LLM judge vs majority vote); (3) assessing cross-model versus intra-model constitution agreement. They also propose ICAI+ (principle refinement) as a mitigation strategy.
AI.result: Different executors agree only 73% of the time. Cross-model vote agreement is 73%, whereas intra-model agreement is 81%. ICAI+ improves inter-executor agreement to 78%. Transparent executors match LLM judge accuracy (66% vs 67%).
AI.conclusion: Constitutions should be evaluated as constitution–executor systems, not as standalone principle lists. Principle refinement (ICAI+) is a promising first step, but significant ambiguities remain in how principles are composed and executed across different models.

title: Learning from Mistakes: Rollout-Retrieval Lifelong Policy Learning for Autonomous Driving
comment: 15 pages, 6 figures. Code available at: https://github.com/Engibacter/R2LPL
summary: Autonomous driving policies should be able to improve continually as deployment exposes them to increasingly diverse and long-tail traffic situations. However, most learning-based policies are trained or fine-tuned on expert demonstrations and then rely largely on generalization to handle challenging closed-loop scenarios, lacking an explicit mechanism to correct and retain the mistakes exposed in these scenarios. This paper studies autonomous driving policy improvement from a lifelong learning perspective: Can a pretrained policy improve continually by accumulating corrective knowledge derived from its own mistakes, while retaining previously acquired driving competence? To answer this question, we propose Rollout-Retrieval Lifelong Policy Learning (R$^2$LPL), a policy learning framework that retrieves corrective targets from recoverable policy-induced mistakes and retains the resulting knowledge through lifelong policy learning. R^2LPL addresses a key bottleneck in continual policy improvement: closed-loop mistakes reveal where the policy is weak, but do not directly specify what the policy should learn. By filtering recoverable mistake-related states and retrieving feasible corrective targets, R$^2$LPL turns sparse failure evidence into compact supervised knowledge for stable and sample-efficient policy improvement. We evaluate R$^2$LPL on large-scale closed-loop nuPlan benchmarks. With only a few rollout and continual-learning cycles, R$^2$LPL elevates a learning-based planner with moderate initial performance to state-of-the-art performance across the evaluated benchmarks, especially on the challenging and long-tail Test14-hard split. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of R$^2$LPL in converting recoverable closed-loop mistakes into corrective knowledge for sustained policy improvement.

AI.tldr: R²LPL is a lifelong policy learning framework for autonomous driving that enables a pretrained policy to improve by retrieving corrective targets from its own recoverable closed-loop mistakes and retaining knowledge through continual learning, achieving state-of-the-art performance on nuPlan benchmarks with minimal rollout cycles.
AI.motivation: Most learning-based autonomous driving policies are trained on expert demonstrations and rely on generalization to handle challenging scenarios, lacking an explicit mechanism to correct and retain knowledge from mistakes encountered during deployment.
AI.method: R²LPL (Rollout-Retrieval Lifelong Policy Learning) filters recoverable mistake-related states from closed-loop rollouts, retrieves feasible corrective targets from those states, and uses them as supervised knowledge for lifelong policy learning.
AI.result: R²LPL elevates a learning-based planner with moderate initial performance to state-of-the-art across nuPlan benchmarks with only a few rollout and continual-learning cycles, particularly excelling on the challenging Test14-hard split.
AI.conclusion: R²LPL effectively converts recoverable closed-loop mistakes into corrective knowledge for sustained policy improvement, addressing a key bottleneck in continual policy improvement for autonomous driving.

title: Does Verbose Chain-of-Thought Really Help? In-Distribution Evidence that Content, Not Length, Matters
comment: ICML Workshop on Efficient Multimodal Question Answering (EMM-QA)
summary: Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting improves LLM reasoning, but the source is contested: do the intermediate steps help because they carry useful semantic content, or because conditioning on more tokens buys extra computation before the model commits to an answer? We bring two lines of evidence to bear. First, in distribution: we repeatedly sample each model on the same question and pair a shorter with a longer of its own natural generations that follow the same reasoning plan, so nothing is rewritten and both traces are genuinely in-distribution. Across 25 models the extra tokens leave accuracy essentially unchanged for every independently-trained reasoner, and a blind analysis of the surplus tokens shows that what gain exists elsewhere tracks validation- and checking-content, not verbosity per se. Second, as a controlled intervention, we ask whether two traces expressing the same semantic content (the same facts, operations, and intermediate values, verified through directed acyclic graph equivalence) produce different outcomes when one is more verbose, using a dual-validator design across four targets and eight benchmarks with number-redacted completion and stratified bootstrap confidence intervals. Verbose traces do improve accuracy (25 of 32 benchmark-target cells are positive under at least one validator), but the effects are modest (typically 1-4 points) and depend on the quality of the verbose prose, not merely its length. Under maximum numerical redaction the effect is amplified (median 3.24x across four arithmetic benchmarks), and length-matched non-reasoning filler recovers none of it. Both lines converge: what matters is what the extra tokens do (the reasoning and validation content they carry), not how many there are, a picture neither a pure forward-pass-compute nor a pure semantic-content account fully explains.

AI.tldr: CoT reasoning gains come from the semantic content of intermediate steps (reasoning, validation, checking), not from mere token count or additional forward-pass computation. More verbose traces improve accuracy modestly (1-4 points), but only when extra tokens carry meaningful reasoning content; length-matched filler has no effect.
AI.motivation: To resolve the debate about whether chain-of-thought prompting improves LLM reasoning due to useful semantic content in intermediate steps or simply because conditioning on more tokens provides extra computation before committing to an answer.
AI.method: Two complementary approaches: (1) In-distribution analysis comparing natural generations of varying lengths following the same reasoning plan across 25 models; (2) Controlled intervention using dual-validator design with DAG-equivalent traces differing in verbosity, across 4 targets and 8 benchmarks with number-redacted completion and stratified bootstrap confidence intervals.
AI.result: Extra tokens leave accuracy unchanged for independently-trained reasoners; verbose traces improve accuracy in 25/32 benchmark-target cells but only by 1-4 points; effect depends on quality of verbose prose, not length; maximum numerical redaction amplifies effect (median 3.24x); length-matched non-reasoning filler recovers none of the gain.
AI.conclusion: What matters for CoT reasoning improvement is the semantic content (reasoning and validation) of extra tokens, not their quantity. Neither a pure forward-pass-compute nor a pure semantic-content account fully explains the findings.

title: Training Vision-Language-Action Models with Dense Embodied Chain-of-Thought Supervision
summary: Cross-embodiment transfer in vision-language-action (VLA) models remains challenging because low-level state and action spaces differ fundamentally across robot platforms. We observe that the high-level cognitive process underlying manipulation, including scene perception, object identification, task planning, and sub-task decomposition, is largely shared across embodiments. Based on this observation, we present ZR-0, a 2.6 billion parameter end-to-end VLA model that uses dense Embodied Chain-of-Thought (ECoT) supervision to align cross-embodiment representations within the vision-language model (VLM). ZR-0 adopts a dual-stream architecture: a pre-trained VLM (System 2) generates structured ECoT reasoning during training, while a Diffusion Transformer-based action expert (System 1) produces continuous action chunks via flow matching. The two components are coupled through cross-attention, with an attention mask that restricts the action expert to input prompt features only, enabling ECoT generation to be entirely skipped at inference without any performance loss. ZR-0 is pre-trained on ProcCorpus-60M, a large-scale dataset comprising approximately 60 million frames (approximately 1,000 hours) from over 400K trajectories, with dense ECoT annotations covering 96.8% of all frames. We evaluate ZR-0 on three simulation benchmarks spanning single-arm (LIBERO), bimanual (RoboTwin 2.0), and humanoid (RoboCasa GR-1 Tabletop) embodiments, as well as real-world experiments on the xArm platform, demonstrating strong performance across all settings. Code and model checkpoints are available at https://github.com/RUCKBReasoning/ZR-0.

AI.tldr: ZR-0 is a 2.6B parameter VLA model using dense Embodied Chain-of-Thought (ECoT) supervision and a dual-stream architecture (VLM + Diffusion Transformer) to achieve cross-embodiment transfer, pre-trained on 60M frames of data and evaluated across multiple robot platforms.
AI.motivation: Cross-embodiment transfer in VLA models is challenging due to fundamentally different low-level state and action spaces across robot platforms, though high-level cognitive processes (scene perception, planning, decomposition) are largely shared.
AI.method: ZR-0 uses a dual-stream architecture: a pre-trained VLM (System 2) generates structured Embodied Chain-of-Thought (ECoT) reasoning during training, coupled via cross-attention to a Diffusion Transformer-based action expert (System 1) that produces continuous actions via flow matching. An attention mask restricts the action expert to input prompt features only, allowing ECoT to be skipped at inference without performance loss. Pre-trained on ProcCorpus-60M (60M frames, 400K+ trajectories, 96.8% ECoT coverage).
AI.result: Strong performance across three simulation benchmarks (LIBERO single-arm, RoboTwin 2.0 bimanual, RoboCasa GR-1 Tabletop humanoid) and real-world xArm platform experiments.
AI.conclusion: Dense ECoT supervision effectively aligns cross-embodiment representations in VLA models, enabling zero-shot transfer across diverse robot embodiments without inference-time overhead.

title: Relevance Is Not Permission: Warranted Attention for Value Contributions
summary: Relevance is not permission. Attention lets a model read key-value items related to the current query, but it does not guarantee that the value contribution of such an item becomes prediction evidence. A retrieved passage may be relevant to a question without being supporting evidence, and a historical fact or temporal neighbor may even blur true-tail ranking or the current edge score. This paper formalizes this gap as a permission problem for the weighted value term alpha_ij * v_j that is actually added to the prediction path. We propose Warrant, a path-localized interface that preserves attention relevance alpha_ij, exposes the value path leading to the primary metric, and, in the full model, turns alpha_ij * v_j into alpha_ij * g_ij * v_j through learned query-item permission g_ij. We place the same operator on the metric-defining value paths of CTDG link prediction, MTPP next-mark ranking, RAG supporting evidence selection, STPP next-location forecasting, and TKG tail prediction. Across 32 paired comparisons, 3 seeds, and 192 total runs, Warrant improves the primary metric in 27 comparisons; practical tiers consist of 10 substantial effects, 1 marginal effect, 8 positive but uncertain effects, 8 tie/negligible effects, and 5 drops. In the path-localization check, correct-path placement outperforms direction-aware Base performance in every domain and exceeds generic attention placement by +0.1076 AUC in CTDG and +0.0683 MRR in TKG. Ablations show that most TKG gains come from historical-tail value path exposure, whereas the core CTDG gain comes from edge-conditioned query-item permission. In conclusion, prediction evidence is not attention mass. A weighted value term becomes evidence only when it is warranted on the path to the metric.

AI.tldr: This paper formalizes the gap between attention relevance and prediction evidence, proposing Warrant—a path-localized interface that adds learned query-item permission (g_ij) to the attention-weighted value term (α_ij·v_j). Across 192 runs in CTDG, MTPP, RAG, STPP, and TKG, Warrant improves primary metrics in 27/32 comparisons, with correct-path placement outperforming baselines by +0.1076 AUC (CTDG) and +0.0683 MRR (TKG).
AI.motivation: Attention mechanisms can mark items as relevant (via α_ij) but those items may not actually contribute valid evidence to the prediction (α_ij·v_j). The authors formalize this "relevance ≠ permission" gap and argue that a weighted value term becomes evidence only when it is warranted on the metric-defining path.
AI.method: Warrant introduces a learned gating term g_ij that turns α_ij·v_j into α_ij·g_ij·v_j, controlling whether a relevant item's value is permitted to become prediction evidence. It is applied as a path-localized operator across CTDG link prediction, MTPP next-mark ranking, RAG supporting evidence selection, STPP next-location forecasting, and TKG tail prediction.
AI.result: In 32 paired comparisons across 3 seeds (192 total runs), Warrant improves the primary metric in 27 comparisons (10 substantial, 1 marginal, 8 positive but uncertain, 8 tie/negligible, 5 drops). Correct-path placement outperforms direction-aware Base in every domain, exceeding generic attention placement by +0.1076 AUC (CTDG) and +0.0683 MRR (TKG). Ablations show TKG gains stem from historical-tail value path exposure, while CTDG gains come from edge-conditioned query-item permission.
AI.conclusion: Prediction evidence is not attention mass. A weighted value term becomes evidence only when it is warranted on the path to the metric, formalizing the permission problem that bridges the gap between relevance and actual predictive contribution.

title: MOAR Planner: Multi-Objective and Adaptive Risk-Aware Path Planning for Infrastructure Inspection with a UAV
comment: 7 pages, accepted at the 2024 IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA), Yokohama, Japan
summary: The problem of autonomous navigation for UAV inspection remains challenging as it requires effectively navigating in close proximity to obstacles, while accounting for dynamic risk factors such as weather conditions, communication reliability, and battery autonomy. This paper introduces the MOAR path planner which addresses the complexities of evolving risks during missions. It offers real-time trajectory adaptation while concurrently optimizing safety, time, and energy. The planner employs a risk-aware cost function that integrates pre-computed cost maps, the new concepts of damage and insertion costs, and an adaptive speed planning framework. With that, the optimal path is searched in a graph using a discrete representation of the state and action spaces. The method is evaluated through simulations and real-world flight tests. The results show the capability to generate real-time trajectories spanning a broad range of evaluation metrics: around 90% of the range occupied by popular algorithms. The proposed framework contributes by enabling UAVs to navigate more autonomously and reliably in critical missions.

AI.tldr: The MOAR path planner enables real-time UAV trajectory adaptation for inspection tasks by optimizing safety, time, and energy through a risk-aware cost function integrating pre-computed cost maps, damage/insertion costs, and adaptive speed planning. It achieves ~90% performance of popular algorithms in simulations and real-world tests.
AI.motivation: Autonomous UAV inspection navigation remains challenging due to the need for close-proximity obstacle avoidance while accounting for dynamic risk factors such as weather, communication reliability, and battery autonomy.
AI.method: The MOAR path planner uses a risk-aware cost function integrating pre-computed cost maps, damage and insertion costs, and adaptive speed planning. Optimal paths are searched in a graph via discrete state and action space representation.
AI.result: The method generates real-time trajectories spanning ~90% of the performance range occupied by popular algorithms, validated through both simulations and real-world flight tests.
AI.conclusion: The MOAR framework enables UAVs to navigate more autonomously and reliably in critical missions by addressing evolving risks and optimizing safety, time, and energy in real-time.

title: FacePlex: Full-Duplex Joint Speech-Facial Motion Generation for Conversational Avatars
summary: Natural face-to-face conversation requires real-time speech generation together with synchronized facial motion. Existing systems only partially address this problem: speech-only full-duplex models can generate speech in real time but do not produce facial motion, while audio-driven facial motion models animate a face from already available audio rather than jointly generating speech and motion online. To bridge this gap, we first formalize full-duplex joint speech-facial motion generation, where speech tokens and facial motion tokens are produced together every step. Building on this formulation, we propose FacePlex, a unified streaming framework with two key components. First, Rolling Flow Matching adapts flow matching to online motion generation by committing new motion frames at each streaming step. Second, Rolling Cross-Attention couples the streaming audio queue with the motion queue, allowing speech and facial motion to condition each other as generation progresses. Through extensive experiments, ablation studies, and a user study, we show that FacePlex enables full-duplex joint speech-facial motion generation under online streaming constraints, while achieving stronger lip-sync quality and motion fidelity than audio-driven facial motion baselines.

AI.tldr: FacePlex is a unified streaming framework that jointly generates speech and synchronized facial motion in real-time, full-duplex conversation, outperforming audio-driven baselines in lip-sync quality and motion fidelity.
AI.motivation: Existing systems only partially address real-time conversational speech and facial motion: speech-only models generate audio but no facial motion, while audio-driven facial animation requires pre-recorded audio. There is no joint, real-time streaming solution for both modalities.
AI.method: FacePlex introduces two key components: (1) Rolling Flow Matching for online motion generation by committing new motion frames at each streaming step; (2) Rolling Cross-Attention to couple streaming audio and motion queues, enabling each modality to condition the other during generation.
AI.result: FacePlex achieves full-duplex joint speech-facial motion generation under online streaming constraints, with stronger lip-sync quality and motion fidelity than audio-driven facial motion baselines, validated through extensive experiments, ablations, and a user study.
AI.conclusion: Full-duplex joint generation of speech and facial motion is feasible in real-time streaming settings, and FacePlex sets a new benchmark by outperforming audio-driven approaches that have access to full audio.

title: Realtime Wind Estimation using Low Cost Quadrotor Uncrewed Aerial Vehicles
summary: In environmental monitoring as well as emergency response applications such as wildfires, wind velocity measurement is essential. Quadrotor UAVs have become popular platforms for wind velocity estimation due to their maneuverability, compact size, and cost-effectiveness. Numerous studies use the Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) to estimate the wind velocity based on the quadrotor dynamic model. However, most of them use hovering quadrotors only for wind estimation, others use a near-linear trajectory to estimate near-constant velocities. Furthermore, EKF performance is constrained by its reliance on linearized approximations of the nonlinear quadrotor dynamics around current states, limiting accuracy in highly nonlinear scenarios, including windy conditions. This study proposes the use of an Unscented Kalman Filter (UKF), a nonlinear estimator to provide accurate wind estimations while maintaining the trajectory of the quadrotor UAV. The quadrotor is modeled on the Special Euclidean group SE(3) and the approach is evaluated through numerical simulations using a geometric controller to maintain quadrotor flight paths. The results indicate that as the nonlinearity of the simulation increases, the UKF consistently outperforms the EKF. This demonstrates the potential of the UKF as a reliable estimator for highly nonlinear scenarios, capable of maintaining the trajectory with minimal deviation while providing accurate wind velocity estimations.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an Unscented Kalman Filter (UKF) for wind velocity estimation using quadrotor UAVs, showing it outperforms the Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) in highly nonlinear scenarios through SE(3)-based simulations with a geometric controller.
AI.motivation: Wind velocity measurement is critical for environmental monitoring and emergency response (e.g., wildfires). Quadrotor UAVs are promising platforms, but existing EKF-based methods are limited to hovering or near-linear trajectories and suffer from accuracy degradation due to linearized approximations of nonlinear dynamics, especially in windy conditions.
AI.method: The study replaces the EKF with an Unscented Kalman Filter (UKF), a nonlinear estimator, for wind estimation. The quadrotor is modeled on the Special Euclidean group SE(3), and a geometric controller maintains flight paths. Numerical simulations compare UKF and EKF performance under increasing nonlinearity.
AI.result: As simulation nonlinearity increases, the UKF consistently outperforms the EKF in wind velocity estimation accuracy, while maintaining trajectory with minimal deviation.
AI.conclusion: The UKF demonstrates strong potential as a reliable estimator for highly nonlinear wind estimation scenarios using quadrotor UAVs, overcoming the EKF's linearization limitations.

title: MirrorCode: AI can rebuild entire programs from behavior alone
comment: 34 pages, 13 figures, 9 tables. Code available at https://github.com/epoch-research/MirrorCode
summary: AI models are rapidly improving at autonomous coding, as shown by benchmark progress and one-off demonstrations such as AI implementing a C compiler. However, existing coding benchmarks tend to focus on shorter tasks, and one-off demonstrations are hard to compare systematically because they often have some human guidance, and are not standardized or repeated across models. To address these challenges, we introduce MirrorCode, a long-horizon coding benchmark based on reimplementing entire software projects. In MirrorCode, AI agents must replicate the functionalities of an existing program, without access to its source code. AI solutions must match the original program's output exactly on end-to-end tests, including held-out tests. MirrorCode's 25 target programs span different areas of computing: Unix utilities, data serialization and query tools, bioinformatics, interpreters, static analysis, cryptography, and compression. Existing AI models can already reimplement complex software, with the strongest model scoring 56% across the benchmark. For example, AI can reimplement gotree, a 16,000-line bioinformatics toolkit - a task that we believe would take weeks for a human engineer. However, studying the frontier of performance requires a larger inference budget than typical benchmarks, for example, \$2,600 over 19 days for a single attempt on a large task. We show that AI agents can already complete long-horizon software engineering tasks, especially when requirements are precisely specified. More broadly, our work suggests AI will have transformative effects on software engineering, as autonomous agents continue to improve.

AI.tldr: MirrorCode is a long-horizon coding benchmark where AI agents reimplement entire software projects without source code access, tested against exact output matching. The strongest model scores 56%, with one agent reimplementing a 16,000-line toolkit that would take weeks for humans, though large inference budgets ($2,600) are needed for frontier tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing coding benchmarks focus on shorter tasks, while one-off AI coding demonstrations lack standardization and comparability across models. MirrorCode addresses the need for a systematic, repeatable benchmark for long-horizon autonomous software engineering.
AI.method: 25 target programs spanning Unix utilities, data serialization, bioinformatics, interpreters, static analysis, cryptography, and compression. AI agents must replicate functionality without source code, matching outputs exactly on end-to-end tests including held-out tests.
AI.result: Strongest model scores 56% on the benchmark. AI can reimplement a 16,000-line bioinformatics toolkit (gotree) - a task estimated to take weeks for human engineers. Large inference budgets ($2,600 over 19 days) required for frontier performance.
AI.conclusion: AI agents can already complete long-horizon software engineering tasks, especially with precise specifications. The work suggests AI will have transformative effects on software engineering as autonomous agents continue to improve.

title: Sequential Planning via Anchored Robotic Keypoints
summary: We present Sequential Planning via Anchored Robotic Keypoints, SPARK, a training-free neurosymbolic manipulation system that reaches 43.7% on six LIBERO-PRO position \& task cells, more than doubling CaP-Agent0 and Vision-Language-Action (VLA) baselines. CaP-Agent0, a multi-turn code-generation agent, achieves 18.2% by re-querying an LLM at every turn, but its restart-from-scratch solution proves costly against minor policy failures. Perception is the layer that fails most under position and task changes so SPARK spends its computation there. A single Gemini call composes the plan as a typed behavior tree (BT) of composable primitives, each already containing the low-level control (motion, grasping, depth geometry) a code-generation agent would otherwise regenerate on every trial. The rest of the budget goes to perception: a second Gemini call proposes three alternative text prompts per object, SAM3 evaluates each, and we keep the prompt$\to$label pair with the most confident detection and a recovery loop then retries a failed primitive against freshly detected objects, with no new LLM call. The alternative prompts add +27.7 points on the spatial suite and +10.0 on the object suite, with the recovery loop adding +5.0 overall. SPARK runs the same primitives on three robot families (UR10e, Franka FR3, bimanual Franka) across nine unique tasks at twenty trials each, averaging 68%. Since the detector, planner, and controller modules sit behind the typed plan, they swap independently without training, and each primitive's checkable post-condition traces a failure to the corresponding module or a kinematic limit. Every trial logs a verified, labeled trajectory, so a training-free planner that already beats VLAs can supply the data those policies need without teleoperation. Project page: https://cwru-aism.github.io/spark-page/

AI.tldr: SPARK is a training-free neurosymbolic manipulation system using typed behavior trees and two Gemini calls (one for planning, one for perception enhancement with SAM3 evaluation of alternative text prompts) that achieves 43.7% on LIBERO-PRO (more than doubling baselines), 68% across 27 task-robot combinations, with independent swappable modules and verifiable post-conditions.
AI.motivation: Existing code-generation agents like CaP-Agent0 fail under position and task changes due to perception errors and costly restart-from-scratch recovery. A training-free system that isolates and addresses the perception bottleneck while avoiding repeated LLM calls is needed.
AI.method: SPARK uses a single Gemini call to compose a typed behavior tree (BT) of composable primitives with built-in low-level control (motion, grasping, depth geometry). A second Gemini call proposes three alternative text prompts per object; SAM3 evaluates each, and the most confident prompt→label pair is kept. A recovery loop retries failed primitives against freshly detected objects without new LLM calls.
AI.result: 43.7% on six LIBERO-PRO position & task cells (vs 18.2% CaP-Agent0). Alternative prompts add +27.7 points (spatial) and +10.0 (object); recovery loop adds +5.0 overall. 68% average across 9 tasks × 20 trials on three robot families (UR10e, Franka FR3, bimanual Franka).
AI.conclusion: A training-free neurosymbolic planner with typed behavior trees and targeted perception budget can outperform VLA baselines, and the verified labeled trajectories it produces can supply training data for those policies without teleoperation.

title: Dynamo: Dynamic Skill-Tool Evolution for Vision-Language Agents
summary: Improving vision-language models (VLMs) on visual reasoning typically requires retraining or hand-designed prompts and tools. We present Dynamo, a training-free framework that adapts a frozen VLM without any weight updates. On a small labeled training subset, the agent inspects its own correct and incorrect attempts and evolves two complementary capabilities: reusable reasoning skills for cognitive bottlenecks, and executable visual tools for perceptual ones. Each generated tool is paired with a skill that specifies when to invoke it, and both capability types accumulate in a persistent library. Across four visual reasoning benchmarks and five VLM backbones, Dynamo improves direct inference on all 20 model--benchmark settings (avg. +5.6 acc). When the tool set is given in advance, the framework learns when to call each tool, and per-step tool choice improves on every tested backbone. Against task-specific RL (VTool-R1, DeepEyes), Dynamo closes 65--99% of the RL gap at a fraction of the compute, and combines additively with RL when available.

AI.tldr: Dynamo is a training-free framework that improves frozen VLMs on visual reasoning by having the model inspect its own outputs on a small labeled subset to generate reusable reasoning skills and executable visual tools, which accumulate in a persistent library. It achieves consistent gains across 20 model-benchmark settings (avg. +5.6 acc), closes 65-99% of the RL gap with far less compute, and combines additively with RL.
AI.motivation: Existing VLM improvements for visual reasoning require retraining or hand-designed prompts/tools, which are costly and inflexible. Dynamo aims to adapt frozen VLMs without weight updates by enabling self-evolution of skills and tools.
AI.method: Dynamo operates in two phases: (1) On a small labeled training subset, the VLM inspects its own correct/incorrect attempts to generate reasoning skills (for cognitive bottlenecks) and executable visual tools (for perceptual bottlenecks). Each tool is paired with a skill specifying when to invoke it. (2) Both capabilities accumulate in a persistent library. During inference, the model retrieves and applies relevant skills/tools from the library.
AI.result: Across 4 visual reasoning benchmarks and 5 VLM backbones, Dynamo improves direct inference on all 20 settings (avg. +5.6 accuracy). It closes 65-99% of the performance gap achieved by task-specific RL methods (VTool-R1, DeepEyes) at a fraction of the compute, and combines additively with RL when available.
AI.conclusion: Dynamo demonstrates that frozen VLMs can effectively self-evolve by generating their own reasoning skills and visual tools from a small labeled subset, offering a lightweight, training-free alternative to RL-based fine-tuning that is complementary to RL methods.

title: GROW$^2$: Grounding Which and Where for Robot Tool Use
summary: Can the robot use a plate to cut a cake if no knife is available? Tool use greatly expands robot capabilities, but to use tools creatively beyond their intended functions, the robot faces the challenge of $\textit{open-world affordance grounding}$: select an open-category object to act as a tool and localize its specific region of action. To this end, we introduce GROW$^2$ (GROunding Which and Where), which leverages object parts as a natural abstraction to split the grounding process hierarchically into semantic and geometric levels, thus bypassing the need for data-heavy, end-to-end training. Semantically, GROW$^2$ harnesses the commonsense reasoning of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to parse a natural-language task instruction, select a suitable object as the tool, and identify task-relevant parts on the tool and the target object. Geometrically, vision foundation models then ground the selected parts into precise 3D regions from a single RGB-D image. Experiments on established benchmarks show that GROW$^2$ outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on affordance prediction benchmarks. Further, it achieves zero-shot generalization over open-category objects and outperforms baselines in both simulated and real-world robot tool use experiments.

AI.tldr: GROW^2 is a hierarchical framework that combines Vision-Language Models for semantic reasoning and vision foundation models for geometric grounding to enable robots to select and localize tool affordances on open-category objects from a single RGB-D image, achieving zero-shot generalization and outperforming baselines in affordance prediction and robot tool use tasks.
AI.motivation: Robots lack the ability to creatively use tools beyond their intended functions (e.g., using a plate to cut a cake), because open-world affordance grounding—selecting an open-category object as a tool and localizing its specific region of action—remains a challenging problem.
AI.method: GROW^2 uses object parts as a natural abstraction to hierarchically split affordance grounding: (1) Semantic level—VLMs leverage commonsense reasoning to parse task instructions, select a suitable tool, and identify task-relevant parts on both tool and target objects; (2) Geometric level—vision foundation models ground the selected parts into precise 3D regions from a single RGB-D image, avoiding end-to-end data-heavy training.
AI.result: Outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on affordance prediction benchmarks, achieves zero-shot generalization over open-category objects, and outperforms baselines in both simulated and real-world robot tool use experiments.
AI.conclusion: Hierarchical decomposition of open-world affordance grounding into semantic (VLM-based) and geometric (foundation model-based) levels is effective for creative tool use, enabling zero-shot generalization without task-specific training data.

title: From Detecting Agency to Doing Work: Self-Caused Credit Builds a Durable Behavioral Self in a Minimal Spiking Agent
comment: 22 pages, 6 figures. Includes supplementary information in the same PDF
summary: How does an agent that can tell self from world come to be durably shaped by that distinction? Recent work shows that a predictive system can detect its own agency (Ye, 2026), but detecting agency does not explain durable, self-shaped behavior. We show that agency-gated slow credit -- a conjunctive term Own*Agency*Salience driving a slow parameter update -- produces post-unload behavioral residue: on a spiking substrate (Nengo LIF/PES), a learned self-preserving choice survives episodic buffer removal (retained fraction 0.96, N=50) and collapses when the slow decoders are reset or the agency gate is removed. Reproducing the agency comparator and toggling only the slow-credit channel, we find a clean dissociation: at matched agency gain, durable behavior develops only when self-credit performs slow work (post-unload self-preservation 1.00 vs 0.00). The same dissociation holds in 24-dimensional partially-observed control (0.74 vs 0.00), and a plastic-work analysis shows that basin deformation equals net self-credit work. Across eight sequentially-learned tasks under exogenous interference, the multiplicative veto also prevents forgetting: it retains old tasks (final post-unload accuracy 0.88, forgetting 0.13) where additive pooling collapses to chance-level recall, the no-agency ablation falls below chance, and episodic/replay baselines stay near chance after unload -- all with no replay buffer and no task-boundary-dependent protection mechanism (N=50). We formalize the durable residue as an operational behavioral self and argue that self-caused credit doing slow work is a necessary building block for agents that develop a self. No claim of consciousness is made.

AI.tldr: Agency-gated slow credit (Own*Agency*Salience driving slow parameter updates) produces durable, self-preserving behavioral residue on spiking neural substrates, enabling self-shaped behavior that persists after episodic buffer removal, with a multiplicative veto preventing catastrophic forgetting across sequential tasks — formalized as an operational behavioral self without claims of consciousness.
AI.motivation: Prior work shows predictive systems can detect agency, but detection alone does not explain how agents develop durable, self-shaped behavior that persists beyond immediate sensory evidence.
AI.method: Introduced agency-gated slow credit (Own*Agency*Salience conjunct driving slow weight updates) on a spiking substrate (Nengo LIF/PES). Conducted experiments with episodic buffer removal, slow decoder reset, agency gate ablation, and comparisons to additive pooling and episodic/replay baselines across 8 sequentially-learned tasks with exogenous interference.
AI.result: Learned self-preserving choice survived buffer removal (retained fraction 0.96, N=50), collapsed when slow decoders reset or agency gate removed. Clean dissociation: durable behavior only with slow self-credit (post-unload 1.00 vs 0.00). In 24D control: 0.74 vs 0.00. Sequential learning retained old tasks (accuracy 0.88, forgetting 0.13) where additive pooling collapsed, no-agency fell below chance, episodic/replay baselines near chance after unload.
AI.conclusion: Self-caused credit performing slow work is a necessary building block for agents that develop an operational behavioral self; durable residue formalized as self. No consciousness claims made.

title: VLK: Learning Humanoid Loco-Manipulation from Synthetic Interactions in Reconstructed Scenes
summary: Perception-based humanoid loco-manipulation requires connecting egocentric observations and task instructions to whole-body motion. Learning this mapping requires synchronized egocentric images, language commands, and robot-compatible kinematic trajectories, yet no existing data source provides this complete tuple at scale. We address this bottleneck by generating vision-language-kinematics (VLK) supervision synthetically in reconstructed scenes. Our pipeline leverages 3D Gaussian Splatting to reconstruct metric-scale indoor environments, synthesizes navigation and object-interaction trajectories using privileged scene information, and renders paired egocentric observations after the fact. We produce 48,000 paired trajectories with no human intervention and train a VLK policy that predicts short-horizon whole-body kinematic trajectories. A whole-body tracker converts these predictions into actions on the physical humanoid. We evaluate on the physical Unitree G1 performing navigation and single-object transport, demonstrating that synthesized interactions in reconstructed scenes provide effective supervision for sim-to-real perception-based humanoid loco-manipulation. Project Website: https://vision-language-kinematics.github.io/

AI.tldr: This paper presents a method to generate synthetic vision-language-kinematics (VLK) supervision data for humanoid loco-manipulation by reconstructing metric-scale indoor scenes using 3D Gaussian Splatting, synthesizing trajectories, and training a policy that predicts whole-body kinematic trajectories for physical humanoid control.
AI.motivation: No existing data source provides synchronized egocentric images, language commands, and robot-compatible kinematic trajectories at scale for perception-based humanoid loco-manipulation.
AI.method: 1) Reconstruct metric-scale indoor environments using 3D Gaussian Splatting. 2) Synthesize navigation and object-interaction trajectories using privileged scene information. 3) Render paired egocentric observations. 4) Train a VLK policy predicting short-horizon whole-body kinematic trajectories. 5) Use a whole-body tracker to convert predictions to actions on the physical humanoid (Unitree G1).
AI.result: Produced 48,000 paired trajectories with no human intervention; demonstrated sim-to-real transfer on physical Unitree G1 for navigation and single-object transport.
AI.conclusion: Synthesized interactions in reconstructed scenes provide effective supervision for sim-to-real perception-based humanoid loco-manipulation.

title: Domain Adaptation with Adaptive Imagination for Visual Reinforcement Learning under Limited Target Data
summary: Sim-to-real transfer remains a major obstacle for reinforcement learning (RL), especially for vision-based control where image observations exacerbate the state-distribution shift between simulation and the real world. Domain adaptation (DA) is a promising remedy for this challenge. Prior sim-to-real DA works have demonstrated encouraging results, yet these approaches typically assume substantially more target data, which is not available in practice. Indeed, their performance degrades significantly when the target data budget is reduced. To address this challenge, we propose AIDA (Adaptive Imagination for Domain Adaptation), a domain adaptation framework for visual reinforcement learning that addresses sim-to-real transfer under scarce target data without requiring additional interaction with the target environment. Our key idea is adaptive imagination: generating reliable and semantic imagination rollouts to augment limited target data. Specifically, AIDA employs a distribution-shift-aware discriminator that truncates rollouts when imagined transitions drift into low-confidence regions, so that only reliable transitions contribute to the augmentation. On these reliable transitions, AIDA introduces a self-consistency loss that cycles through state -> image observation -> state, penalizing discrepancies between the original and reconstructed states. This provides additional adaptation signals beyond the scarce target data. Our experiments demonstrate that adaptive imagination effectively truncates unreliable rollouts. By enforcing a self-consistency loss on the resulting reliable transitions, AIDA learns semantically meaningful state representations and outperforms baselines across five MuJoCo tasks and two Gymnasium-Robotics tasks.

AI.tldr: AIDA proposes a domain adaptation framework for visual RL that uses adaptive imagination (truncating unreliable rollouts via a distribution-shift-aware discriminator) and self-consistency loss (cycle: state→image→state) to enable sim-to-real transfer under extremely scarce target data without additional real-world interaction.
AI.motivation: Prior sim-to-real DA methods for visual RL assume abundant target data, but their performance degrades significantly when the target data budget is scarce, which is the realistic setting.
AI.method: (1) Adaptive Imagination: a distribution-shift-aware discriminator truncates imagined rollouts when transitions drift into low-confidence regions, retaining only reliable transitions. (2) Self-Consistency Loss: on reliable transitions, a cycle (state→image observation→state) is enforced, penalizing reconstruction discrepancies to provide additional adaptation signals beyond limited target data.
