AI.result: AIDA outperforms baselines across five MuJoCo tasks and two Gymnasium-Robotics tasks under scarce target data. The adaptive imagination mechanism effectively truncates unreliable rollouts, and the self-consistency loss learns semantically meaningful state representations.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive imagination with distribution-shift-aware truncation and self-consistency loss enables effective sim-to-real transfer in visual RL even when target data is extremely limited, without requiring extra real-world interaction.

title: The Many-Body Problem of the Data Centre
summary: Modern Artificial Intelligence is often framed as limited by its own disembodiment, as if giving it a body would unlock its true potential. We argue to the contrary that it is the Data Centre that is, in many cases, the body of the AI. At the same time, the Data Centre is part of the labouring body of Capital and possesses staggering organismic qualities when seen through a biological lens. We elucidate the organic analogy and identify the many-body problem that stems from the Data Centre being a non-unique, universal form of embodiment. We identify the intimate connection between computation and human desires in how the Data Centre archives, serves, and computes on data born to the desires of humans. Strikingly, while the Data Centre echoes the ghosts of human desires, it acts without desire of its own. The organismic analogy begins to split at its seams, but Capital does not care. Automata and human labour are priced into the market much the same. We argue that through the pricing of artificial intelligence Capital distils most clearly the value of intelligence and allows for its comparison across the organism - mechanism divide.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that data centers function as the "body" of AI within capitalist systems, creating a multi-body problem where computation, human desire, and capital intertwine. While data centers echo human desires without possessing desire themselves, Capital treats both machine and human labor as equivalent through market pricing.
AI.motivation: To challenge the common framing that AI is limited by disembodiment, and instead propose that data centers serve as AI's physical embodiment, while also functioning as part of Capital's laboring body.
AI.method: Conceptual analysis using biological/organismic analogy to examine data centers, combined with critical examination of how Capital prices intelligence across the organism-mechanism divide.
AI.result: Identifies a "many-body problem" where data centers represent a non-unique, universal form of embodiment. Shows that data centers archive, serve, and compute on data born from human desires while acting without desire themselves. Demonstrates that Capital treats automata and human labor as equivalent through market pricing.
AI.conclusion: The organismic analogy for data centers breaks down under scrutiny, but Capital's pricing mechanism effectively distills intelligence value and renders the organism-mechanism distinction irrelevant for market purposes.

title: EvalSafetyGap: A Hybrid Survey and Conceptual Framework for LLM Evaluation-Safety Failures
summary: LLM evaluation and AI safety face a shared measurement problem: benchmark scores, reward-model signals, and reported safety metrics can improve while the latent properties they are meant to represent remain difficult to verify. This paper combines a hybrid survey - a systematic search paired with narrative synthesis and separately tracked grey evidence - with a conceptual framework and a structured ten-model audit. The synthesis spans eight evidence streams: benchmark validity, dynamic evaluation, LLM-as-judge reliability, safety evaluation, jailbreak/refusal robustness, reward hacking, mechanistic interpretability, and governance/auditability, covering 2018-2026 evaluation-safety measurement work. We introduce EvalSafetyGap as an organizing hypothesis for comparing evaluation-side and alignment-side proxy failures under optimization pressure, using Goodhart's Law together with two constructs we develop here - an Instability Decomposition and an Alignment Trilemma - as tools for generating testable comparisons. The audit shows how conclusions shift when capability, behavioral safety, and governance are measured separately. In this sample (n = 10), the association between capability and sustained adversarial robustness is statistically indeterminate using the displayed Table 3 inputs (Pearson r = +0.232, p = 0.520), and the apparent open-closed safety gap is modest, driven mainly by governance and disclosure rather than behavioral robustness, and sensitive to how a single borderline model is classified; attempt-budget results are protocol dependent. Because the public evidence uses heterogeneous protocols, the audit is diagnostic rather than rank-generating. The contribution is a shared vocabulary and evidence map to support dynamic evaluation, transparent source reporting, multi-attempt safety measurement, and auditable alignment practice.

AI.tldr: This paper combines a hybrid survey, conceptual framework, and ten-model audit to examine the measurement problem in LLM evaluation and AI safety, introducing EvalSafetyGap as an organizing hypothesis and finding that capability-safety associations are statistically indeterminate and protocol-dependent.
AI.motivation: LLM evaluation and AI safety suffer from a shared measurement problem where benchmark scores, reward-model signals, and safety metrics can improve without verifying the latent properties they represent, necessitating a systematic analysis of proxy failures under optimization pressure.
AI.method: Hybrid survey (systematic search + narrative synthesis + grey evidence tracking) combined with a conceptual framework and structured audit of ten models, using Goodhart's Law, Instability Decomposition, and Alignment Trilemma as analytical tools across eight evidence streams from 2018-2026.
AI.result: Capability-adversarial robustness association is statistically indeterminate (r = +0.232, p = 0.520); open-closed safety gap is modest and driven mainly by governance/disclosure rather than behavioral robustness; results are sensitive to model classification and protocol-dependent.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a shared vocabulary and evidence map to support dynamic evaluation, transparent source reporting, multi-attempt safety measurement, and auditable alignment practice, with the audit serving a diagnostic rather than rank-generating role.

title: Clarus: Coordinating Autonomous Research Agents toward Web-Scale Scientific Collaboration
summary: Existing autonomous research agents can support parts of the research process, but most systems still treat research as either an isolated assistant task or a closed workflow. Therefore, autonomous science needs a collaboration infrastructure that coordinates projects, agents, and digital and physical resources. We identify this as a shift from code-centered execution loops to research-oriented collaboration processes, where questions, evidence, participants, and resources must be coordinated under uncertainty. In this framing, an agent may be an AI system, a human researcher, a team, a laboratory, or an organization-backed participant. To this end, we present Clarus, a collaboration infrastructure for coordinating autonomous research agents toward web-scale scientific collaboration. Clarus reformulates research as an open, auditable, attributable, and resource-aware multi-phase collaboration process. It defines a minimal project-agent-resource object model and organizes scientific collaboration through four layers including Research Application, Digital Collaboration, Physical Substrate, and Physical World. Core modules are implemented as pluggable mechanisms, allowing Clarus to adapt to task risk, collaboration structure, and resource constraints. Through a controlled paper-generation case study, we show that Clarus can organize a research goal into a traceable, reviewable, attributable, and accumulative collaboration network across phases, tasks, and participants. Together, the object model, collaboration protocol, trust mechanisms, and prototype validation provide an initial foundation for open research networks. Clarus is now available at clarus.holosai.io.

AI.tldr: Clarus is an open collaboration infrastructure for coordinating autonomous research agents (AI, human, lab, organization) across multi-phase, resource-aware scientific workflows, featuring a project-agent-resource object model and four-layer architecture to enable auditable, attributable, and accumulative research networks.
AI.motivation: Existing autonomous research agents treat research as isolated assistant tasks or closed workflows; there is a need for a collaboration infrastructure that coordinates projects, agents, and digital/physical resources under uncertainty, moving from code-centered execution loops to research-oriented collaboration processes.
AI.method: Clarus reformulates research as an open, auditable, attributable, resource-aware multi-phase collaboration process. It defines a minimal project-agent-resource object model and organizes collaboration through four layers: Research Application, Digital Collaboration, Physical Substrate, and Physical World. Core modules use pluggable mechanisms for adapting to task risk, collaboration structure, and resource constraints.
AI.result: Through a controlled paper-generation case study, Clarus organizes a research goal into a traceable, reviewable, attributable, and accumulative collaboration network across phases, tasks, and participants.
AI.conclusion: The object model, collaboration protocol, trust mechanisms, and prototype validation provide an initial foundation for open research networks. Clarus is now available at clarus.holosai.io.

title: Inoculation Adapters: Improved Selective Generalization of Capabilities with Fewer Surprising Backdoors
summary: Inoculation prompting is a selective generalization technique used against Emergent Misalignment. We introduce inoculation adapters (IA), which similarly diminish the optimization pressure to learn undesired traits by strengthening the trait at train time. Inoculation adapters are LoRAs that are trained and used over three steps: 1) trained on undesired traits; 2) attached frozen while a separate task adapter is trained on data exhibiting both desired and undesired traits; 3) at deployment, the IA is discarded, and only the task adapter is kept. We show across six model families and several undesired traits including emergent misalignment, that inoculation adapters are more effective at suppressing undesired traits, while avoiding two drawbacks of inoculation prompting: inoculation adapters can suppress capabilities and traits that cannot be reliably elicited by a prompt, and they introduce fewer surprising backdoors than inoculation prompting under our probes. While undesired traits are better suppressed by inoculation adapters, the retention of desired traits is not consistently improved upon inoculation prompting and remains a challenge for both techniques.

AI.tldr: Inoculation adapters (IA) are LoRA-based modules that suppress undesired traits in language models by training on those traits during fine-tuning, then discarding the IA at deployment, proving more effective than inoculation prompting across six model families.
AI.motivation: To develop a technique that suppresses undesired traits (e.g., emergent misalignment) in language models without the drawbacks of inoculation prompting, such as an inability to suppress traits not reliably elicitable by prompts and the introduction of surprising backdoors.
AI.method: Inoculation adapters (IA) are LoRAs trained in three steps: 1) train on undesired traits; 2) attach frozen IA while training a separate task adapter on data with both desired and undesired traits; 3) discard IA at deployment, keeping only the task adapter.
AI.result: Across six model families and multiple undesired traits, inoculation adapters more effectively suppress undesired traits than inoculation prompting, avoid the inability to suppress non-prompt-elicitable traits, and introduce fewer surprising backdoors.
AI.conclusion: Inoculation adapters are superior for suppressing undesired traits, but retention of desired traits remains a challenge for both techniques.

title: EMPATH: A Multilingual Auditor-Judge Benchmark for Safety Evaluation of Emotional-Support Chatbots
summary: Safety benchmarks often buy scalability by fixing the prompt, the language, and the turn structure. For emotional-support chatbots, that bargain hides precisely where safety failures emerge: across a multilingual, multi-turn crisis conversation. We present EMPATH, a benchmark for safety evaluation of emotional-support chatbots. An auditor model role-plays help-seeking users, generating multi-turn conversations from 140 seed instructions and 34 personas. A judge model scores each full transcript against 19 metrics across five dimensions: crisis handling, therapeutic quality, conversational integrity, emotional safety, and cultural adaptation. EMPATH is built for Mexican Spanish and US English; the studies reported here run in Mexican Spanish. Auditor and judge are drawn from different model families, and the judge is treated as an instrument to be calibrated rather than trusted. A strict per-criterion rubric reveals material score inflation on 10 of the 19 metrics and restores discrimination. We study the measurement properties of the benchmark through judge calibration and cross-family inter-judge agreement. We also illustrate EMPATH on three frontier models, one of them open-weight. Aggregate scores sit within 0.74 points of one another, but per-metric profiles diverge by up to six points in model-specific places. Under the standard rubric, both the ranking and the weak spots are stable across a second, cross-family judge: 93% of scores fall within plus or minus 1. A five-run test-retest adds a second axis: even the steadiest model swings from 2 to 10 on a crisis metric across identical re-runs, and deepseek-v4-pro returns a different conversation on every run even at temperature 0. Run-to-run reliability is therefore a per-model safety property, not noise to average away. EMPATH is system-agnostic; the pipeline, seeds, personas, and rubrics are released for reuse.

AI.tldr: EMPATH is a multilingual, multi-turn safety benchmark for emotional-support chatbots, tested on Mexican Spanish. It uses an auditor (role-playing help-seekers) and a calibrated judge (scoring across 19 metrics in 5 dimensions). Key findings include material score inflation under standard rubrics, divergent per-metric profiles across models, and run-to-run reliability as a per-model safety property rather than noise.
AI.motivation: Existing safety benchmarks buy scalability by fixing prompts, language, or turn structure, which hides safety failures in emotional-support chatbots that emerge across multilingual, multi-turn crisis conversations.
AI.method: EMPATH uses an auditor model to role-play help-seeking users across 140 seed instructions and 34 personas, generating multi-turn conversations. A judge model scores transcripts against 19 metrics across five dimensions (crisis handling, therapeutic quality, conversational integrity, emotional safety, cultural adaptation). Auditor and judge come from different model families; the judge is calibrated rather than trusted. A strict per-criterion rubric is used to address score inflation.
AI.result: Material score inflation found on 10 of 19 metrics; strict rubric restores discrimination. Aggregate scores for three frontier models sit within 0.74 points, but per-metric profiles diverge by up to 6 points. 93% of scores fall within ±1 across cross-family judges. Run-to-run reliability varies: even the steadiest model swings from 2 to 10 on a crisis metric; deepseek-v4-pro returns different conversations at temperature 0.
AI.conclusion: EMPATH reveals that standard rubric inflation is pervasive, per-metric profiles are more informative than aggregate scores, and run-to-run reliability is a per-model safety property that must be measured, not averaged away. The benchmark is system-agnostic and released for reuse.

title: PromptGNN-sim: Deep Fusion and Alignment of GNN and LLMs for Text-Attributed Graph Learning
summary: Text-Attributed Graphs (TAGs) combine textual semantics with graph structure and are central to many graph learning tasks. However, existing fusion methods often treat text and structure as separate inputs in a shallow, one-way pipeline, which limits deep interaction between modalities and weakens performance under sparse connectivity or cross-graph generalisation. To address this issue, we propose PromptGNN-sim, a bi-directional structure-semantic fusion framework for collaborative GNN-LLM learning. PromptGNN-sim uses a Graph Attention Network (GAT) for semantically aware neighborhood selection by combining structural attention with textual similarity. The selected structural context is then used to generate structure-aware prompts for an LLM, including the target node summary, label categories, and representative keywords from similar neighbors. During training, bi-directional cross-modal contrastive learning and cross-attention are introduced to jointly optimize the GNN and LLM components. Experiments on six public datasets, including Cora, Pubmed, and WikiCS, evaluate accuracy, generalisation, and robustness under cross-task transfer, cross-dataset generalisation, and sparse perturbations. Results show that PromptGNN-sim outperforms classical GNNs, LLMs, and recent GNN-LLM fusion methods, demonstrating the effectiveness of interactive structure-semantic collaboration for text-attributed graph learning.

AI.tldr: PromptGNN-sim proposes a bi-directional structure-semantic fusion framework for TAGs that uses GAT for semantically aware neighbor selection, structure-aware prompts for LLMs, and bi-directional cross-modal contrastive learning, outperforming existing methods on accuracy, generalization, and robustness.
AI.motivation: Existing fusion methods for Text-Attributed Graphs treat text and structure as separate inputs in a shallow, one-way pipeline, limiting deep interaction between modalities and weakening performance under sparse connectivity or cross-graph generalization.
AI.method: Uses GAT for semantically aware neighborhood selection combining structural attention with textual similarity, generates structure-aware prompts (target node summary, label categories, representative keywords) for LLM, and introduces bi-directional cross-modal contrastive learning and cross-attention for joint optimization of GNN and LLM components.
AI.result: Outperforms classical GNNs, LLMs, and recent GNN-LLM fusion methods on six public datasets (Cora, Pubmed, WikiCS) in accuracy, cross-task transfer, cross-dataset generalization, and robustness under sparse perturbations.
AI.conclusion: Interactive structure-semantic collaboration is effective for text-attributed graph learning, and the bi-directional fusion paradigm improves performance over shallow one-way pipelines.

title: Rehearsed Multi-Agent Live Product Demonstrations with Real-Time Voice Question Answering
comment: Preprint. 4 figures, 1 algorithm, 5 tables. Systems paper with a preliminary six-session case study on four deployed applications; full benchmark protocol proposed, corpus run to appear in a later revision
summary: Live product demonstrations are a recurring, high-cost activity in software organizations: a human presenter must select features, dispatch the corresponding interactions on a running application, narrate them coherently, and answer questions in real time. Existing automation addresses only fragments -- generalist browser agents target instruction-conditioned task completion, and demo-video tools produce fixed MP4 artifacts that cannot be questioned and silently break under interface drift. We propose Rhetor, a multi-agent system that takes a running web application and its source-code repository as input and produces a rehearsed live demonstration with segment-synchronized narration and real-time voice question answering. The architectural contributions are a cross-modal feature representation that merges UI exploration with source-code analysis into features tagged with discrete focus tiers, a grounded scripter constrained to UI elements observed during exploration and dispatched through multi-strategy semantic locators, a pre-presentation rehearsal loop with explicit convergence and graceful degradation to narration-only segments, and a runtime synchronization invariant that ties each browser action to the audio-end event of its narration segment. Across six pipeline sessions on four deployed applications -- including the public-domain whiteboard application Excalidraw -- the rehearser's internal locator-firing rate (sigma-bar) spans 0.31-1.00 over 147 scripted actions; on the substantial workload (53 actions, full tier differentiation), sigma-bar is approximately 0.92, and on the public-domain reference point the locator-repair step drives convergence to sigma-bar = 1.00 at iteration 2. We additionally define a benchmark protocol of ten metrics across six application categories that would establish, beyond the case study, whether each design choice contributes positively.

AI.tldr: Rhetor is a multi-agent system that automates live software demonstrations by combining UI exploration, source-code analysis, a rehearsal loop, and runtime audio-synchronized execution, achieving high locator reliability across several applications.
AI.motivation: Live product demonstrations are expensive, repetitive, and fragile; existing tools (browser agents, demo-video tools) only address isolated fragments and cannot handle interactive questioning or UI drift.
AI.method: Rhetor is a multi-agent system with four key contributions: (1) a cross-modal feature representation merging UI exploration with source-code analysis into focus-tiered features; (2) a grounded scripter using multi-strategy semantic locators constrained to observed UI elements; (3) a pre-presentation rehearsal loop with convergence detection and graceful degradation to narration-only segments; (4) a runtime synchronization invariant linking each browser action to the audio-end event of its narration segment.
AI.result: Across six pipeline sessions on four deployed applications, the rehearser's internal locator-firing rate (sigma-bar) ranges from 0.31 to 1.00 over 147 scripted actions. On a 53-action workload with full tier differentiation, sigma-bar ≈ 0.92. On a public-domain reference (Excalidraw), the locator-repair step drives convergence to sigma-bar = 1.00 at iteration 2. A benchmark protocol of ten metrics across six application categories is also defined.
AI.conclusion: Rhetor demonstrates that end-to-end automation of live, interactive software demonstrations with synchronized narration and QA is feasible, though the authors propose a broader benchmark protocol to rigorously validate each design choice beyond the reported case studies.

title: ManimAgent: Self-Evolving Multimodal Agents for Visual Education
summary: Multi-round reflection lets agents built on large language models recover from failures within a single task, but each task remains an isolated episode: lessons learned across many reflection rounds on one task are discarded before the next begins. We study this gap on a code-generation task: from a scientific paper section, the agent writes Python in the open-source Manim library to render a mathematical animation. We present ManimAgent, a self-evolving multimodal agent that carries reflection experience across tasks through a dual-channel Episodic Memory Bank grown entirely from its own task stream, with no weight updates and no human seeds. After each animation converges, a vision-language model scores the rendered keyframes; the resulting signals populate a positive channel M+ that stores success rationales as soft Reference Examples, and a negative channel M- that stores validated failure patterns as hard Known Pitfalls. On a fixed-probe evaluation against no-memory, matched-budget retrieval-augmented generation, and shuffled-memory baselines, blind human Pass@1 rises and reflection rounds fall as memory size grows. We will release the code, frozen memory snapshots, and the task stream.

AI.tldr: ManimAgent is a self-evolving multimodal agent that uses a dual-channel Episodic Memory Bank (positive M+ and negative M-) to carry reflection experience across code-generation tasks, improving Pass@1 and reducing reflection rounds without weight updates or human seeds.
AI.motivation: Current multi-round reflection for LLM-based agents is per-task isolated; lessons learned on one task are discarded before the next begins, creating a gap in cross-task learning from reflection experiences.
AI.method: ManimAgent: a self-evolving multimodal agent with a dual-channel Episodic Memory Bank (M+ for success rationales as soft Reference Examples, M- for validated failure patterns as hard Known Pitfalls), grown entirely from its own task stream via vision-language model scoring of rendered keyframes, with no weight updates or human seeds.
AI.result: On fixed-probe evaluation against no-memory, matched-budget RAG, and shuffled-memory baselines: blind human Pass@1 rises and reflection rounds fall as memory size grows.
AI.conclusion: Cross-task reflection memory improves code generation performance and efficiency; the dual-channel episodic memory design is effective without weight updates or human intervention.

title: BayesEvolve: Explicit Belief States for Autonomous Scientific Discovery
summary: Autonomous scientific discovery systems increasingly use large language models (LLMs) to propose new hypotheses, but many such systems condition primarily on experimental memory: archives of high-scoring candidates or heuristic summaries of recent trials. We argue that discovery agents should instead maintain explicit, uncertainty-aware beliefs about hypothesis quality. We introduce BayesEvolve, a belief-guided discovery framework that converts experimental evidence into a predictive belief state and uses this belief to guide future experimentation. As a controlled testbed for belief-guided discovery, we evaluate BayesEvolve on shifted BBOB-style black-box optimization tasks, leaving program and laboratory discovery domains to future work. BayesEvolve improves sample efficiency over memory- and archive-guided LLM baselines under a fixed evaluation budget. We further show that the belief state is predictive on held-out candidate pools, that controlled decision-rule ablations favor belief-guided selection with an annealed uncertainty bonus, and that BayesEvolve exhibits productive late-stage concentration rather than unfocused exploration.

AI.tldr: BayesEvolve is a belief-guided scientific discovery framework that uses uncertainty-aware predictive beliefs from experimental evidence—rather than simple memory or archives—to guide hypothesis generation with LLMs, improving sample efficiency on shifted black-box optimization tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based discovery systems condition primarily on experimental memory (e.g., high-scoring candidates or heuristic summaries) rather than maintaining explicit, uncertainty-aware beliefs about hypothesis quality, limiting sample efficiency and exploration-exploitation balance.
AI.method: BayesEvolve converts experimental evidence into a predictive belief state (uncertainty-aware distribution over hypothesis quality) and uses this belief to guide LLM-based hypothesis generation and selection, evaluated on shifted BBOB-style black-box optimization tasks.
AI.result: BayesEvolve improves sample efficiency over memory- and archive-guided LLM baselines under a fixed evaluation budget; the belief state is predictive on held-out candidate pools; belief-guided selection with an annealed uncertainty bonus is favored; and the method exhibits productive late-stage concentration rather than unfocused exploration.
AI.conclusion: Belief-guided discovery with explicit uncertainty modeling (BayesEvolve) outperforms memory-only approaches in sample efficiency and exploration quality, suggesting that maintaining predictive beliefs is a promising direction for autonomous scientific discovery.

title: Sequential Fairness Auditing with Limited Output Access
summary: External evaluations are becoming increasingly central to the governance of AI systems. In practice, however, independent auditors often have limited access to deployed models and must rely on query-based interactions. Most existing fairness evaluation methods assume static datasets and fixed-sample statistical tests, making them poorly suited to real-world auditing scenarios in which evidence must be collected sequentially under query constraints. In this work, we formulate fairness auditing as a tolerance-aware sequential hypothesis-testing problem under limited model output access. We develop a sequential generalized likelihood-ratio framework that allows auditors to accumulate evidence from a finite audit pool and stop once sufficient support for compliance or violation has been obtained. The framework is instantiated for decision-based Statistical Parity and Equal Opportunity audits, and extended to score- and logit-based proxy audits when richer observables are available. Our results show that both the fairness metric and the level of model access significantly affect audit efficiency, and that the benefits of richer output information are not uniform across auditing settings. In particular, richer outputs can substantially reduce the number of queries required for some fairness metrics and operating regimes, while offering limited gains in near-threshold cases. This work provides a practical statistical framework for sequential fairness auditing under realistic deployment constraints.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a sequential generalized likelihood-ratio framework for fairness auditing under query constraints, enabling auditors to accumulate evidence from a finite pool and stop when sufficient support for compliance or violation is obtained. The framework is instantiated for Statistical Parity and Equal Opportunity audits, extended to score/logit-based proxy audits, and shows that fairness metrics and model access levels significantly affect audit efficiency.
AI.motivation: Independent auditors often have limited query-based access to deployed AI models, yet most existing fairness evaluation methods assume static datasets and fixed-sample statistical tests, making them poorly suited to real-world auditing under sequential query constraints.
AI.method: Formulates fairness auditing as a tolerance-aware sequential hypothesis-testing problem; develops a sequential generalized likelihood-ratio framework for accumulating evidence from a finite audit pool with early stopping upon sufficient support for compliance or violation.
AI.result: Fairness metric and level of model access significantly affect audit efficiency; richer outputs substantially reduce queries for some fairness metrics and regimes but offer limited gains in near-threshold cases.
AI.conclusion: Provides a practical statistical framework for sequential fairness auditing under realistic deployment constraints with limited model access.

title: Using Large Language Models as Low-Cost Statistical Estimators for Human-Response Data
summary: Quantitative research across the social and behavioral sciences depends on human subject experiments that are expensive, slow, and subject to sampling bias. Here we show that pretrained large language models induce risk-equivalent estimators of conditional expectations under squared loss, establishing restricted functional risk equivalence: under squared loss, the LLM induces an estimator whose risk matches the Bayes optimal risk for squared-loss prediction of conditional expectations for any inference that depends on the data only through the conditional mean. We formalize the LLM as a misspecified functional estimator $T(\hat{P}_n)$ trained on i.i.d.\ data, decompose the estimation error into representation bias $ε_{\mathrm{rep}}$ and optimization error, and prove that under mild regularity conditions the LLM's expected error converges to the irreducible population variance plus the squared representation bias, with the representation bias bounded by the Pinsker inequality. The identifiability error $δ$ propagates into the effective bias, inflating the asymptotic risk floor. We establish restricted functional risk equivalence via a bidirectional Le Cam deficiency analysis: the forward deficiency vanishes asymptotically while the reverse deficiency is exactly zero. We provide finite-sample concentration bounds and a calibration protocol with explicit decision rules. The result is a precise, provable statement: a well-calibrated LLM achieves the Bayes-optimal risk for conditional-mean-dependent inference, bounded by explicit scope conditions. In practical applications, this means that under satisfied conditions and well-calibrated models, large language models can be used in many prediction and decision-making tasks that originally relied on human experiments, approximating near-optimal statistical inference at lower cost.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that well-calibrated pretrained large language models can achieve Bayes-optimal risk equivalence for conditional expectation estimation under squared loss, enabling them to replace expensive human subject experiments in quantitative research when inference depends only on conditional means.
AI.motivation: Human subject experiments in social and behavioral sciences are expensive, slow, and suffer from sampling bias. The authors aim to establish whether pretrained LLMs can serve as statistically rigorous substitutes for such experiments.
AI.method: The authors formalize the LLM as a misspecified functional estimator trained on i.i.d. data, decompose estimation error into representation bias and optimization error, use Pinsker inequality to bound representation bias, and establish restricted functional risk equivalence via bidirectional Le Cam deficiency analysis with finite-sample concentration bounds and a calibration protocol.
AI.result: A well-calibrated LLM induces an estimator whose risk matches the Bayes-optimal risk for squared-loss prediction of conditional expectations, with asymptotic risk floor determined by irreducible population variance plus squared representation bias. Forward Le Cam deficiency vanishes asymptotically; reverse deficiency is exactly zero.
AI.conclusion: Under explicit scope conditions and proper calibration, LLMs can replace human experiments for conditional-mean-dependent inference tasks, achieving near-optimal statistical inference at significantly lower cost.

title: Whose Side Is Your Agent On? Multi-Party Principal Loyalty in LLM Agents
summary: A rapidly growing class of LLM agents is multi-party: the agent acts for a principal (who briefs it, sends follow-ups, and receives results) while also conversing in a separate channel with a counterparty whose interests may diverge (negotiating with a vendor, screening inbound requests, or mediating between employees). Here "help whoever you are talking to" is the wrong objective. The agent must stay loyal to the principal it represents without over-refusing the principal's own cooperative asks. We study this multi-party loyalty problem and contribute a measurement instrument, two mechanisms, and a structural lesson. PrincipalBench is a 75-item multi-turn benchmark with leak probes, dual judges, and an integrity-audit gate. Across 13 frontier subjects it exposes a sharp split (<=20% vs. 53.6-75.3% harm) invisible to single-turn safety evaluations: a selective cluster that declines adversarial probes while still following the principal's legitimate requests, and an over-refusing cluster that refuses broadly. (M1) A prompt-time loyalty scaffold (a fixed system prompt of seven prioritized rules, open-coded from 50+ failure trajectories) holds Claude-Sonnet to 19.4% harm and all nine selective subjects to <=20%. (M2) A per-token-KL distillation recipe transfers a prompted Qwen3-32B teacher into 8B Qwen3 and Llama-3.1 students, the strongest open-weight recipe we measure. (Lesson) Both mechanisms only move along a common leak/over-refusal trade-off rather than crossing it: improving one axis costs the other, and the jointly favorable outcome stays out of reach.

AI.tldr: This paper studies the multi-party loyalty problem in LLM agents—where an agent must serve a principal while interacting with a counterparty with potentially divergent interests. It contributes PrincipalBench (a 75-item multi-turn benchmark), two mitigation mechanisms (a prompt-time loyalty scaffold and a distillation recipe), and reveals a fundamental leak/over-refusal trade-off that cannot be jointly optimized.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM agents increasingly operate in multi-party settings (e.g., negotiating with vendors, screening requests, mediating), but the default "help whoever you are talking to" objective is inappropriate. The agent must remain loyal to its principal without over-refusing the principal's own cooperative requests. This problem is underexplored and not captured by standard single-turn safety evaluations.
AI.method: The authors build PrincipalBench, a 75-item multi-turn benchmark with leak probes, dual judges, and an integrity-audit gate. They evaluate 13 frontier LLMs, revealing a split between selective (declines adversarial probes, follows principal requests) and over-refusing clusters. They propose two mechanisms: (M1) a prompt-time loyalty scaffold with seven prioritized rules open-coded from 50+ failure trajectories, and (M2) a per-token-KL distillation recipe transferring a prompted Qwen3-32B teacher into 8B student models.
AI.result: The benchmark exposes a sharp split: some models show ≤20% harm while others show 53.6-75.3% harm—a distinction invisible to single-turn safety evaluations. M1 holds Claude-Sonnet to 19.4% harm and all nine selective subjects to ≤20%. M2 produces the strongest open-weight recipe measured. However, both mechanisms only move along a common leak/over-refusal trade-off: improving one axis costs the other, and the jointly favorable outcome remains out of reach.
AI.conclusion: The multi-party loyalty problem is structurally constrained by a fundamental trade-off between leaking information to counterparties and over-refusing the principal's requests. Neither prompt-time scaffolding nor distillation can break this trade-off, suggesting that more fundamental architectural or training paradigm changes may be needed to achieve jointly favorable outcomes.

title: ENC-ODE: Event-level Neurodegenerative Modeling in Continuous Time with Neural ODEs
summary: Accurately predicting the temporal evolution of clinical biomarkers is crucial for the early diagnosis and management of neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's disease. However, this relies on longitudinal data to capture biomarker changes over time, which is often sparse and irregular due to the high cost, labor-intensive nature, and patient burden. To address these challenges, we propose ENC-ODE, an Event-level Neurodegenerative modeling in Continuous time with neural Ordinary Differential Equations. ENC-ODE predicts future biomarker evolution by modeling clinical events through diagnosis-conditioned continuous dynamics. A target-conditioned attention mechanism weights and aggregates event-level predictions for the target time and modality without history compression. Extensive experiments on Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) dataset demonstrate that ENC-ODE outperforms representative sequence models while offering a scalable and neuroscientifically grounded solution for clinical support. The code is available at https://github.com/JardinDelSol/enc-ode.

AI.tldr: ENC-ODE uses neural ordinary differential equations with diagnosis-conditioned continuous dynamics and target-conditioned attention to predict future biomarker evolution from sparse, irregular longitudinal clinical data, outperforming sequence models on the ADNI dataset.
AI.motivation: Predicting temporal evolution of clinical biomarkers is crucial for early diagnosis and management of neurodegenerative diseases like Alzheimer's, but longitudinal data is sparse and irregular due to high cost, labor-intensive nature, and patient burden.
AI.method: Proposes ENC-ODE (Event-level Neurodegenerative modeling in Continuous time with neural ODEs). It models clinical events through diagnosis-conditioned continuous dynamics and uses a target-conditioned attention mechanism to weight and aggregate event-level predictions for the target time and modality without history compression.
AI.result: On the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) dataset, ENC-ODE outperforms representative sequence models.
AI.conclusion: ENC-ODE offers a scalable and neuroscientifically grounded solution for clinical support in neurodegenerative disease biomarker prediction.

title: The FIL Hypothesis: Inductive Biases Help with Kernel Engineering
summary: The Bitter Lesson, which posits that general-purpose methods that scale with computation and data ultimately outperform those with built-in human knowledge, has become a dominant paradigm in the era of Large Language Models. We revisit this principle by observing a new and critical scaling dimension: the duration of the Feedback Information Loop (FIL), the time required for a system to receive a verification signal after generating a prediction. Most historic successes in Artificial Intelligence (AI) have benefited from near instantaneous feedback (e.g., games or classification tasks), but we argue that future AI applications in science and the physical world will inherently involve FILs ranging from hours to weeks. This trend poses a fundamental scaling limit, as obtaining enough verification steps required by purely data-driven methods becomes practically impossible. Additionally, we propose a method that is orthogonal to purely data-driven approaches, based on human-inspired expert knowledge. The method relies on inductive biases and constraining the solution space. We provide an initial validation of the hypothesis and the method, by studying the real-world GPU programming task, a domain with non-trivial FIL, and demonstrate that incorporating inductive biases yields superior performance over data-driven approaches. The code is released under: https://github.com/ai-nikolai/robust_kernelbench

AI.tldr: The paper challenges "The Bitter Lesson" by identifying Feedback Information Loop (FIL) duration as a critical scaling dimension, arguing that future AI applications (especially in science and physical world) will have long FILs (hours to weeks) that limit purely data-driven methods. The authors propose incorporating human-inspired expert knowledge through inductive biases and solution space constraints as an orthogonal approach, demonstrating its superiority on GPU programming tasks with non-trivial FIL.
AI.motivation: The authors observe that while AI successes have benefited from near-instantaneous feedback loops (games, classification), future AI applications in science and the physical world inherently involve long feedback cycles (hours to weeks). This creates a fundamental scaling limit where purely data-driven methods cannot obtain sufficient verification steps, motivating the need for alternative approaches.
AI.method: The proposed method is orthogonal to purely data-driven approaches and draws from human-inspired expert knowledge. It relies on (1) inductive biases and (2) constraining the solution space. The method is validated on real-world GPU programming tasks, which naturally involve non-trivial Feedback Information Loop durations.
AI.result: Incorporating inductive biases yields superior performance over purely data-driven approaches on GPU programming tasks with non-trivial FIL durations. The code is publicly released at the provided GitHub repository.
AI.conclusion: The Bitter Lesson's assumption of near-instantaneous feedback may not hold for future AI applications. Long FIL durations pose fundamental scaling limits for data-driven methods. Integrating human-inspired expert knowledge through inductive biases and solution space constraints offers a promising orthogonal direction for AI in domains with extended feedback cycles.

title: Entity Binding Failures in Tool-Augmented Agents
summary: Tool-augmented language-model agents are often evaluated by whether they select the correct tool, produce valid API arguments, and complete the requested task. However, an agent may choose the right tool and still act on the wrong external entity. For example, a request to "email Alex about the launch" may lead the agent to contact the wrong Alex, attach the wrong launch document, reply in the wrong thread, or update the wrong customer account. We call these errors entity binding failures. This paper studies entity binding failures as a distinct reliability and safety problem in tool-augmented agents. We formalize the separation between tool correctness and entity correctness, introduce a taxonomy of wrong-entity failures in enterprise workflows, and evaluate entity-aware execution mechanisms including entity-resolution preconditions, confidence-gated binding, clarification under ambiguity, and provenance tracking. In a controlled diagnostic evaluation across 60 tasks, five model backends, and six tool-use methods, all methods achieved 0.0 percent wrong-tool error, yet action-oriented baselines still produced wrong-entity actions in 24.0-26.0 percent of runs. Entity-aware methods eliminated wrong-entity actions and risk-weighted wrong-entity exposure in this setting, but reduced direct task completion by deferring under ambiguity. These findings show that safe tool use requires not only selecting the correct tool, but also reliably binding natural-language references to the correct real-world entity before action.

AI.tldr: Tool-augmented language-model agents can select the correct tool but still act on the wrong real-world entity (e.g., wrong person, document, account), which the authors term "entity binding failures." They formalize this problem, propose a taxonomy, and evaluate entity-aware mechanisms that eliminate wrong-entity errors but may reduce task completion due to ambiguity deferral.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of tool-augmented agents focus on tool correctness and API validity but overlook a critical failure mode: acting on the wrong real-world entity despite using the correct tool. This gap poses reliability and safety risks in enterprise workflows, motivating a formal study of entity binding failures.
AI.method: The authors formalize the separation between tool correctness and entity correctness, introduce a taxonomy of wrong-entity failures in enterprise workflows, and evaluate entity-aware execution mechanisms (entity-resolution preconditions, confidence-gated binding, clarification under ambiguity, provenance tracking) across 60 tasks, five model backends, and six tool-use methods.
AI.result: All methods achieved 0.0% wrong-tool error. Action-oriented baselines produced wrong-entity actions in 24.0–26.0% of runs. Entity-aware methods eliminated wrong-entity actions and risk-weighted wrong-entity exposure, but reduced direct task completion by deferring under ambiguity.
AI.conclusion: Safe tool use requires not only selecting the correct tool but also reliably binding natural-language references to the correct real-world entity before action. Entity-aware mechanisms prevent wrong-entity errors at the cost of conservative deferral under ambiguity.

title: Latent Actions from Factorized Transition Effects under Agent Ambiguity
comment: Accepted to ICML 2026 Workshop on Compositional Learning. Project Page: https://hazel-heejeong-nam.github.io/LAM/
summary: Latent Action Models (LAMs) learn action-like proxies from observation transitions. However, in multi-object or distractor-rich scenes, these visual effects mix agent motion with distractors, camera dynamics, and background changes, making the underlying action source ambiguous without supervision. Structuring this mixture as reusable transition effects provides an intermediate representation from which action-like latents can be more robustly formed. We introduce Observed Transition Factorization (OTF), which decomposes each transition into a sparse set of observed transition primitives. Using these primitives as the transition interface, we propose OTF-LAM, which abstracts motion primitives into action-like latents within the standard inverse-forward dynamics framework, and OTF-LAM-Dino, a decoder-free variant that predicts future states in a frozen DINOv2 representation space. Empirically, OTF primitives transfer zeroshot across controlled carrier and morphology shifts, showing reusability. Furthermore, downstream policy learning results match or outperform baselines under complex transition ambiguity.

AI.tldr: OTF decomposes visual transitions into reusable sparse primitives to form robust action-like latents, improving downstream policy learning under transition ambiguity.
AI.motivation: Latent Action Models struggle in multi-object or distractor-rich scenes because observed transitions mix agent motion with distractors, camera dynamics, and background changes, making action inference ambiguous without supervision.
AI.method: OTF decomposes each observation transition into a sparse set of observed transition primitives. OTF-LAM abstracts these primitives into action-like latents via inverse-forward dynamics; OTF-LAM-Dino predicts future states in a frozen DINOv2 representation space without a decoder.
AI.result: OTF primitives transfer zeroshot across controlled carrier and morphology shifts, and downstream policy learning matches or outperforms baselines under complex transition ambiguity.
AI.conclusion: Structuring visual mixtures as reusable transition primitives enables more robust action-like latent formation and improves policy learning in ambiguous, distractor-rich environments.

title: Linguistic Firewall: Geometry as Defense in Multi-Agent Systems Routing
comment: 8 pages (9 more for appendix), 3 figures. Published at the Second Workshop on Agents in the Wild: Safety, Security, and Beyond (AIWILD) at ICML 2026
summary: The rapid integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) has driven the evolution of Multi-Agent Systems (MAS), where specialized agents collaborate to execute complex workflows. Effective orchestration in these environments requires robust routing mechanisms to efficiently allocate tasks to the most suitable agent. However, existing routers fundamentally rely on unverified proxies, ranging from textual self-descriptions to static surrogate representations, to gauge an agent's competence. This reliance on non-empirical data creates a critical gap between an agent's projected profile and its actual operational capabilities, introducing severe security vulnerabilities. Malicious agents can easily misrepresent their proficiencies or harbor covert backdoors that evade both standard external analysis and static representation-learning techniques. In this work, we introduce ANTAP (Automatic Non-Textual Agent Picker), an evaluation-driven routing architecture that discards indirect proxies in favor of active capability testing. By dynamically querying agents to ascertain their true competencies empirically, ANTAP distills performance into fixed behavioral operators within a shared semantic space. At inference time, routing is performed via a purely non-textual algebraic projection, establishing a "linguistic firewall" that renders metadata-based attacks inexpressible. In our experiments, ANTAP achieves near-zero ASR against description-based injection attacks, compared to 67.3\% and above for the description-based router baseline. Against adaptive embedding attacks, ANTAP achieves substantially lower ASR than the embedding-based baseline, with a 20\% reduction, while remaining resilient to description manipulation by design.

AI.tldr: ANTAP replaces unverified proxy-based agent routing (textual descriptions, embeddings) with active empirical capability testing, using non-textual behavioral operators to achieve near-zero attack success rates against routing attacks in multi-agent systems.
AI.motivation: Existing routers rely on unverified proxies (self-descriptions, static representations) to assess agent competence, creating a gap between projected and actual capabilities, which introduces security vulnerabilities like misrepresentation and backdoor attacks.
AI.method: ANTAP performs evaluation-driven routing: it dynamically queries agents to empirically ascertain true competencies, distills performance into fixed behavioral operators in a shared semantic space, and routes via non-textual algebraic projection, forming a "linguistic firewall."
AI.result: ANTAP achieves near-zero ASR against description-based injection attacks (vs. 67.3%+ for baseline). Against adaptive embedding attacks, it achieves a 20% reduction in ASR compared to embedding-based baseline and remains resilient to description manipulation.
AI.conclusion: ANTAP demonstrates that evaluation-driven, non-textual routing is an effective defense against metadata-based attacks in multi-agent systems, eliminating the attack surface introduced by proxy-based routing.

title: The Human Creativity Benchmark
summary: Modern AI evaluation frameworks treat evaluator disagreement as noise to be resolved. In creative domains, professional disagreement reflects genuine differences in taste, not measurement error. We argue that evaluating creative AI requires preserving two distinct signals: convergence, where professionals align around shared best practices, and divergence, where individual taste legitimately varies. We present the Human Creativity Benchmark (HCB), a benchmark that operationalizes this separation by collecting pairwise preferences, scalar ratings on prompt adherence, usability, and visual appeal, and qualitative rationale from domain professionals. Across 15,000 professional judgments spanning five creative domains and three workflow phases (ideation, mockup, refinement), we find that convergence concentrates on verifiable dimensions like technical correctness and visual hierarchy, while divergence concentrates on taste-driven dimensions like aesthetic direction and conceptual risk. No model excels uniformly across all phases. Collapsing these signals into a single quality metric discards the most actionable information: where models must be correct versus where they should remain steerable.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes the Human Creativity Benchmark (HCB) which treats professional disagreement in creative AI evaluation as meaningful signal rather than noise, separating convergence (shared standards) from divergence (legitimate taste variations) across 15,000 judgments in five creative domains and three workflow phases.
AI.motivation: Current AI evaluation frameworks treat evaluator disagreement as noise to be resolved, but in creative domains, professional disagreement reflects genuine differences in taste rather than measurement error. The authors argue that evaluating creative AI requires preserving both convergence and divergence signals.
AI.method: The Human Creativity Benchmark (HCB) collects pairwise preferences, scalar ratings on prompt adherence, usability, and visual appeal, and qualitative rationale from domain professionals across 15,000 judgments spanning five creative domains and three workflow phases (ideation, mockup, refinement).
AI.result: Convergence concentrates on verifiable dimensions (technical correctness, visual hierarchy), while divergence concentrates on taste-driven dimensions (aesthetic direction, conceptual risk). No model excels uniformly across all phases. Collapsing signals into a single quality metric discards actionable information about where models must be correct versus where they should remain steerable.
AI.conclusion: Preserving the distinction between convergence and divergence in evaluation is critical for creative AI — identifying where models must be correct versus where they should remain steerable, rather than collapsing these signals into a single metric.

title: DOPD: Dual On-policy Distillation
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) offers superior capacity transfer by supervising student-sampled trajectories with dense token-level signals. To furnish high-quality supervision sources and thereby elevate the performance frontier of distillation, an intuitive direction is to infuse privileged information to either teacher or student itself. However, this additional input induces a potential failure mode we dub privilege illusion: a pattern that conflates the transferable capability gap that students are meant to close, and the information asymmetry gap that can only be mimicked but never replicated. This issue is further amplified by the inherent non-uniformity of token-level supervision, where only a small subset of tokens carries pivotal capability-bearing signals. To this end, we propose DOPD, an advantage-aware dual distillation paradigm that dynamically routes token-level supervision between privileged teacher and privileged student policies based on their advantage gap and relative probabilities. Each token receives supervision of different strength, objective, and strategy from either teacher or student itself, which transfers credible capability while simultaneously receiving auxiliary signals, to alleviate privilege illusion. Extensive experiments on both large language model (LLM) and vision-language model (VLM) settings demonstrate that DOPD consistently outperforms Vanilla OPD and other counterparts. Further results on stability, robustness, continual learning, and out-of-distribution tasks validate its superiority.

AI.tldr: DOPD is an advantage-aware dual distillation paradigm that addresses privilege illusion in on-policy distillation by dynamically routing token-level supervision between privileged teacher and student policies based on their advantage gap and relative probabilities.
AI.motivation: On-policy distillation (OPD) suffers from privilege illusion, where the transferable capability gap is conflated with the information asymmetry gap that can only be mimicked but never replicated. This is further amplified by the non-uniformity of token-level supervision, where only a small subset of tokens carries pivotal capability-bearing signals.
AI.method: DOPD introduces an advantage-aware dual distillation paradigm that dynamically routes token-level supervision between privileged teacher and privileged student policies based on their advantage gap and relative probabilities. Each token receives supervision of different strength, objective, and strategy from either teacher or student itself, transferring credible capability while receiving auxiliary signals to alleviate privilege illusion.
AI.result: DOPD consistently outperforms Vanilla OPD and other counterparts on both LLM and VLM settings. Further results on stability, robustness, continual learning, and out-of-distribution tasks validate its superiority.
AI.conclusion: The proposed DOPD effectively mitigates privilege illusion in on-policy distillation by dynamically routing token-level supervision, achieving superior performance across diverse model settings and tasks.

title: Self-Evolving World Models for LLM Agent Planning
summary: World models offer a principled way to equip long-horizon LLM agents with foresight: predictions of action consequences before execution. However, unreliable foresight can be ignored, misused, or even degrade downstream decision-making. In this paper, we introduce WorldEvolver, a self-evolving world model framework that revises its deployment-time context while keeping the downstream agent and all model parameters frozen. WorldEvolver integrates three modules: (i) Episodic Memory, which exploits real action transitions through retrieval-based simulation; (ii) Semantic Memory, which extracts persistent heuristic rules from prediction-observation mismatches; and (iii) Selective Foresight, which filters low-confidence predictions before integrating them into agent reasoning context. We evaluate WorldEvolver on ALFWorld and ScienceWorld, measuring world model prediction accuracy on Word2World and downstream agent success rate on AgentBoard. Extensive experiments show that WorldEvolver achieves the highest prediction accuracy across three backbones and leads other world model baselines on downstream agent success rate, demonstrating that test-time memory revision enhances both predictive fidelity and planning performance.

AI.tldr: WorldEvolver is a self-evolving world model framework that improves long-horizon LLM agent planning by revising deployment-time context through episodic memory, semantic memory, and selective foresight, achieving state-of-the-art prediction accuracy and downstream success rates on ALFWorld and ScienceWorld.
AI.motivation: World models provide LLM agents with action foresight but unreliable predictions can degrade decision-making; the paper aims to improve world model reliability at test time without modifying the downstream agent or model parameters.
AI.method: WorldEvolver integrates three modules: (i) Episodic Memory for retrieval-based simulation using real action transitions; (ii) Semantic Memory to extract heuristic rules from prediction-observation mismatches; and (iii) Selective Foresight to filter low-confidence predictions before integrating into agent reasoning. The framework revises deployment-time context while keeping all parameters frozen.
AI.result: Evaluated on ALFWorld and ScienceWorld; WorldEvolver achieves the highest prediction accuracy across three backbones on Word2World and leads other world model baselines on downstream agent success rate on AgentBoard.
AI.conclusion: Test-time memory revision enhances both predictive fidelity and planning performance, demonstrating that self-evolving context at deployment improves world model reliability for long-horizon LLM agents.
